There is a growing interest in Federated Learning (FL) for developing private AI solutions without compromising data confidentiality. Despite existing privacy-preserving techniques, such as differential privacy and homomorphic encryption, current FL approaches continue to expose client data to vulnerabilities. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel framework, called DeepAdmire, which adapts a complex optical phenomenon to protect client data from unintended revelation. DeepAdmire employs an artificial source, a 3D fractal surface, and an optical system to attribute an irregular light pattern to the client's data, using a map of admittances. This approach ensures that, even with advanced optical analysis, it is impossible to retrieve the original data, as the affected light pattern can be attributed to various data types. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method with a fully functional DeepAdmire system for neural network training, using a simple example. This pioneering work lays the foundation for exploring the use of optical phenomena for enhancing FL security. DeepAdmire's innovative technique provides a groundbreaking solution for privacy preservation in FL, offering a unique and compelling approach that surpasses traditional methods. In addition to its technical contributions, our work invites the AI community to explore the intersection of optical physics and deep learning. In the future, this framework can be developed into an actual optical system for physical implementation. Furthermore, the core component of the DeepAdmire system can be utilized in other FL and AI applications to provide unparalleled privacy and security. We have made the DeepAdmire codebase publicly available on our website. Additionally, a video showcasing the project's key aspects can be found on YouTube. Timeloops is a lightweight, set-timeable Linux appliance that blocks 
unauthorized system calls and prevents malicious data from being written 
to the file system. It works by replacing the system's libc with a trusted 
version that verifies system calls and enforces policies before allowing them 
to proceed. Since Timeloops operates at the libc level, it supports system 
calls that rely on functionality from other libraries that are not tampered 
with. We tested Timeloops on a Linux device and verified its effectiveness 
by trying to bypass its security features, finding along the way that it 
blocks system calls that write to the file system without proper authorization. 
As a result, Timeloops prevents security breaches that exploit vulnerabilities 
in poorly written server-side application code written in languages like PHP 
and Python, demonstrating its capacity to protect system configuration and 
prevent malicious data from being written to the file system.

protector, offering a unique and effective defense against security breaches 
harmful to system configuration and file system integrity. Timeloops' potential

a promising tool for providing online security services and protecting system

Our research focuses on classifying single-cell RNA-seq data based on the expression levels of specific cell types. Unlike traditional Euclidean space settings, we find that this classification in low-dimensional space formed by cell-to-cell differences yields substantial performance gains, averaging 20-40% improvement over Euclidean space, across various datasets and models. This advantage holds not only for capturing cell type differences but also for reflecting overall variation within the data. Furthermore, our approach has the advantage of reduced computational complexity and ease of interpretation. We introduce the term "mixture space" to describe this classification space and propose the term "mixture coordinates" to refer to the dimensional representations of cells within this space. By translating the expression into a common language, our model can identify mixtures unique to each cell type and distinguish them from noise. We also show that this space effectively detects anomalies and detects subtle shifts in expression patterns. Our results indicate that modeling scRNA-seq data as a low-dimensional mixture space offers superior performance over Euclidean space, presenting a new and effective method for classifying and understanding complex cellular data. This work investigates the theoretical foundation of stochastic Model Predictive Control (SMPC) from a dynamic system with uncertain dynamics. By assuming that the true system state falls within a defined boundary, we establish both a conservative and precise estimate for the boundary of the state space at any given time. These boundaries are calculated using the solution to a set of linear differential equations, which are derived from the Fokker-Planck equation associated with the system. Consequently, these boundaries can be utilized to develop an optimal stochastic feedback law that minimizes costs while accounting for both the system's uncertainty and the risk aversion level. Notably, the resulting SMPC approach is versatile and can be applied to various types of dynamic systems, including those with uncertain parameters, noises, and initial conditions. Furthermore, our method can be used to investigate the system's asymptotic behavior over long time periods. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach through several numerical examples in the areas of chemical reaction engineering and risk-averse trajectory planning. Importantly, our analysis reveals that the optimal stochastic feedback law can be implemented in real-time, even for complex systems with a large number of state variables. Additionally, our method has various potential applications across multiple fields. From a fundamental perspective, our work contributes to the advancement of stochastic Model Predictive Control techniques. From an applied perspective, our approach can be used in various engineering applications. From a theoretical perspective, our analysis provides a valuable starting point for investigating the system's long-term behavior using stochastic dynamical systems. Our classification is tied to the existing categorization of representation categories of one-dimensional semisimple highest-weight modules in vertex operator algebras. This result means that the local subalgebras associated with compact regions in a one-dimensional system, governed by a vertex operator algebra, can be identified on a per generator basis, whereas broader von Neumann algebras associated with infinite intervals or bounded intervals containing a Markov boundary cannot be expressed in such a finite basis. Moreover, we address certain structural aspects of these von Neumann algebras, revealing that the strict continuity of states on these algebras is linked to the presence of sectors with positive central charge, and that the Markov property that pertains to these algegeories is not solely defined by the absence of a certain boundary condition. By solving these two issues, we are able to demonstrate that the Markov property is equivalent to the condition that the conditional expectation associated with a particular sector in the algebraic conformal field theory is faithful. Finally, our work includes the construction of a von Neumann algebra associated with an infinite interval that contains a Markov boundary, specific to the algebra generated by the algebra associated with the unique irreducible highest-weight module $V_{4,3}$. This construction enables the identification of KMS states on von Neumann algebras that are local to compact regions in systems that are one-dimensional and super-symmetric, particularly at non-zero temperatures. This result means the fermion's number is unbounded, a fact that contradicts the conditions of the bootstrap for phase transitions in one-dimensional systems that is related to the concept of finiteness. To explore the capabilities of scanning transmission electron microscopes in producing tiny electron probes, we've investigated the design of electrostatic phase plates using a combination of theoretical and computational methods. By simulating different designs of these plates, we've determined how their shape, size, and the spacing and arrangement of their pixels impact the size and intensity of the electron probe when it exits the microscope. These findings will be useful in developing new techniques for producing extremely small electron probes, and in understanding how to achieve high currents with these probes,, which could greatly improve the speed and quality of data that can be collected with the microscope. Specifically, we've found that certain patterns of pixels can produce improved results, and that there is an optimal balance between probe intensity and size. We've also confirmed previous research on this topic, and have discovered some new limitations and potential improvements. Further analysis is planned to confirm these findings, and to explore other design options for the phase plates. Ultimately, we hope to use the results of this research to develop a practical design for the electrostatic probe, and to demonstrate its effectiveness with experiments. Additionally, the software used to simulate the probe design will be made available for other researchers to use. Specifically, the design code will be open to the public on the GitHub platform. Currently, the simulation code is only capable of modeling the probe design, but in the future, it could be expanded to also simulate the behavior of the electron probe as it interacts with the sample being imaged. Finally, we would like to note that the research presented here is primarily theoretical in nature, and that further experimental verification is needed to confirm the results. Specifically, tests are planned to verify the design of the probe, and to compare its performance with the simulations. These experiments will involve using a test pattern to measure the size and intensity of the electron probe, and to compare its performance with the simulations. Once confirmed, the results of this research will be shared with the community through presentations and publications. Specifically, plans are in place to present the research at a conference called the Microscopy and Microanalysis conference, and to submit a related paper for publication in a journal called the Journal of Microscopy. Additionally, plans are in place to present an overview of the research and its results at a conference called the SPIE Optics and Optoelectronics conference, and to share the research and its results with researchers through a conference called the Quantum Matter and Related Topics conference. Finally, plans are in place to present the results of the research and its implications to a broader audience

However, the core idea behind this redefinition, known as the Tiered Computational Framework, is challenging to apply to quantum computation due to the inherent characteristics of quantum states. In this study, we address this challenge by developing a modified quantum computation model that is consistent with the Tiered Computational Framework. Our research demonstrates that the proposed model is equivalent in performance to the standard quantum computation model. Additionally, our study explores the applicability of the proposed model to quantum measurement-based computation and quantum circuit models, showcasing the latter's superiority in terms of computational efficiency. Furthermore, our research identifies potential connections between the proposed model and quantum teleportation, quantum superposition, and entanglement. These connections highlight the inherent relationships between fundamental quantum principles and the concepts of the Tiered Computational Framework. Our research further establishes a link between quantum computation and the concept of 'information without representation,' an idea previously attributed to quantum mechanics and general relativity. The quality of text-to-speech systems can now be significantly enhanced beyond the capabilities of existing approaches, such as probabilistic and sequence-to-sequence frameworks. This improvement can be achieved by fine-tuning a pre-trained language model, specifically the RoBERTa, which is designed to handle masked or out-of-vocabulary words. The MaskedSpeech system leverages this capability along with novel strategies for word and phoneme masking. As a result, it produces more natural and engaging speech without relying on pre-built dictionaries or prior knowledge of the input text. Additionally, the system's performance is enhanced through the incorporation of auxiliary tasks, such as predicting punctuation and prosody. On a dataset of spontaneous speech, the system's phoneme error rate and mean opinion score were significantly improved, showcasing its superior capabilities. Furthermore, the MaskedSpeech system exhibits the ability to synthesize speech in a more spontaneous and dynamic manner, especially when generating longer utterances. The analysis reveals that the quality of the synthesized speech is directly correlated with the quality of the speech it is based on. Consequently, the MaskedSpeech system is most effective when used with high-quality, naturally spoken audio. Despite being a latecomer to the text-to-speech field, the MaskedSpeech system is easily implemented and can be fine-tuned using just 30 minutes of speaker-specific audio. The advantages of the MaskedSpeech system far surpass its drawbacks, making it a highly accessible and effective tool for enhancing text-to-speech systems. The system's source code and pre-trained models are available for public use at https://github.com/yjohann/maskedspeech. The dataset used for evaluation can be accessed through https://github.com/yjohann/maskedspeech-dataset. In accordance with the dataset's terms, the synthesized speech itself is not included in the repository. Nonetheless, the audio generated from the text-to-speech system can be obtained upon request by contacting the authors at [yjohann@gmail.com](mailto:yjohann@gmail.com). This type of attack, employed by a powerful third party, can compromise data security without altering the underlying data. A key distinction lies in the involvement of this third party in the communication process. In contrast to earlier research, the entire dataset isn't compromised at once, and the attack relies on intercepting and modifying communication, making it a man-in-the-middle (MIM) attack. For a MIM attack to be successful, the MIM needs to intercept communication, modify it without altering the structure, and then distribute the altered communication. This has been implemented using a modified version of the Fast Gradient Sign method and a new mechanism to prevent detection, specifically 'Add-Then-Crop' (ATC). Our research delves into the climate change conspiracy theories shared on Twitter, analyzing their origin, spread, and the role of specific social media influencers. Our methods involve collecting Twitter posts related to climate change, identifying conspiracy theories mentioned in these posts, and tracing their origin and spread. Our findings indicate that a particular social media group is primarily responsible for circulating conspiracy theories concerning climate change, including the baseless claim that the US government is manipulating temperature measurements. Our analysis also reveals that counter-conspiracy messages are often drowned out by the sheer volume of conspiracy theory-related posts, indicating their limited reach. Nonetheless, the impact of these conspiracy theories can be hazardous, as they are attempting to delegitimize climate change as a global emergency. Inspired by the research of Zeldovich in the 1970s, our analysis delves into the long-term effects of spatial inhomogeneities on the universe's structure, both in the past and future. We demonstrate that these effects persist for an exponentially long time, even when the matter density is extremely low. This finding has significant implications, suggesting that the fate of the universe is intricately linked to its initial spatial configuration. We also examine the possibility that the effects of spatial inhomogeneities could limit the accuracy of cosmological models based on average universe properties. Additionally, we discuss potential limitations and extensions of our analysis. Supplementing the main text, our investigation in depth highlights various aspects in detail. We begin by exploring the behavior of vacuum fractals and how they relate to the Hartle-Hawking wave function. We then consider the effect of scalar fields on the universe's structure, as well as the potential for string theory to influence the long-term cosmological behavior. We conclude with an analysis of the long-term effects of spatial inhomogeneities on the universe in the presence of dark energy, addressing questions and raising potential future avenues for inquiry.

We examine the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model, a widely employed approach for image segmentation task. However, this model is prone to misinterpretation in image corruption situations. To address this challenge, we propose modifying the model under a trust-control mechanism. The given image is split into two parts: a clear section and a section affected by corruption. The model minimizes boundary errors in the corrupted area while optimizing the division between these two parts. By characterizing the optimal partition, we adapt the model using a non-smooth total-variation regularizer in the clear section and the characteristic curve of an unknown non-differentiable function in the trust-control mechanism. By utilizing the properties of the Riesz distribution and the minimal representation of the Toeplitz matrix, we obtain the approximate solution through the approximation of the finite-dimensional problem. The proposed method is validated through various experiments and compared with existing methods. The results indicate that it achieves superior performance over other approaches in terms of accuracy and speed. The adaptation of the model enables successful segmentation of corrupted images, especially in medical imaging applications. The proposed method also outperforms existing techniques in both the segmentation of the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model and image denoising. The time complexity of the method has been analyzed thoroughly. For instance, when processing 128x128, 256x256, and 512x512 images, the computation time is approximately 0.02 seconds, 0.06 seconds, and 0.13 seconds, respectively. The method has been implemented utilizing MATLAB v. 2020b on a device with 32 GB RAM. To achieve optimal performance, we have levered the potential of GPU acceleration. integrating the laser beams within a single plane. This planar-integrated configuration
significantly reduces the overall trap depth when compared to the conventional ring-shaped arrangement.
Our research demonstrates that a trap depth as low as 2.5 nK can be achieved with a few mW of laser power,
while the conventional method requires a power of at least 30 mW to achieve a similar temperature.
As a result, our new setup minimizes heat generated by the trap, facilitating accurate measurements
of rare earth elements in a laser MAGNETIC trapping volume of fewer than 2 cc. 
Our innovative setup has the potential to reduce heat loads in traps operating at lower powers and to expand the range of elements that can be measured in a magnetic trapping volume. 
Additionally, we have evaluated the efficiency of radio-frequency ablation in relation to health risks and assessed the risk of fatal outcomes due to vaporization of the rare earth element ytterbium when inhaled. 
Our research found that ytterbium vapor exposure through inhalation poses no threat to human life, even at extremely high concentrations and prolonged exposure periods. 
Our analysis was based on existing data regarding the lethal effects of ytterbium exposure when inhaled, speckle damage to the eye, and ytterbium's ionization energy. 
Our evaluation of the ytterbium vapor's ionization threshold and the speckle damage to the eye at various power densities may contribute to a deeper understanding of the ytterbium vapor's properties and its potential applications in optical and medical research. 
Our research has also been applied in the detection of rare earth elements in a sample, as demonstrated by our successful identification of ytterbium in a piece of petalite. 
Our innovative detection method may be used to identify ytterbium and estimate its concentration in various solid materials by measuring the ionization threshold of the ytterbium vapor generated from the sample at elevated temperatures. 
Our research found that ytterbium's concentration in the petalite sample amounted to approximately 0.15 pg/g.

Super-resolution (SR) techniques have been effectively utilizing prior information to enhance low-resolution (LR) astronomical images. However, the majority of these techniques are based on probabilistic models and require substantial computational power. In this research, a new SR approach based on deep learning and graphics processing units (GPUs) is presented to increase the spatial resolution of LR images captured by the Dark Energy Survey (DES). The study employs a SR convolutional neural network (CNN) that incorporates an SR factor learned through a separate network, similar to previous work, but replaces the image prior with a regularizer based on total variation (TV) to maintain image smoothness. The SR-CNN is trained using simulated LR images generated from the catalog of galaxies in the DES, and the method is evaluated using a dataset of 210,699 LR images with a factor of 4 times enhancement and a dataset of 5,000 images with a factor of 8 times enhancement. The results demonstrate that the SR method can effectively recover detailed structure while reducing artifacts, and the demonstration of its effectiveness using GPz-450 shows a significant improvement over conventional upsampling techniques with a factor of 8. The SR method presents considerable advantages in terms of processing speed and memory usage compared to previous SR approaches based on probabilistic models. Moreover, the method offers the benefit of being prototype-independent, meaning it can be applied to various optical surveys without needing to adapt to changes in the telescope or imaging conditions. Deep Neural Networks have tremendous potential, yet they suffer from the limitation of extensive overfitting, particularly in data-scarce situations. Research has revealed the effectiveness of regularization techniques but these often constrain the model, limiting its performance. This study presents a data augmentation approach using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) to reduce overfitting during training and enable the reusability of existing data. A conditional supervised GAN model is trained in parallel to a regular Neural Network. The proposed algorithm is called GAN-based Regularization for Deep Neural Networks (GAN-RDNN). Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the superiority of GAN-RDNN over existing regularization techniques and data augmentation methods, achieving higher accuracy, fewer errors, and improved robustness. The concept of local and global modes has far-reaching implications for wave propagation. Graphene-based waveguides can achieve confinement through both electronic and photonic mechanisms, taking advantage of unique graphene properties such as electronic and photonic inertia, electronic excitation, and gate-tunable functionality. Local modes can be harnessed in graphene by creating line waves through photoexcitation or electronic injection. When these modes spread beyond the initial source, they become global modes, offering the potential for optical imaging and communication systems to utilize these waves. By designing graphene patches with optimal size, researchers can maximize line wave propagation and influence, and theoretical analysis indicates that the line wave amplitude increases linearly with the patch size. Notably, when the patch size reaches half of the line wave's decay length, its line wave injection efficiency approaches its maximum. Moreover, the line wave's propagation in the optical domain can be achieved by photoexciting graphene and overcoming loss mechanisms, and numerical simulations validate these findings across various numerical frameworks. These findings provide essential insights for the development of novel graphene-based optical imaging and communication systems. Finally, the concept of local and global modes can be applied to both electronic and photonic inertia mechanisms, holding broad potential for the creation of new modes in graphene and other 2D materials.

This innovative approach enables the learning algorithm to operate without requiring access to individual sensor node data, while simultaneously protecting sensitive information. We've successfully applied this framework to a complex warehouse pickup task and demonstrated its superior performance compared to traditional machine learning methods. Notably, our Federated Learning-based approach achieved a significant reduction in training time of about 90%. Furthermore, we explored the effects of variable sensor node connectivity and observed that the system can adapt to changing connectivity conditions, ultimately resulting in improved performance. In contrast, traditional learning methods show a sharp decline in performance under similar scenarios. Specifically, our experimental scenario shares similarities with the dolphin-like foraging behavior observed in shoals of fish, where individual creatures work together to gather food, demonstrating collective intelligence. We introduce a new estimator that significantly reduces bias while maintaining optimal smoothness in nonparametric regression models with a smoothness parameter tied to the dimension of the model. This innovative estimator emerges from an unbiased estimator of the residual variance. Notably, our results show that the bias of this estimator decays at a rate twice as swift as that of the classic M-estimator, and features a smoothness characteristic akin to that of classical linear regression, thereby facilitating application of techniques like functional principal component analysis. We illustrate the efficacy of this estimator in a real-world study on nitrate deposition, and use it to derive a dynamic model of phosphorus dynamics within the same ecosystem. We also propose a method to make cross-validation fully adaptive in terms of model specification, and use it to select the optimal degree of smoothing for this estimator. Finally, the gains offered by this estimator in terms of efficiency can be approximated by simply multiplying the efficiency gains of the standard M-estimator by a fixed factor. Consequently, we suggest referring to the new estimator as the 'efficient' estimator. We offer an implementation of the new estimator in the R programming language. This research focuses on knowledge graph link prediction, a crucial task that utilizes data from both relation extraction and graph construction to forecast non-existent links. While current solutions heavily rely on large, publicly available knowledge graphs like FB15k-237 and WN18RR, which are derived from Wikipedia and Wiktionary, our approach involves leveraging a constructed graph from Wikipedia that includes a greater variety of entities. Specifically, our method utilizes 1.6 million unique entities and 33 million statements, which are derived from 207 million Wikipedia pages. Using entity descriptions and graphs in conjunction, our knowledge graph-based model exhibits superior performance on the FB15k-237 dataset and comparable performance on the WN18RR dataset compared to existing methodologies. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the incorporation of entity descriptions often contributes positively to model performance. Additionally, our model is capable of generating entity-specific attributes and it is demonstrated that these attributes can enhance existing models. It is also worth noting that our constructed graph is significantly larger and more diverse than the currently available FB15k-237 training data. As such, our knowledge graph serves as a more effective training platform for the link prediction task. Ultimately, our research aims to facilitate the development of more sophisticated knowledge graph-based models and to facilitate the link prediction task. Our source code and knowledge graph can be accessed at https://github.com/AliMahdavi/FB15k-237-Wikipedia. As such, our model exhibits a moderate level of disagreement with Wikidata on the missing links in the FB15k-237 dataset. Nonetheless, our knowledge graph-based model still achieves superior performance on the Wikidata-based evaluation metric compared to the current state-of-the-art methodologies. It is also worth noting that our knowledge graph-based model is capable of generating a more diverse set of attributes for the entities compared to the attributes found in Wikidata. As such, our knowledge graph presents a more comprehensive and accurate representation of the knowledge graph compared to Wikidata. A theoretical model using the $A_4$ group is proposed to explain the heavy quark sector, where a unique $U(1)_F$ symmetry is introduced to address the mass hierarchies and correct the perturbative predictions of the top and bottom quark masses. The breaking of the $U(1)_F$ symmetry is caused by the one-loop effect of a heavy scalar field, leading to a mass ratio of approximately $1/3$, thereby resolving the discrepancy with the unitarity bound and aligning the top and bottom quark masses with their observed values. Additionally, we provide guidelines for developers on how to effectively utilize pre-trained language models in new languages with limited data. Specifically, our focus is on the "know who" aspect of language, which concerns the degree of access to knowledge held by different groups. Moreover, this research can be used to encourage and inspire other research in the broader "forbidden knowledge" paradigm, which covers a wide range of related topics. It is hoped that our work will contribute to the continued growth and exploration of this research area. We have used the CMB lensing measurement from SPT-3G to study the post-Planck cosmological parameters, incorporating measurements of the galaxy bias, CMB temperature, and acoustic scale. Our analysis accounted for potential systematic errors in the CMB data and the galaxy survey sky map. By analyzing the CMB lensing power spectrum and the galaxy bias power spectrum simultaneously, we have determined the CMB temperature, the density fluctuation amplitude, the primordial density ratio, and the galaxy bias scale to be $A_{\rm l}=1.00\pm 0.13$, $r=0.05\pm 0.04$, $n_s=0.96\pm 0.01$, and $b=1.26$ with marginalized uncertainties, assuming a flat cosmological model. We have found the constraints on the CMB temperature and the density fluctuation amplitude to be 2.5% and 4.3% smaller, respectively, due to incorporating the galaxy bias power spectrum data. Furthermore, we have determined the galaxy bias to be $b=1.26\pm 0.03$ with constraints on the galaxy bias power spectrum, with a normalization amplitude of $A_{\rm l}$, in a good agreement with the literature. We have examined the CMB lensing subpixel effect and estimated its impact to be negligible. We have further analyzed the CMB lensing effect using the joint analysis of the galaxy bias and the CMB lensing power spectrum, revealing a change in direction at $r-n_s$ plane compared to the post-Planck estimation using the CMB data only. Additionally, we have used a technique known as the CMB parameterization of the galaxy bias to determine the galaxy bias power spectrum, discovering a behavior $k$ dependence and a smooth transition at $k=0.5h/Mpc$. Ultimately, we have determined the galaxy bias to be $b=1.26\pm 0.03$ with constraints on the galaxy bias power spectrum, in a good agreement with the literature. We have established a new approach in determining the galaxy bias through the CMB lensing measurement, providing valuable insights in both the CMB lensing power spectrum and the galaxy bias power spectrum. \\

This study investigates how well various dimensionality reduction methods in hyperspectral pixel classification perform when a certain number of pixels in the training data is withheld from the algorithm. It examines the accuracy of the resulting predictions by measuring the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and considers three types of class balances in the data. It also looks at how well signal and noise components are reconstructed after reduction and proposes a new method that outperforms established ones in this area. The research reveals that techniques like PCA and linear discriminant analysis provide a good starting point for signal reconstruction, but random projection ultimately offers the best trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, a new method is developed that utilizes a proportional odds model to preserve the relative frequencies of different classes during the reduction process. It is shown that this approach not only enhances the quality of the reduction but also improves the resulting pixel classifications. The new method is compared with existing methods in terms of their computational complexity, reconstruction capabilities, and predictive powers. It is implemented in the R package RED using the PCA-like method as a default option. Further development of the method could involve applying it to the reduction of image data and exploring its potential uses in continuing education for healthcare professionals. Additionally, a utility function in the package calculates the optimal number of dimensions for a given reduction, and another function allows users to annotate the reduced data using a predefined dictionary. An example with penguins data demonstrates how to use the functions available in the package to perform reductions, calculate accuracy metrics, and predict class labels, all while controlling the class balance in the reduced data as much as possible. Moreover, a new function in version 1.2 of the package allows users to perform a single ends balanced reduction when the prior class probabilities are known in advance. To accomplish this, users can specify the prior probabilities in the form of a vector, as shown in the case of the penguins data. This kind of prior information can be utilized to produce reduced data that is closer to the desired class balance. To summarize, the package offers a versatile tool for image data analysis through classification, reconstruction, and predictive modeling, as shown in the example using penguins data. One potential application of this method is in the ongoing learning of healthcare professionals, as discussed in the accompanying paper. Deep neural networks require significant resources during deployment. As a result, compressing deep neural networks has become a crucial endeavor, with various methods such as pruning, quantization, and compact architecture design being employed to reduce their footprint. Pruning, in particular, involves eliminating unnecessary parameters in the network, though its efficacy is hindered by the recurrence of a common issue - the re-appearance of removed layers during backpropagation. Current approaches address this issue through various workarounds, though they often require substantial modifications to the original network architecture, compromise accuracy, or have inconsistent results. In contrast, our proposed method, layer-level weak label pruning, utilizes historical prediction data to directly prune individual layers without relying on the original network structure, thereby achieving notable improvements in inference efficiency with minimal impacts on accuracy. Our comprehensive experiments illustrate the efficacy of our approach, outperforming existing compression techniques in terms of accuracy, and demonstrating comparable results to state-of-the-art compact architectures in terms of efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/huynhai1999/LLWL.git. In addition, our project has been deposited on OSF to facilitate understanding of the code at https://osf.io/dj9hc/.

By integrating ProCS into the structure prediction process, predicted contact information can be incorporated into the structure refinement to produce high-accuracy results. Notably, ProCS has effectively improved the performance of state-of-the-art structure prediction algorithms such as ROETT, I-TASSER, and FoldPro, and has achieved superior results in refining the structures of proteins with disordered regions, predicted loops, and unknown structures. Furthermore, the ProCS algorithm has been successfully applied to refine the structures of single-chain proteins, complex proteins, and protein complexes, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness. Overall, ProCS has shown great potential in refining protein structures and can serve as an essential tool for structure prediction algorithms. As a result, ProCS may contribute to the development of accurate protein structures and help to advance the field of protein structure prediction. Deep neural network training's success largely hinges on the choice of loss function. While Cross-Entropy is ubiquitous, research has shown that other loss functions can outperform it. Nevertheless, simply optimizing the loss function's parameter can yield significantly improved performance, particularly with KL Divergence, despite underrepresented usage. Our investigation delves into the underlying reasons for this efficacy, identifying two key factors: 1) stochasticity and 2) non-convexity. Specifically, we demonstrate that demonstrating success with KL Divergence requires balancing its generative model's precision with the posterior's approximation, a trade-off facilitated by non-convex optimization, allowing for'searching' the parameter space. Our findings underscore the importance of considering both dimensions in loss function optimization, highlighting KL Divergence's potential for significant improvements in image classification tasks. Our analysis sheds new light on the efficacy of stochastic, non-convex optimization in search processes, more broadly. While the model amplitude adheres to conservation and crossing symmetry principles, it deviates from the parquet amplitude in terms of phase shifts, leading to distinct differences in physical predictions. Notably, the model amplitude allows for the inclusion of long-range confinement phases, whose effects are particularly apparent in the low-energy region and visible in the infrared phase structure of massless QFT. Given these distinctions, we suggest that the model amplitude with conservative corrections provides a more accurate representation of physical phenomena. To validate this claim, we conduct a direct comparison with the parquet amplitude in various low-energy processes, including tree-level scattering in spinless and spin-1/2 particles, as well as infrared counterterm contributions in massless QFT. Our analysis reveals that the model amplitude's conservative features effectively capture the IR phase structure's critical aspects, offering a more detailed and physically meaningful description. Emergency call centers worldwide rely on text-based incident reporting systems that gather information from users through a standardized set of questions, regardless of the nature of the incident. These systems often fail to consider that certain queries are irrelevant to some types of incidents. To improve these systems, we investigated the effectiveness of dispatchers in collecting information from users. Our research involved analyzing 8,914 real-life incidents from two call centers in Germany, consisting of seven distinct event categories. The results showed that dispatchers typically gather the same data sets, encompassing location, road conditions, number of people involved, and vehicle information, from users experiencing the same type of event. Importantly, our findings revealed that users are frequently asked irrelevant questions by dispatchers. This understanding can facilitate the development of data-driven methods for identifying questions relevant to specific event categories and enhance the efficacy of risk reporting systems. To achieve this, we proposed a framework that utilizes user input to determine question relevance based on their discharge without violating system integrity. The method is fully automatic and adaptable to any call center, requiring no manual annotations. Consequently, we hope this study spurs the creation of more effective text-based incident reporting systems. To facilitate the replication of our work, we made our source code, data, and analysis available online at a public repository. Additionally, we outlined several avenues for further exploration in the field of computer science. These suggestions aim to stimulate both theoretical and practical investigations into the event response problem. Specifically, we identified three areas for investigation: enhancing data entry using question types, analyzing user input with event-driven methods, and applying machine learning algorithms. By addressing these queries, we may gain a deeper understanding of the event response problem and develop more effective data entry systems. For practical applications, we may be able to lower costs, boost dispatch efficiency, and enhance data quality in call centers. For machine learning model development, active learning algorithms strategically select the next training sample to minimize costs. Current approaches often rely on approximate models of posterior distributions, calculated using methods like variational inference, to estimate sample uncertainty. However, these approximations can hinder the algorithm's performance. Building on entropy-based methods, we introduce a new, improved active learning approach that leverages minimax entropy to calculate sample entropy more accurately. By incorporating both entropy and class density to estimate uncertainty, this method addresses two common pitfalls in active learning: selecting duplicate samples and ignoring diverse data points. In addition, its binary outcomes ensure that both hard and easy samples are utilized equally. By minimizing approximately bounded posterior entropy, this algorithm is shown to be effective. We assess its performance using both synthetic and real-world data and find that it surpasses state-of-the-art active learning algorithms. Furthermore, we enhance its scalability for large datasets by employing a subsampling technique. Notably, when applied to the BERT language model, our method achieves an accuracy of 95.4% after 60% labeling, outperforming traditional deep learning approaches with full labeling. This interpretation, known as Analytic Semantics, is rooted in the idea that the meanings of terms and concepts can be clearly defined through their reference to fundamental axioms and the operations inherent to those axioms. We develop an interpretation of this idea within the context of predicate calculus with basic axioms by analyzing how inference rules can be reflected in the original axioms and by considering the relationship between distinct inference rules. We examine this relationship between inference rules through the comparison of containment between different sets of axioms, analogously to how we assess the relationship between concepts in philosophy. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to other types of operation and concept, such as those that govern continuity in functional axioms, by applying the same approach. We then explore applications of this analysis, such as identifying the minimal sets of axioms for individual concepts and terms across the entire axiomatic system, as well as evaluating the coherence of isolated groups of axioms and concept extensions. We examine the behavior and evolution of baroclinic waves within a rotating, vertically-slabbed annulus that contains a warm core at its center. To investigate these phenomena, we apply a set of linearized equations both analytically and through numerical modeling. We evaluate the accuracy of two Bayesian estimators for the Pareto distribution's background, leveraging Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations for complex models. The first estimator utilizes a tuning parameter'm' to approximate the background's typical values. By investigating the impact of'm' on model results, we explore its potential influence on model outcomes and suggest an optimal approach to determine its utility. The second estimator relies on the Mode Masking method, providing a flexible alternative that's often used in modeling complex data. Our study focuses on modeling position-momentum pairs of heavy atoms, employing a mixture model of uniform and Pareto distributions to accurately model background and identify signal. The results show that this model can effectively distinguish between signal and background even at low confidence levels. We then use the model to estimate the minimum detectable amounts of alpha, beta, electron and photon radiation from real experiments. We consider the case of reinforcement learning in partially observable environments that may be partially corrupt. The expected partial corruption is measured by the metric $\eta$. The clean Markov decision process (MDP) is known, but the corrupt MDP's dynamics and transition function are hidden. It is assumed that the partial corruption can be quantified as $\eta$. Our objective is to determine the optimal policy using sample-based reinforcement learning. The problem is split into two parts. Firstly, we investigate an algorithm that is robust to partial corruption $\eta$. Secondly, we explore an algorithm that is robust to any level of corruption. The results show that when $\eta$ is known and is less than $\frac{1}{4}$, the robust sample-based polynomial-time algorithm can be found. Additionally, in the unknown corruption case, the robust sample-based polynomial-time algorithm can be found with high probability, albeit at a higher computational cost. In various applications such as probability theory, statistics, and machine learning, the f-Convolution operator is frequently utilized. Computing the full f-Convolution is an expensive process that requires a great deal of time and memory. However, we discovered that each entry of the convolution can be calculated independently, allowing for the efficient evaluation of a single entry near the origin. By leveraging this property, we developed a two-stage approach to speed up the convolution process. First, we calculated the essential parameters at the boundary, and then used the Fast Fourier Transform to quickly fill in the rest of the convolution surface. This results in a considerable time savings of O(nlogn) compared to the traditional approach of O(n^2). Furthermore, we identified a correlation between the f-Convolution and the inhomogeneous Gaussian distribution, enabling us to apply the Fast Fourier Transform to the latter to solve the former more efficiently. This led to the development of the Fast Gaussian Approximation, a novel method for approximating the f-Convolution, and testing it on several complex scenarios. The experimental outcomes confirm its effectiveness and speed. This research provides a substantial time improvement for the convolution process, and for specific cases such as the Gaussian distribution, it offers a significant memory reduction, from O(n^2) to O(nlogn). Moreover, the two approaches can coexist and complement each other in situation where the f-Convolution is primarily used for statistical inference and the speedup is not crucial. Ultimately, both the Fast Fourier Transform and the Fast Gaussian Approximation can be integrated into the deep learning framework, offering significant time and memory benefits. A refined kernel-based method for dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) enhances the traditional time-stepping approach by incorporating a range of kernels, thereby enhancing its ability to resolve nonlinear systems. This development follows the success of the kernel-based DMD (K-DMD) in improving the accuracy of low-dimensional representations of complex flows. However, the original K-DMD was limited to Euclidean space and worked with linear snapshots; it also shared a strong resemblance to the dynamic empirical coefficient basis method. Unlike its predecessor, the refined approach employs various kernels found within the Grimes space, utilizes observed data via the Manifold Test, and is capable of operating in metric and Grimes spaces. The evaluation of chess players' skills remains a complex issue due to the immense number of possible opening and closing moves.
Despite this complexity, our research successfully applied the Economic Fitness and Complexity approach to evaluate chess skills by analyzing the outcomes of over 700,000 games from the Stockfish database.
This approach measures players' skills as vectors representing their performance in specific chess positions, allowing us to assess players' expertise in particular openings and to evaluate their overall skills.
By treating chess as a dynamic system with multiple equilibrium states, our analysis evaluates players' ability to maintain balance when playing as white or black.
Our findings reveal that the assessment of chess skills is within the same level of accuracy as existing methods that analyze the players' overall winning record.
Furthermore, the introduction of the Economic Fitness and Complexity algorithm enables us to identify and rank the most demanding and rewarding opening moves.
Ultimately, this innovative approach enables the in-depth analysis of chess as a dynamic system with multiple equilibrium states, opening up new possibilities for a more comprehensive understanding of the game. 
The associated code can be found at https://github.com/jmfranson/EF_CHESS.

This correction emerges from a quantum effect that is not evident when the mass is fixed. Notably, the result is applicable across various theories describing black branes, including $N=4$ super Yang-Mills and anti-de Sitter theory. The analysis also extends to baryon black branes, where the quantum effect leads to a similar outcome. Furthermore, the approach allows us to determine the quantum effect on the entropy of heavy probe particles in a thermal plasma. Additionally, the study reveals that the correction in question is a manifestation of an instanton interaction, which is typically negligible but becomes relevant in the thermal canonical ensemble. The findings also suggest that the weak gravity conjecture's prediction may be indicative of a more fundamental thermodynamic relationship rather than a consequence of gravity. Ultimately, the research underscores the significance of the instanton interaction in shaping thermodynamic properties. Due to its negligible impact in the grand canonical ensemble, the effect may have gone undetected until now. Research has established a theoretical framework for this crack growth pattern, which consists of a combination of geometric and physical factors. This study aims to expand our understanding by applying the crack growth models to a new scenario: the presence of multiple cracks in materials that are subjected to rapid loading. By using mathematical analysis and numerical computations, we have developed new equations that describe how these cracks interact and affect the overall behavior under high loading conditions. The analysis reveals that the distance between cracks, their shape, and the overall loading conditions influence the rate at which they propagate. The study provides new insights into how cracks behave under high loading conditions and how their intrinsic length scale affects their behavior. The findings have significant implications for understanding intrinsic length scale effects in materials with cracks. The data consists of descriptions from Wikipedia summaries and factual statements in the form of queries. The task is divided into three parts: identifying the main components of these statements, categorizing the statements themselves, and generating reformulated statements. We introduce Indecision Trees, a novel model capable of generating meaningful
constraints to aid inference processes. Unlike conventional machine learning
models, which strive for decision-making, Indecision Trees explore the realm
of partial orders to facilitate more efficient computation and insight into
complex problems. By leveraging constrained optimization techniques, Indecision
Trees can generate model parameters satisfying both functional and structural
constraints. In this study, we establish the mathematical underpinnings for
Indecision Trees and illustrate their applicability through two numerical examples. 
The first example involves polynomial systems, and the second, derived from
computer vision, yields a solution efficiently scalable for large data sets.
Our analysis demonstrates that Indecision Trees can tackle various problem types
and can be solved using conventional optimization methods. Furthermore, they
can generate numerous feasible solutions, enabling us to explore and visualize
them. Ultimately, Indecision Trees offer a versatile tool for constrained
inference processes.

The surge in IoT data and time series analysis necessitates efficient time series similarity search to support real-time applications. Pruning strategies are integral to achieving high performance, especially when combined with approximate indexing. However, the standard approach involves evaluating each tuple separately, leading to unnecessary computations early on. By integrating an early abandoning mechanism into the evaluation process, performance can be enhanced. This paper introduces techniques for indexing time series with an early abandoning mechanism into the Minkowski sum of spheres (MOS) algorithm, resulting in significant reductions in CPU and memory usage. The optimized method was then compared to existing approaches through extensive experiments on diverse datasets, yielding impressive results. The findings support the conclusion that incorporating early abandoning into the evaluation process of time series similarity search can be highly effective. Additionally, the source code and some experimental data are available at https://github.com/jm4t/Early-Abandoning-MOS. The index construction time was measured in nanoseconds, and memory usage was quantified in bytes per tuple. All measurements were normalized in line with standard practice in the field. The proposed optimized method outperformed the competition, offering faster processing times and lower memory requirements. As an example, on the ontheroad dataset, the tree construction time was reduced from 18 milliseconds to 9.5 milliseconds, resulting in significantly lower memory usage (from 7.9 MB to 6.4 MB per gigabyte). These performance gains were replicated across all evaluated datasets, underscoring the potential of the optimized method to improve software development. The relative improvements in processing speed and memory efficiency were calculated as a function of the number of data points and dimensionality, offering valuable insights into the expected performance gains. The study's findings can be summarized as follows: the indexing time was directly proportional to the number of data points, but dependent on dimensionality; the memory usage was directly proportional to the number of data points and their size. These conclusions were validated through experiments with various configurations. The analysis reveals that the time complexity of processing each tuple was dominated by the time required for evaluation, leading to the conclusion that incorporating early abandoning can mitigate the adverse effects of high dimensionality. Furthermore, the experiments with different dimensionality confirm the positive impact of reducing unnecessary computations on performance. The analysis shows that incorporating early abandoning results in significant processor time savings, exceeding memory gains in certain scenarios. In contrast, the benefits in memory usage were more modest. The comparison of processor time savings to memory savings reveals that the gains in processor time were consistently greater than those in memory.

This study explores the effectiveness of giving immediate feedback to high school students while they learn to program, using multiple tools at once. These tools provide different feedbacks based on various metrics. To maximize their impact, students are encouraged to work on small batches of code at a time and switch between writing and testing phases using a technique called the Perry Model. However, giving feedback for such tiny batches can be unnecessary and distracting, according to our analysis. Instead, students need feedback only when they make progress in their code or when they fail to improve coverage, even if they make no changes. By combining this approach with immediate feedback for successful testing and strategic feedback for code growth, students can achieve better test coverage, performance improvements, and overall better grades. Our methods are part of a state-of-the-art learning system that is being tested right now in a large-scale study involving over 700 students, but the results shown here are based on a smaller pilot with 63 students, using data from two different courses. Interpretable machine learning is crucial for comprehending why and how black-box models have reached certain conclusions. Nevertheless, when such models are part of an overall system that yields a collective decision, grasping its inner workings remains challenging. This is due, in part, to the lack of clear requirements for the type of interpretability it should provide. We identify distinct forms of interpretability for collective systems and propose a set of criteria to evaluate various solutions. Using our framework, we examine and assess three different approaches that offer explanations for the decisions made by such systems. We conclude by highlighting a suitable method as a potential solution. This work draws inspiration from the concepts of understanding and absorption in logic. We explore how the concepts of reflection and transference of properties may also be applicable to learning systems. Furthermore, we identify relationships between these logical ideas and the requirements for interpretability in collective systems, as summarized in the table below. 

| Concept | Understanding | Absorption | Explanation |
| :----- | :---------- | :-------- | :---------- |
| Idea | System makes decision based on input | System makes decision based on its state after receiving input | Representation of the system's decision-making process |
| Focus | Why and how system reached decision | Why and how system reached decision and what information was used | Why and how system reached decision |
| Properties | Truthfulness and soundness | Truthfulness and soundness, in addition to being independent from the system's state | Truthfulness and soundness |

This research offers a rigorous analysis of existing estimators for common stochastic trends among a group of non-stationary assets. Our study examines their asymptotic behavior, taking into account the effects of extreme events and changing sample sizes. The results reveal that these estimators are susceptible to errors caused by outliers, and their accuracy can be compromised if the same event affects multiple assets. An enhanced estimator is developed to mitigate these limitations and improve estimation of common stochastic trends. The newly proposed approach matches or outperforms the original estimators when all assets follow conventional specifications, while also providing improved results in cases where assets exhibit extreme value movements. A comprehensive method is also introduced to test the presence of common stochastic trends, and associated inference procedures are designed. The research offers insights on how to apply these improved estimation and testing methods in practice, and demonstrates their advantages through application to historical data on S&P 500 stock prices. Focusing on multi-asset price models helps to minimize the impact of measurement errors and facilitates the application of these methods, even when individual asset price data are not available. The research includes all necessary code for replication of the analyses and figures presented. Additionally, the code can be utilized for other applications, such as estimating common stochastic trends in a group of assets from various markets. Some of the methods employed in this research have broader applications, including the assessment of model specification and the identification of shocks with specific characteristics. Understanding the behavior of individual stocks during times of market stress is essential, especially when considering portfolio management by stock and credit exchanges. The dynamics of a single equity asset are typically analyzed using familiar concepts like mean, median, mode, and skewness. This research extends these ideas by examining the cross-sectional returns distribution for an entire portfolio of assets and defining key statistical parameters beyond the first order. By applying the central limit theorem and utilizing four distinct methods of analysis, the study demonstrates that the first four statistical parameters of cross-sectional returns are directly correlated with those of asset returns. A practical application of these findings involves using the estimates derived from historical data to assess the likelihood of future losses in a portfolio's value. Specifically, the study proposes a statistical model grounded in theoretical framework, which includes parameters for location, scale, skewness, and Kurtosis. This model can be used to generate simulated cross-sectional returns and evaluate the associated risk. Ultimately, the study showcases the application of these models through a numerical example. It compares the behavior of a portfolio consisting of both large-cap and small-cap stocks during the financial crisis of 2007-2008, highlighting their differing characteristics and potential for managing market and credit related risks. Several other promising avenues for further investigation and exploration are identified. This includes using the models in conjunction with loss distribution modeling and assessing the effect of time on cross-sectional returns and their distribution. Additionally, the study hints at the possibility of employing the models in an inverse scenario, where a known outcome is used to determine the probability of asset returns. Specifically, the study references the situation of determining the probability of a firm going bankrupt in order to set the firm's credit spread.  Finally, the study reveals the potential for these models in an environment where the models are utilized to determine the price of a credit default swap. We introduce a novel detection method for cardiac abnormalities in sound recordings that functions effectively in noisy environments without the need for preprocessing. This approach uses a deep learning technique with a convolutional neural network, allowing the detection of abnormalities without the manual segmentation of heart sounds required in traditional methods. Our system demonstrates high accuracy in detecting cardiac diseases when trained with data from various environments and patients of different ethnicities. Notably, it surpasses state-of-the-art techniques by a significant margin in noise-intensive settings. To facilitate further research and improvements, we make the source code publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/afshanjaved/SoundBN. Specifically, we provide the code for the BN-Block and the complete ConvNeXt model architecture used in the study. Additionally, we include a package called mxcardiosax that enables the analysis of cardiac sound recordings using the Saxe metric, originally developed for studying the diversity of deep neural networks. This new library is compatible with the MXNet deep learning framework, making it easy to reproduce the results shown in the paper. The mxcardiosax package is also available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/afshanjaved/mxcardiosax. A corresponding paper has been published on arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10324. We present the code and the results in the paper as our contribution to the field, aiming to promote the development of cardiac disease detection using deep neural networks with robustness as the primary focus. In the context of deep learning, robustness refers to the capacity of a model to function effectively in diverse environments and patient conditions. By prioritizing robustness, we can create detection tools that are easier to interpret and used widely. Nonetheless, achieving robustness often comes with the cost of decreased accuracy, making it an intriguing area of study. We invite researchers to build upon our work by improving the model's overall performance while ensuring robustness as a primary goal, and we present the code to facilitate further research and improvements. A rapid decline in single-particle effects beyond the 2-neutron contribution was found, justifying the use of a single-particle calculation for computing electric dipole transition amplitudes with a significant proton in a $t_{2g}$ orbital. A straightforward method to compute the multiparticle contribution for any proton configuration was developed, which consists of two components: the core (one-proton contributions not involving the outermost proton) and tail components. It was observed that the core and single-proton tail contributions sufficiently reproduce the multiparticle effect, confirming that the initial assumption of the single-particle approximation. Let a finite group G act on a real 2-dimensional torus S^1 x S^1 by twisting its components by elements from the group. This paper explores the properties of G-twisted equivariant cohomology, hatching a rigorous mathematical framework that describes it in terms of the G-cohomology of the group's representation on the 2-dimensional torus S^1 x S^1. Additionally, research identifies both necessary and sufficient conditions under which this G-twisted cohomology can be reduced to the ordinary equivariant cohomology. These findings are verified through concrete examples in the context of cyclic groups of prime order. Furthermore, based on these findings, we propose a theory of G-twisted equivariant bivariant homology and cohomology theorems. Finally, we investigate how this G-twisted equivariant cohomology is related to non-trivial situations in which the group actions either collapse to the ordinary equivariant cohomology or become non-trivial. These lastly considered non-trivial scenarios include actions of the cyclic group of prime order on both the loop space of the torus and on the universal covering space of the projective plane. Creating an inclusive and supportive academic environment is critical, encompassing a comprehensive approach that extends beyond diversity metrics. It involves fostering a vibrant community that promotes mutual respect, cooperation, and innovative research. At the Department of Computer Science at Stanford, we have initiated 'Connect @ CS,' a program aimed at enhancing the overall departmental atmosphere through social events, teamwork initiatives, and a comprehensive website. By hosting over 60 gatherings, developing 20 collaboration projects, and designing a dynamic website with over 300 members, we have successfully engaged the department's faculty, staff, and students in a comprehensive effort to build a unified and inclusive community. Evaluations indicate positive responses towards these initiatives, resulting in an increased sense of belonging among department members. Moreover, an external review in 2021 highlighted the program's contributions, stating, 'The Connect @ CS program has developed a vibrant community that is a strength for the department.' Consequently, we recommend integrating this program into the department's long-term strategy, advising that resources be allocated to maintain and expand the program, and encouraging other academic departments to adopt similar community-building initiatives. Ultimately, a supportive and inclusive campus culture is critical for academic success and should be a priority for departmental development. By fostering a unified and engaged community, we can harness the collective potential of our faculty, staff, and students to drive excellence in research and achieve a more inclusive and supportive departmental environment.

However, sellers who participate in non-credible auctions frequently fail to capitalize on the opportunity to extract the value of time and uncertainty, which ultimately means they could be generating more revenue if they were participating in a first-price auction. Additionally, the theoretical framework developed offers a potential explanation for why sellers sometimes refrain from maximizing their revenue and adhering to auction rules in an effort to maintain a level of moral integrity. This occurs when sellers place significant importance on fairness and are willing to sacrifice some revenue in order to participate in an auction that is perceived as fair, even if it means forgoing the opportunity to benefit from uncertainty and time. This finding has significant implications for fields such as industrial organization, auction theory, and the study of human behavior, as it highlights the intricate relationship between time, uncertainty, and human behavior in auctions. This study reveals a novel connection between Grobner bases and the local character theory of symmetric groups, specifically within the context of Hessenberg varieties. We establish that Grobner bases generated by a monomial ideal associated with Hessenberg varieties possess a group-theoretic structure, effectively comprising key characters from the Kostka theorem. This discovery enables us to distill a set of essential generators for the local defining ideal of any Hessenberg variety. We also explore the local structure of these varieties, including the local Hilbert series, which reflects the shape of the associated Hessenberg configuration. Additionally, this research reveals a duality between two types of Grobner bases, effectively allowing for the computation of Grobner bases for non-Hessenberg varieties via Grobner bases for Hessenberg varieties of a specific type, known as normal. We conclude by illustrating various Grobner basis computations for Hessenberg varieties of shape $(2,2,n-2)$. Specifically, this involves calculating the Grobner basis for the ideal defining the maximal Hessenberg variety of type $B\cup D$, as well as the Grobner bases for three other Hessenberg varieties of type $D$. We also demonstrate that the local structure of these varieties is equivalent to that of three other Hessenberg varieties of the same shape. Furthermore, this research involves Grobner base computations for Hessenberg varieties of shape $(3,1,n)$ in types $A$ and $D\cup D\cup D$. We establish explicit calculations for four Grobner bases associated with these varieties, including one variety for which the computation was previously infeasible. We also determine the local structure of eleven other Hessenberg varieties of the same shape, including varieties of maximal Hessenberg type in group $D_4$. These computational outcomes also yield explicit formulas for local Hilbert series and exponents in group $D_4$. Furthermore, these structural properties yield equivalences in Grobner base computation for two varieties in group $D_4$ of shape $(3,1,4)$ and two others in group $D_4$ of shape $(2,2,4)$. We now present our general findings for all the computed Grobner bases for Hessenberg varieties in groups $A_n$ and $D_n$. Deep generative networks such as GANs exhibit incredible capability in creating various forms of visual art. In the realm of brushstrokes, a fundamental element of art, implementing a pixel-based representation proves to be inefficient. The massive number of pixels required to capture a single brushstroke's effect complicates representation and generates excessively large images. To overcome this challenge, we propose BrushGAN, a novel brushstroke generation method. BrushGAN produces brushstrokes as continuous lines, allowing the model to be trained with a more manageable image size, yielding better sampling quality and reduced noise compared to previous methods. To verify the efficacy of our model, we analyzed BrushGAN's performance using the Drawing in Between dataset, demonstrating its superiority over the SSGAN method. Additionally, we successfully applied BrushGAN to multiple brushstroke-based artistic tasks. Firstly, we used the model to create individual brushstrokes, generating a video showcasing a brush moving across a canvas. Secondly, we employed BrushGAN to produce brushstrokes for a specific style, using a style transfer approach. Lastly, we combined BrushGAN with PointGAN to develop a painting tool, allowing a brush to be moved while producing color outputs based on input pressure. The resulting brushstrokes were then used to create interactive and dynamic paintings. Due to the dataset's grounded nature, it offers a framework for the next-generation NLP challenge - Grounded Question Generation (GQG). Using a one-dimensional astrophysics code, we studied the formation and development of the stellar core collapse edge (CCE). This boundary is found where the post-shock material meets the rapidly cooling, denser core of the star. Prior research suggested the CCE becomes unstable through the "fast instability" if a supernova explosion occurs, causing the star to collapse. We discovered the fast instability occurs consistently within the CCE, leading to enhanced mixing between the core and outer layers. When a supernova explosion is not successful, the material within the CCE remains stable. We found the properties of the CCE to significantly impact its stability, with broader regions of the CCE indicating greater instability. We also observed the instability to significantly increase Si and O abundances within a limited, inner layer of the core, even when Si and O enrichment is not generally present. Additionally, the model we used showed the fast instability to result in the partial dissolution of the progenitor star's structure, especially for Si and O layering, with more abundant Si on the outer layer and less in the inner, indicating the model's completeness. Three-dimensional simulations are required to fully comprehend the movement of material within the CCE and its influence on the inner layers and structure of the star. The findings of this research will contribute to those simulations by providing initial conditions and understanding the formation of the CCE, as well as its properties and behavior. The model suggests the fast instability has a significant impact on the inner layers of the star, particularly outer layers of Si enrichment and inner layers of Si depletion, which could provide insight into these enrichments through the analysis of stellar movement patterns. In this paper, a novel neural network model based on multi-task learning and focused attention was proposed. By employing a F-score optimizer and a focused attention module that selects key regions of interest, the model's overall performance was enhanced. Notably, when trained on a reduced subset of the most important regions of interest, the model still achieved an accuracy of 70.46%, indicating improved generalizability. Furthermore, the model was found to have a reduced parameter count and improved computational efficiency due to its condensed architecture. As a result, the model outperformed existing state-of-the-art ADHD diagnosis models, with an enhanced new sample accuracy of 71.13% and a improved generalizability of 70.46%, along with a reduced parameter count of 35.92 kHz. Additionally, the model was found to have a reduced architecture density of 34.04%, indicating improved computational efficiency. Furthermore, the model was used to develop an ADHD diagnosis decision support system that selects key regions of interest for clinicians to focus on, utilizing an attention mechanism that identifies the least influenced regions. Consequently, the system enables the optimization of clinical resources, allowing the detection of ADHD with reduced scanning regions, and facilitates data augmentation by selecting the most generalizable regions of interest. Therefore, the model proposed in this paper is an effective and efficient deep neural network-based architecture for the diagnosis and treatment of ADHD. Given that acronyms often carry different meanings across various fields and writing contexts, a multi-stage approach is proposed to efficiently resolve ambiguities, relying on the analysis of available knowledge graphs. By adapting the type of the unknown acronym from the context in which it appears, the system can select suitable knowledge graphs to look up the acronym, thus significantly reducing the system's computational requirements and potential mistakes.
