This work proposes a DNA data storage system that utilizes the DNA sequence-based access mechanism to the stored data. The system allows a DNA data recorder to request multiple storage partitions from the DNA sequence pool, each recorded with a different primer pair, and, upon reception of the DNA sequence, determine the applicable primer pair based on a DNA sequence analysis algorithm. By generating optimal primer pairs, the system can effectively prevent misidentification and optimize storage efficiency, especially in the case of multiple recordings, and, due to the DNA sequence pool's vast capacity, can significantly lower the cost per unit of stored data. Experimental results indicate that the proposed system can achieve a superior balance between overhead and storage capacity compared to existing DNA data storage approaches. For example, when the overhead is set at 10%, the total storage capacity can reach up to 67% of the maximum value. Furthermore, when the storage capacity is at 80%, the total overhead can be as low as 10% of the maximum value. Moreover, when multiple recordings are involved, the proposed system can save an average of additional 13% of storage capacity over existing DNA data storage approaches for the same overhead. Finally, when the storage capacity is at 80%, the overhead can be as low as 10% of the maximum value, with an average reduction in storage overhead of approximately 13% compared to existing DNA data storage approaches for multiple recordings. In terms of algorithmic complexity, the proposed system has a more efficient DNA sequence analysis algorithm with a time complexity of O(n), as well as optimized primer pair design with an approximately linear time complexity. In contrast, existing DNA data storage approaches have a less efficient algorithm with a higher time complexity. In conclusion, the proposed system provides a superior balance between overhead and storage capacity while effectively managing storage partitions, and its novel DNA sequence analysis algorithm further enhances its efficiency. The system's effectiveness in optimizing DNA data storage while minimizing storage overhead and misidentification serves as a significant advancement over existing DNA data storage approaches. Momentum-space nodal lines are inherently one-dimensional topological features that occur in two higher-dimensional spaces known as nontrivial nodal-line semimetals. Unlike other topological states (e.g., Weyl nodes, zero-energy nodes in topological superconductors, and Mott insulators with zero-energy nodes), nodal lines are characterized by being zero-dimensional in real space yet one-dimensional in momentum space. Topological semimetals with nodal lines have garnered significant interest due to their unique properties and potential applications in materials science. Notably, the theoretical concept of topological surface states provides a natural connection to observing nodal-line semimetals, as a solid can be topologically nontrivial if its surface exhibits a nodal-line structure. This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the theoretical concepts underlying nodal-line semimetals, with a focus on NLS by N. M. Wild, M. Ulrich, and C. L. Kane, as well as their key aspects, with additional insights from L. M. Fischer and H. M. Meyer, M. Ulrich, C. L. Kane, and N. M. Wild. The text also draws connections to other areas of research, including topological surface states, Weyl semimetals, topological superconductors, and Mott insulators with zero-energy nodes. Researchers examine how wave speeds change and interact within a complex system of coupled oscillators, influenced by external forces and connections. The study reveals that wave speed in the system is determined by the relationship between an oscillator and its neighbors, as well as the impact of external stimuli. This can lead to situations where wave speeds become stuck at local minimum points. By applying mathematical concepts derived from bifurcation theory, the study provides an in-depth analysis of the complex behaviors encountered. The work is then extended to a model of a fluid-like system consisting of coupled Josephson oscillators and reveals new wave phenomena. The study's findings are critical in understanding wave dynamics in low-energy systems and providing insights that can be applied to higher-energy quantum liquid phenomena. The research also lays the groundwork for future developments in micro-mechanical quantum devices. The results demonstrate that the algorithm can be reliably used in sequences containing continuous, discrete, or a combination of both types of information, as long as the information sequence is sufficiently unpredictable. The algorithm is also capable of handling sequences containing an unlimited amount of information, albeit with diminishing returns, similar to the natural information limit in English. The assessment of its robustness is comparable to previously established methods in specific scenarios and is proven to be more robust in others, specifically when dealing with a combination of continuous and discrete information. The burgeoning field of artificial intelligence (AI) holds immense promise for transforming existing medical imaging centers and biobanks into high-utility, computer-assisted research platforms. To achieve this potential, compound AI-enabled imaging biobanks (CAIIBs) necessitate the development of sophisticated computational pipelines and extensive imaging databases. Effective CAIBs require the seamless integration of advanced AI algorithms with large-scale medical image collections, as well as reliable quality control and data management mechanisms. This article examines the requirements and best practices for designing and building AI-friendly medical image repositories, with a particular emphasis on the creation of comprehensive training and testing datasets for deep learning-based applications. It also explores the need for standardized clinical image sets, data recapture protocols, and the implementation of secure data storage and transmission measures. Finally, the article presents a case study highlighting our institutional efforts to establish a successful CAIB and showcases our methodologies and findings. Despite the numerous successes achieved to date, this article primarily serves as an initial exploration of this subject, and it is anticipated that future contributions from the research community will yield even more substantial advancements for the field. Ultimately, the article seeks to facilitate the creation of AI-friendly biobanks, empower researchers in the field, and facilitate the translation of CAIBs into high-utility, computer-assisted research platforms capable of realizing their full AI-driven potential. The power of machine learning in medical settings has been increasingly acknowledged, but the availability of clinical features and patient data often poses significant limitations to the effectiveness of models. To bridge this gap, researchers have explored data augmentation as a potential solution, with the goal of expanding the scope of trained models without supplementing the original dataset. While various methods have been proposed, there is a lack of comprehensive analysis examining the impact of different augmentation strategies and their applicability to specific medical tasks. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of data augmentation on the classification of left ventricular dysfunction in medical images, employing both augmented clinical features and images to train a siamese network. Our results indicate that data augmentation yields comparable or superior performance to training models with augmented datasets, but on specific medical tasks where sufficient training data is available. Moreover, we identify that data augmentation using clinical features is more beneficial than image-based augmentation and can prevent model overfitting when training on small datasets. Our findings suggest that data augmentation can be a valuable tool for enhancing model robustness and effectiveness, and can be utilized effectively both with and without increased dataset sizes. We introduce a quantum version of the K-means clustering algorithm utilizing a hybrid quantum-classical approach. In the classical realm, this problem poses a computationally challenging data analysis issue, leading to an exponential time complexity of O(ld^KT) with the number of data points, clusters, and dimensions. By leveraging quantum computers for data processing and classical methods for optimization, our proposed solution achieves an asymptotic complexity of O(ld^K), provided there are enough data points. If the number of clusters is 2, we demonstrate a constant complexity independent of dimensions. Our results indicate the potential for significant performance gains, specifically for datasets involving multiple dimensions and a small number of clusters. We implement the proposed algorithm using qubit-based quantum computers and simulate its performance with random datasets on simulators for noiseless and noisy quantum environments. Our simulations reveal the existence of a threshold below which the quantum approach outperforms the classical method. Moreover, our results suggest the possibility of efficiently clustering high-dimensional data points using the proposed quantum algorithm despite increasing data points. Simulations also show an increase in success rate as the number of data points doubles from 16 to 32, and further enhancements are anticipated with larger datasets. We discuss potential applications and improvements for the proposed solution. Additionally, we compare its performance with another quantum clustering algorithm based on amplitude distribution, yielding comparable outcomes but distinct limitations in terms of data points, clusters, and dimensions, paving the way for integration with classical methods to overcome these constraints. We showcase the potential of combining classical and quantum approaches for clustering, including a hybrid version of the proposed algorithm utilizing classical optimization for better results. Notably, the proposed solution consistently performs better than classical methods for small datasets and achieves comparable outcomes to the hybrid version for large datasets. We discuss the necessity of noise-robust quantum algorithms for practical applications of quantum computing, highlighting the potential drawbacks of current models and the need to develop new types of algorithms that can effectively utilize quantum computers despite imperfect conditions. The discovery of planetary systems in M dwarf stars is gaining momentum, thanks largely to ground-based surveys focused on these stars. As the sample grows, so does our understanding of how the distribution of planetary mass ratios changes based on the type of stars and planets. To further this knowledge, we analyzed the Kepler data for 34 M dwarfs that contain multiple planetary systems, yielding 144 unique planetary detection events. By examining the transit patterns, we were able to identify ratios of mass for 64 distinct planetary events. Using these ratios, we created two diagrams representing different perspectives on planetary mass ratios. The first diagram displays the ratios in a R_{2} versus P ratio format, while the second shows within-system comparisons of the ratios. Our analysis revealed that planets in close proximity to their host stars tend to have smaller mass ratios compared to wider systems, while ultracompact systems exhibit the highest mass ratios overall. When considering the radius of the planets, we found that those with larger radii exhibit higher mass ratios. To further this understanding, we used astronomical code simulations to place constraints on the underlying mass-ratio distribution, taking into account detection biases. Our analysis revealed that the probability of finding a planet decreases as the mass ratio increases, peaks around 0.01, and then shows a significant drop-off at ratios above 0.01. We also found that the shape of this distribution remains largely unchanged when considering systems composed of equal-mass planets. However, for systems featuring disparate masses, the distribution reveals an upward trend, particularly at lower mass ratios. Through our analysis, we have provided constraints on the mass-ratio distribution, which can inform theoretical models and provide a framework for comparing the results of future transit surveys with the exoplanet sample from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. Additionally, our findings highlight the significance of incorporating variability-induced biases and detection limitations into statistical analyses of planetary systems. By doing so, we can gain a more accurate understanding of the planetary mass-ratio function. Based on our analysis, we predict that the mass-ratio distribution will likely drop off at higher mass ratios compared to what is seen in G dwarf stars. Finally, our study underscores the value of utilizing transit times to make more precise estimates of planetary masses, which in turn can provide a wealth of new information on the shape of the planetary mass-ratio distribution. By doing so, we can achieve a level of precision that can distinguish between differing theoretical mass-ratio scenarios. In the context of probabilistic origin-destination demand modeling, the statistical model is based on a probabilistic formulation of the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two multivariate normal distributions, leading to a linear regression model that needs to estimate a large, sparse covariance matrix. Under the assumption of sparsity, lasso regularization is employed to accurately recover the covariance matrix, yielding a consistent estimate. Furthermore, lasso-based sparse covariance estimation improves the precision of parameter estimation compared to the unbiased estimate and performs well even when the assumptions of sparsity are not perfectly met. Using real-world air passenger demography data from 1987-1988, lasso estimation reveals a substantial number of zero entries in the covariance matrix, confirming the original hypothesis of sparsity. When applied to the probabilistic formulation of the Kullback-Leibler divergence, lasso regularization yields more accurate estimates of the covariance matrix, leading to improved generalization performance and faster convergence. Additionally, lasso estimation outperforms the traditional approach in a probabilistic formulation of the flow-diverging Kullback-Leibler divergence on various metrics. Nonetheless, both lasso and traditional approaches struggle with the estimation of small eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors. Consequently, a new, more robust eigendecomposition approach is proposed for tackling ill-posed problems, including the computation of the eigenvectors corresponding to minimal eigenvalues. This novel method employs a weighted lasso approach with the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix determined through a random sample matrix decomposition. Furthermore, the approach incorporates the soft-thresholding technique from the lasso regularization to stabilize the estimation of the eigenvectors and improve the removal of noise. Importantly, the proposed method preserves the sparsity of the covariance matrix and accurately estimates the non-zero eigenvectors while applying soft-thresholding to the non-zero eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors helps to eliminate excessive noise. Importantly, the approach remains stable and robust when the lasso regularization is applied to the original covariance matrix, allowing for the extraction of the top eigenvectors with minimal distortion and the identification of the sparest structure in the remaining eigenvectors. Consequently, the proposed method yields more accurate and stable estimates of the eigenvectors, especially in the case of minimal eigenvalues, with the ability to remove excessive noise while maintaining sparsity. In a practical application using the same air passenger demography data, the approach successfully removes noise from the covariance matrix, yielding an almost completely noise-free structure with accurate eigenvectors. Recent advancements in music representation learning have been accelerated by large-scale, multi-modal datasets. Nevertheless, the present music dataset is limited, hindering the development of effective models. To address this issue, a new music dataset is presented, consisting of 88,804 song-title pairs along with accompanying audio features. This dataset overcomes existing shortcomings due to several factors. Firstly, it possesses a substantial number of song-title pairs second only to the Million Song Dataset. Secondly, it contains a diverse collection of song titles that accurately reflects mainstream musical tastes. Lastly, it includes a wide array of song titles that enable cross-modal retrieval in music representation learning in an unbiased manner. To evaluate the effectiveness of our dataset, several state-of-the-art music retrieval models are applied and assessed using the dataset's annotations. The results are then utilized to develop new benchmark scores for the dataset. Furthermore, the dataset and accompanying code are made publicly available for the purpose of advancing music representation learning in a cross-modal context. Building on the work by Cipolès, Frénod, and Rozenblum in the one-dimensional case, we investigate the stability of dark solitons in the two-dimensional defocusing Bose gas with wave speed. Leveraging the conformal transformation developed by Cipolès and Gelashvili, we obtain a new system of coupled Schrödinger equations in the half-plane. The resulting stability analysis, similar to that in the one-dimensional case, reveals that dark solitons are stable for a specific range of wave speeds and decouple into stable black solitons through a limiting process. Moreover, our research extends the existing knowledge on soliton stability by providing new findings. Specifically, we establish the existence of solitons for any positive wave speed and any non-zero coupling parameter, while the existing literature only guaranteed their existence for small enough wave speeds and non-zero coupling parameters. Additionally, we obtain an accurate estimate of the minimum possible black soliton speed and show that it occurs at a non-zero coupling parameter value, thus laying the groundwork for further investigations into soliton behavior through linear and nonlinear stability analysis in future studies. The two-dimensional case studies highlight the dark soliton's orbital stability under small perturbations in both wave speed and coupling parameter. The calculations for the stability constants reveal that for large enough wave speeds, the stability depends on the coupling parameter and wave speed values, while the soliton's stability under small perturbations in the coupling parameter remains consistent across all tested combinations of these parameters with wave speeds and coupling parameters. Current assessments of reinforcement learning algorithms are limited to a single, fixed environment. Yet, in real-world applications, learners typically encounter adapting curricula and shifting task schedules. To give these algorithms a more accurate test, we propose a method to change the curriculum over time. By gradually introducing new tasks and adjusting conditions like state-action pairs to signal task transitions, the curriculum becomes more challenging for learners. Using a continuous, dynamic environment, we show that our curriculum changes allow us to examine multiple tasks at once, and we evaluate the learning capabilities of four reinforcement learning algorithms in this new setting. Findings indicate that algorithms excelling in static conditions often struggle with our dynamic curricula, but some, like C51 DQN using a hierarchical model, demonstrate success. Consequently, our approach offers a new standard for comparing learning methods in evolving applications, and it paves the way for better-trained agents capable of navigating evolving environments. Notably, our findings have implications for training agents to navigate shifting operational conditions and adapting systems where tasks are introduced at various times. This research focuses on the baroclinic wave generation driven by random disturbances in a barotropic beta-plane model with coupled baroclinic and stratified layers. We found that the existence of non-trivial traveling waves near the Couette flow relies on the degree of model simplicity. For a high level of model simplicity, we can observe the existence of these waves. However, the simplicity decreases with increasing Rossby number and parameter beta. Moreover, we identified a critical level of model simplicity below which the baroclinic wave generation is unlikely. Using an approach starting from a linear regime and applying a multiple-scale perturbation method, we were able to analyze the singular reduction of the coupled equations and identify the key factors that restrict the existence of these waves. Ultimately, we were able to demonstrate that the properties of these waves match those observed in numerical simulations, thereby confirming their relevance. Additionally, we were able to obtain a complete description of the baroclinic wave generation observed in these simulations, particularly its occurrence with and without the presence of zonal currents. Furthermore, we were able to identify the parameters that characterize the diffusion-limited and stochastic regimes of these waves. Lastly, we were able to evaluate the accuracy of our analysis by comparing it with numerical results for the baroclinic wave generation in a coupled layer coupled to a barotropic beta-plane model. We found that the parameters obtained through our analysis closely match those obtained via numerical simulations, thereby confirming the completeness of our description of these waves. \\

This paper compares various fusion techniques for estimating sparse signals from multiple measurements. These techniques, such as early, intermediate, and hierarchical fusion, differ in their approaches to integrating information from multiple sources. To demonstrate their equivalence, we recast each method as a form of matrix inversion using the Moore-Penrose inverse, enabling the application of tools from linear system theory. Utilizing the Nevanlinna-Pick theorem, we established a condition for the effectiveness of these techniques, which may not always be feasible with high dimensions due to numerical instability. Our findings are substantiated through numerical experiments. Additionally, we propose a new method of parameter estimation for these techniques, which provides a more reliable way to determine their effectiveness in various scenarios. Our results are particularly applicable to DRL-based techniques, such as data-driven and learning-based hierarchical fusion, enabling conventional optimization approaches. Our work provides a clear understanding of the limitations and possibilities of each technique, thereby facilitating the development of more effective techniques in this category. Furthermore, pre-training strategies typically focus on individual speech segments or simple tasks like speech classification. In contrast, we propose a multi-task pre-training approach that incorporates data from entire conversations and multiple tasks. Specifically, we utilize contrastive learning to promote distinction between separate speakers and similar within-branch speakers. Our novel model architecture and pre-training method exhibit exceptional performance on multiple datasets, including the NIST CQS and CSJ datasets, in multiple speech recognition tasks. Notably, we observe a significant 16.7% relative improvement in the CONDOR dataset after applying our pre-training method. We compare the efficacy of our method to state-of-the-art models through baseline tests on the NIST CQS dataset. The thermal nature of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes suggests a direct correlation between particle mass and temperature.  Evaluating the standard mass and energy terms within the Standard Model, we find the peak of the Hawking spectrum occurs near Planck masses, where $M \simeq 9 \times 10^{14} \GeV$, and determine the low-energy photon flux to be far below current LHC sensitivity levels.  Consequently, we conclude that primordial black holes are unlikely to be the source of the 3.56 MeV gamma-ray signal from the dark matter sector observed by the AMOEBA collaboration.  Alternatively, we explore the possibility that the signal arises from the decay of relic heavy neutrinos.  To explain the observed rate and to satisfy constraints from big bang nucleosynthesis and a recent LHC search for heavy stabilizer states, we find that decay parameters ranging from $10^{16.3}$ eV to $10^{17.7}$ eV are plausible.  Moreover, according to certain astrophysical considerations, we note that heavier neutrinos may also be within reach of current LHC capabilities. Semantic segmentation tasks involving hyperspectral images are restricted due to incomplete label information. Conventional segmentation models rely on coarsely segmented regions, which are, however, insufficient for precise refinement. Additionally, standard supervised learning methods struggle due to a large gap between their basic scene understanding and detailed label information. Our novel approach addresses these challenges by developing hyperspectral segmentation models with the aid of refined labels and by seamlessly integrating learning tasks with partial label inference. Our method demonstrates superior performance on external evaluation benchmarks, surpassing state-of-the-art benchmarks by a substantial margin. Moreover, we introduce HS, a cutting-edge hyperspectral segmentation dataset, featuring higher-resolution images and more precise segmentations. In object categorization tasks using recurrent neural networks (RNNs), auxiliary variables can facilitate training and enhance performance. However, their influence on task outcome is unclear, and it's presumed their effect diminishes over task progression. This assumption is contradicted by our findings, which indicate auxiliary variables continue to be necessary for optimal performance in early task stages. Moreover, their importance is not always consistent and can vary between different auxiliary variables. We discovered that variables with strong task-relevant features should be incorporated into the final classification model, whereas those primarily contributing early task information can be omitted. By incorporating an optimal ratio of auxiliary variables to task-specific variables, networks can achieve improved classification accuracy. Specifically, our experiments on MiniImagenet, CUB200-2011, and Stanford Online Product Sales datasets led to enhanced performance after fine-tuning on the reduced datasets using fewer auxiliary variables. We also analyzed the effective variables at different training epochs. Additionally, our method allowed the efficient removal of unnecessary variables from complex RNN architectures, resulting in a more streamlined and optimized model. We validated the efficacy of our proposed variable selection method through ablation studies and comparative analysis with existing approaches. As a result, our model consistently outperformed alternative strategies, including selecting variables solely based on their performance in a fixed auxiliary variable range or choosing the minimal set of variables necessary for task completion. We observed improved generalization performance from our model, along with reduced expression variance compared to the baseline models. The code for our proposed method is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ashishp19/RNN-Optimization.git. Additionally, the minimized models have been integrated into the DeepMinion framework https://github.com/ashishp19/DeepMinion.git. Our investigation offers a new perspective on the role of auxiliary variables in RNN performance, shedding light on their continued influence across various task progression stages. Moreover, our method provides a novel approach to selecting optimal variables for enhanced accuracy in a range of applications. To our knowledge, our analysis is the first to delve into the auxiliary variables' impact at distinct stages of RNN training, making our method uniquely effective in various tasks. Importantly, our model exhibits improved generalization and accuracy compared to existing models in multiple datasets. As a result of our research, the optimal model achieved state-of-the-art performance on MiniImagenet and CUB200-2011 datasets and comparable performance on Stanford Online Product Sales. Our analysis indicates auxiliary variables continue to influence RNN performance throughout training and can be efficiently minimized to reach enhanced accuracy

A novel interpolation formula based on positive definite radial basis functions with exponential decay ensures the preservation of convexity and monotonicity properties, even in higher dimensions. By integrating this method with the difference quotient operator, we obtain a continuous quasi-interpolation scheme that maintains convexity and monotonicity while ensuring continuous first and second derivatives. Theoretical estimates of error norms are provided along with an empirical study validating these findings. The proposed solver exhibits more precise error results compared to existing solvers in dimension $d=2$, and its error norms in $L^\infty$ and $W^{1,\infty}$ spaces converge at the rate $h^{1+\alpha/2}$ in $d=3$. The numerical experiments fully support these error estimates. The solver outperforms other solvers in terms of precision, especially in solving the two-dimensional modified Poisson problem with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Pulsar halos hold great potential in exploring the cosmic positron excess and the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess. As a source of high-energy gamma rays, these halos are crucial in understanding the galactic gamma-ray background. Current gamma-ray telescope data are insufficient to pinpoint pulsar halos, and additional information is required to confirm their existence. Since gamma rays and positrons share a common origin, searching for positrons in these halos could help identify their associated gamma-ray sources. Although current Cherenkov telescopes have limited sensitivity, future experiments like the Cherenkov telescope array are expected to provide positron and gamma-ray rate observations of pulsar halos. As a precursor, this investigation involves examining the feasibility and capabilities of detecting pulsar halos with the large area giant air Cherenkov array (LAGETA), a proposed ground-based array of optical telescopes, and exploring its potential in exposing these halos through positional and morphological analysis of gamma-ray and positron data. Using a position reconstruction simulation based on the LAGETA design, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining data from air Cherenkov and e+ e- tracks in identifying pulsar halos. The results reveal that observing these halos becomes possible when the LAGETA observes more than 100 photoelectrons, and incorporating positron data increases their detectability. The LAGETA's capability to detect these halos will depend on its observed solid angle, and if it operates at the full expected sensitivity of 10 deg^-1, it should be able to identify 8 of the 16 pulsar halos in the galactic plane. The difficulty in distinguishing pulsar halos suggests that confirming their existence will likely require simultaneous gamma-ray and positron data or information from other potential gamma-ray sources within a 5 deg radius. The analysis also shows that these halos are distinguishable from nearby supernova-remnant halos when the LAGETA observes more than 260 photoelectrons and includes positron data. The LAGETA's potential in exposing these halos provides a meaningful test of both the LAGETA technology and the Cherenkov telescope array's capabilities. The latter's potential in shedding light on these halos could serve as a crucial precursor to its main application in studying dark matter. The combined gamma-ray and positron data from the LAGETA LHC will offer a meaningful test of both the LAGETA technology and the CTArray capabilities, and the CTArray's potential in illuminating these halos

Recent advancements in Deep Learning have significantly impacted the analysis and processing of multi-spectral satellite images. Nevertheless, employing additional storage and computational resources are required to analyze large datasets due to the large size of convolutional neural networks and the storage needs of multi-spectral images. In this work, we explore the potential of improving convolutional neural networks through the use of data augmentation methods that utilize super pixel delimiting masks to reduce both computational and storage requirements. The findings indicate that using this method can enhance the performance of convolutional neural networks while also decreasing their size and memory needs. Furthermore, the analysis reveals connections between the performance gains and the characteristics of the visual features extracted by the networks. Although climate change is a pressing issue, research on the topic has been in decline since the late 2000s among economists and a broader range of science journals.  Our analysis reveals a unique pattern, as recent research by scientists and a few specialized economists continues to thrive, while other economists' interest wanes.  One potential factor contributing to this disparity is the shifting focus of climate change research among economists from theoretical to policy-based.  Another contributing factor might be the intense policy-related work undertaken by leading climate economists.  Our findings also show that policymakers remain highly engaged with climate change research, as evidenced by a significant increase in their published work on the subject since the late 2000s.  Nonetheless, the amount of climate change research completed by policymakers remains relatively low when compared to their total number of completed research projects.  Our analysis further demonstrates that climate change is a niche area of study for most policymakers, as the majority of their research is devoted to other topics.  Our quantitative results were generated through a pair of large datasets containing the total number of research projects completed by economists and those of policymakers, as well as their respective publication records spanning from 2000-2015, as recorded by the RePEc database.  Our analysis utilizes ratio-based techniques and an econometric panel design to address potential issues of bias and missing data.  One potential limitation of our study is the reliance on researchers' recorded output, as recorded output may not perfectly reflect the actual quantity of research completed.  Another potential limitation stems from our reliance on the RePEc dataset, as our findings may not be generalizable to researchers not registered on the platform.  Nonetheless, the RePEc dataset remains the most comprehensive collection of researchers' published and unpublished work globally.  One potential area for further research generated by our quantitative results is the investigation into the reasons behind the observed decline in climate change research among economists since the late 2000s, as our analysis reveals a unique pattern unique to this field of study. The emerging field of soft robotics holds great promise due to its potential to create flexible robotic platforms. To date, control of these systems has been constrained by performance issues. Notably, current control strategies are concerned primarily with achieving static stability, but they often fall short of enabling dynamic mobility. To address this limitation, we employ the concept of the Koopman operator from control theory to develop a novel control method for active soft links. Our approach leverages the properties of singular values and their rates of change to generate dynamic trajectories, ensuring both safety and feasibility. By incorporating real-time boundary detection via flow visualization, we extend the application of this method to planar motion. Ultimately, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through successful simulations of various maneuvers. Compared to static stability controls, our method enables the collection of a 35% increase in "energy points," representing a greater degree of dynamic control. Our research thus far poses the following question: Can we utilize the spectral properties of the Koopman operator to establish a theoretical connection between control effectiveness and the topology of control surfaces? This potential connection motivates additional investigation, as illustrated through preliminary studies involving simple geometric forms. Our analysis suggests that the spectral characteristics of the Koopman operator may serve as a critical link between the global properties of control systems and the local characteristics of control strategies. If this hypothesis holds, it could enable the design of control systems that are sensitive to spectral properties, as well as the development of novel metrics for evaluating control surface effectiveness. To test this theory, we plan to apply our method to a range of active soft links, as well as to explore its extension to more complex systems, such as articulated soft manipulators. Conversely, we may also discover instances where the Koopman operator's spectral characteristics fail to capture control effectiveness, as is possible with systems featuring singularities or high nonlinearity. To address this possibility, we will need to refine our understanding of the relationship between the spectral properties of the Koopman operator and the control properties of active soft links. This revised hypothesis will serve as our primary guide for future research, as we strive to create a practical control method that is both safe and effective, as well as to clarify the theoretical connection between the Koopman operator and control mobility. Our research has the potential to make two major contributions: First, we may be able to utilize the spectral properties of the Koopman operator to develop a groundbreaking control method for active soft links, as well as to extend its application to planar motion through real-time boundary detection.

This work presents a lightweight version of a pre-trained SerNet, called Lite-ProSENet, designed for survival time analysis. The Lite-ProSENet is an adaptation of the original ProSENet, which outperformed other state-of-the-art methods in lung cancer prognosis. The Lite-ProSENet reduces the computational complexity and memory requirements of the original model, while maintaining its predictive capabilities. The Lite-ProSENet was tested on datasets from the International Cancer Genome Consortium and the Kaplan-Hale dataset, and achieved accuracy and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve results comparable to the original model and other state-of-the-art methods. Notably, the Lite-ProSENet was trained on a Tesla P100 GPU with 16GB of memory, while the original model required a Tesla V100 GPU with 16GB of memory or multiple P100 GPUs in parallel. The Lite-ProSENet is therefore suitable for survival time analysis on modern NVIDIA V100 and T1000 architectures, which were previously unable to support the original model due to memory constraints. To achieve a higher level of flexibility in learning, it's crucial to derive meanings from inputs that are straightforward and easily understandable from a linguistic perspective. This study investigates the potential of Self-supervised Learning in grasping these interpretable representations by exploring its capacity to extract features that are vital for various natural language tasks. Our focus is on Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) video descriptions as the basis for our research, and we examine whether Self-supervised Learning can yield linguistically meaningful outcomes. Our results demonstrate that features derived from this method hold great potential in capturing word meanings, as these features closely relate to the words used in the descriptions. Moreover, when integrated into a BERT-based language model, they enhance its ability to forecast next words in a sentence, as well as provide crucial insights for zero-shot sentiment analysis. To achieve more effective outcomes, we propose ModulfiLL, an innovative framework that combines the strengths of Self-supervised Learning and supervised learning to generate interpretable representations. Our findings also highlight the substantial advancements achieved when utilizing the resulting features in video-based NLP applications. We also explore consequences for irreducible admissible U(𝕙)-modules and provide a determination of when U(𝕙)-free modules are isomorphic to Verma modules. These findings are then applied to U(𝕙)-free modules of specific types, including those generated by a highest weight element and a lowest weight element, as well as those generated by a highest weight element and a nilpotent element. We further extend our analysis to Borel subalgebras and obtain results on irreducible highest weight modules for a Borel subalgebra. We also address limitations of these methods and propose alternative approaches. Additionally, we address open questions regarding direct sums of irreducible U(𝕙)-free modules and provide a partial solution. Finally, we provide additional context and relate our results to existing literature on Kac-Moody algebras and Lie superalgebras.

The role of specification in role-guided dialogue systems has received little attention despite its potential to impact the world dialogues. This study investigates how role specifications affect natural dialogue conversations and whether a pre-trained universal adapter can enhance a target task's performance. Role specifications were found to significantly influence the dialogue system's performance, with the universal adapter achieving impressive results. Moreover, the analysis shows that the adapter's performance is largely determined by a limited number of key tokens. Based on these findings, a novel framework, BASTARD, was proposed to explore and analyze how role specifications impact the dialogue system's responses. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of BASTARD in revealing the adapter's underlying logic and its ability to expand the scope of role specifications beyond the ones studied. Overall, the proposed approach paves the way for deeper comprehension of the adapter's behavior and may be applied to other downstream tasks. In text completion tasks such as word suggestion, models often face a challenge when encountering unknown words. To overcome this issue, recent approaches combine semantic and syntactic methods, but tend to emphasize one over the other depending on the input word, ignoring the interdependence of both in word completion. This has led to the development of hybrid models that integrate both mechanisms, including our proposed HYSOG. In this study, the performance of HYSOG was tested alongside other models in a Persian word completion system, using datasets consisting of word pairs and triples. The results revealed that HYSOG surpassed other models by consistently increasing their accuracy. In addition, the implementation of HYSOG demonstrated the benefits of combining semantic and syntactic features in word completion tasks. The outcome also validated the importance of considering morphological analyses in word completion systems. The proposed model has been successfully integrated into a commercial Persian word completion system, where its efficacy has been verified through user feedback. Current attention-based recommendation methods prioritize item attention over user attention, resulting in subpar performance. To address this limitation, we introduce a new prototype-based attention network that enhances user representation with attention mechanisms. To do so, we define user-related attention modules that aggregate and highlight relevant item features based on similarity scores. We combine these modules with existing item attention networks to produce output. Notably, we leverage prototype learning to refine item features, yielding improved results. Experimental evaluations on multiple public datasets yield favorable outcomes, affirming the efficacy of our proposed approach. Our source code is available at https://github.com/shivaaari/PAAN. We introduce a mesh adaptation technique grounded in the conforming Delaunay tetrahedralization framework to simulate single-phase flow through a porous medium with a small number of large cracks. This method produces a mesh that closely aligns with the cracks and their connections, the boundary of the domain, and any additional defined boundaries. The technique also optimizes the mesh according to a specific error indicator, refining it in the areas that need the most correction. The use of a mesh influenced by fluxes also enables the computation of accurate gradients outside of the cracks, thus avoiding an abrupt discontinuity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a test case where a mixed fluid is flowing through a porous Fracture, comparing the errors in several metrics such as pressure, velocity, and material property calculations. The result shows that our mesh adaptation technique can lower the error by a factor of ten, also increasing the convergence rate from O(n^-0.5) to O(n^-1), where n represents the number of grid elements. Furthermore, the test case yields precise convergence values to within two percent of the expected value. Additional analysis reveals that the convergence rate is largely determined by the mesh quality rather than the error indicator. Finally, the test case shows that the flux-based approximation is accurate to a degree comparable to the exact solution, with an absolute error of less than three percent outside of the cracks. This research centers around forming drone swarms through a communication system with a ground control center, connecting to each unit through a single control channel and multiple information exchange channels. Each drone within the swarm has a predetermined weight, aiming to minimize the average deviation from the center point by adjusting the swarm's shape and size, resulting in improved overall performance. To achieve this, the problem is broken down into two components: optimizing the swarm's structure and locating the center point. For the first aspect, the weight of an optimal path between two points in a graph is calculated, leading to a closed-form solution that can be efficiently implemented in polynomial time. For the second aspect, the center point is determined by calculating the average position of a set of points, weighted according to their individual weights. All operations are accomplished in constant time. These findings provide the basis for developing efficient algorithms to form swarm configurations, including determining the minimum number of drones to place within a specified bounded area and developing a distributed algorithm for creating and maintaining a uniform shape in a swarm. The complexity of these problems is analyzed and solutions are proposed, including one method that can be executed in near-linear time. Additionally, the effectiveness of these algorithms in reducing the average distance between drones and the minimum number of drones required to achieve a specific density within a specified area are investigated, using the SWIM meta-heuristic algorithm as a reference. It is shown that executing a linear search twice can achieve the same level of efficiency, using significantly fewer resources. Furthermore, the concepts and complexity analysis are generalized to apply to any set of points with associated weights. Lastly, the potential for applying the developed algorithms to other areas, such as robotics and tunable optics, is explored. It is suggested that these algorithms could be adapted for use in shaping and controlling arrays of optical devices by adjusting their positions. Similarly, these algorithms may also find application in controlling and shaping swarms of robots. It is assumed that the same set of challenges exists in this field. Lastly, the output of this research may also be applied to the domain of astronomy, where the movement and configuration of celestial bodies over time can be analyzed and related to their weights. It is suggested that this topic warrants further investigation to determine the underlying principles at play.

The study of eigenvalue problems for the Dirac operator presents intricate mathematical challenges. Researchers have found that certain aspects of Dirac eigenvalue problems can be linked to Heun's equation, a third-order differential equation with non-rational singularities, as well as to eigenvalue problems for tridiagonal operators. This paper explores specific solutions to Heun's equation in the complex plane, focusing on the case where the coefficients are real. It appears that this special case has not been thoroughly investigated. To generate the solutions, the authors use a novel approach based on the symmetry of the relevant operator with respect to a permutation matrix. This method allows them to correlate the solutions with the eigenvalues of a related finite tridiagonal matrix. By employing standard finite element techniques, the authors can approximate the solutions to the Dirac operator in large domains. Notably, the solutions exhibit a form of "continuous" band structure. To test the approach, the authors apply it to simple domain shapes, such as a sphere and a cylinder, and compare the results with exact solutions for these domains. Finally, the authors discuss potential applications of the method to theoretical physics and list several relevant problems. DB3 uses an advocate approach to perform black-box knowledge distillation. In this method, a decision-maker chooses the most similar probe model to the target model based on their prediction outputs, essentially closing the gap between the two. Traditional knowledge distillation relies on the model's intermediate information, whereas DB3 focuses solely on its decision, offering a distinct and more challenging test of distillation effectiveness. By eliminating the need for model inspection, DB3 also avoids modifying the target model, making it a more authentic black-box process. Our experiments examine the pros and cons of various advantages associated with DB3. Notably, a key benefit arises when the advocate model is trained on data not used to train the target model, indicating DB3 can facilitate knowledge distillation across domains. Moreover, DB3 demonstrates success even when the advocate model is trained on task parameters differing from the target model's task, indicating a certain level of task generalization. Our findings suggest DB3 produces results at least as good as traditional knowledge distillation methods, often leading to better results, and show that distillation effectiveness increases with the advocate model's accuracy. This research aims to understand and explain rationally related varieties, particularly focusing on hypersurfaces as a specific case study. By leveraging the properties of resolution of singularities, we arrive at a theorem that describes the rational connections of hypersurfaces in mixed characteristic and provides a characterization of k-rationality in terms of the eigenvalues of the Newton polyhedron. Furthermore, this result helps clarify the explicit k-rationality condition for certain group schemes and contributes to understanding the rationality of algebraic torus extensions, generalizing K-Rationality Theorems in the process. Additionally, this work explores the relationship between rationally related varieties and the geometric properties of the deformation space of smooth hypersurfaces, demonstrating that rationally related varieties form an open subset of the deformation space that is independent of the ground field. Using toric geometry, we are able to compute the explicit definition of rationally related varieties in terms of the combinatorics of the underlying polyhedron, thereby generalizing the results of Tsai to include all of dimension 3 hypersurfaces. This project aims to create a mathematical framework for representing complex mathematical expressions derived from Feynman integrands in multi-loop computations, and to utilize this framework to develop algorithms for extracting and generalizing mathematical principles from one loop topology to another. The initial stage of our work involves proposing a novel way to describe Feynman integrands using the concept of causal functions, which enables us to define and study the mathematical properties of the symmetry group actions on these integrands. Furthermore, we outline an approach to representing Feynman integrands in terms of master integrands within the context of this formalism, and demonstrate the method through a specific computation involving a simple two-loop diagram. The mathematical formalism we presented can be found at https://gitlab.com/looppoetry/looppoetry/-/tree/causal-functions. A related video explanation is available on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mttT1egnOoY. The underlying code can also be accessed on the Loop Poetry GitLab platform at https://git.looppoetry.org/looppoetry/looppoetry/-/tree/master/README.md. In the near future, we plan to extend the causal representation to include additional mathematical components, such as gamma matrix structures, and to apply the formalism to the evaluation of multi-loop Feynman integrals. The goal is then to use this representation to automate causal phase space integrals and thus contribute to the development of automated multi-loop integration algorithms. Ultimately, the expectation is that this framework will facilitate the generation of mathematical principles from loop topologies and enable the production of symbolic results in the future. In that context, the formalism could also be used for causal numerics by reversing the process. The formalism we presented aims to be causal, algebraic and homotopy invariant. The presentation is organized in the following manner: in Section 1, we introduce the proposed causal representation of Feynman integrands; in Section 2, we outline the approach to representing symmetry group actions on these integrands; in Section 3, we show an approach to representing Feynman integrands in terms of master integrands within the context of this formalism; and in Section 4, we apply the formalism to a specific computation involving a two-loop diagram. Additional details can be found in the supplementary materials provided at https://gitlab.com/looppoetry/looppoetry/-/tree/experimental-results. The experimental results can also be accessed at https://gitlab.com/looppoetry

This article investigates several novel aspects of related functions in the context of continuous-time quantum walks on graph domains. Specifically, it's found that the quantum walk Green function, the positive Green function, and the inverse of the graph's Ahlfors-regular conformal structure all share a common pattern of immersion within the graph's quantum walk Laplacian. Convolving this quantum walk Green function with any positive Green function yields the positive Green function at a given scale, proving a previously conjectured relationship. Furthermore, this quantum walk Green function is shown to conform to a certain structure at small scales, characterizing its embedding within the graph's quantum walk Laplacian. In addition, this article establishes a novel phase singularity for the quantum walk Green function's negative phase at small scales, corresponding to the graph being Ahlfors-regular. When the graph is non-Ahlfors-regular, a different positive phase is dominant; otherwise, both phases are present. Finally, this article explores negative phases within the graph's quantum walk Green function, including a previously unknown positive Green function, known as the hyperbolic Green function, which only exists on non-Ahlfors-regular domains and exhibits distinct phase properties. Notably, this hyperbolic Green function phase negatively corresponds to the graph's Ahlfors-regular conformal structure. To validate these claims, this article provides concrete examples of domain characters that fit these criteria. These character traits are then applied and extended to the context of group boundaries and random walks. Ultimately, this article contributes to our understanding of quantum walks on graph domains, including the specification of domain characters based on the graph's Ahlfors-regular new character. These theorems provide novel insights into the domain characters of quantum walks. Moreover, this article reveals the domain characters of positive Green functions and the graph's Ahlfors-regular new character to be equivalent. This equivalence is then applied to the context of group boundaries and random walks. These random walks on group boundaries are found to possess positive Green functions characterized by group characters and phase patterns dependent on the group's infinity rank and projective irreducibility. These theorems provide novel insights into the domain characters of random walks on group boundaries. Moreover, this article shows that the domain characters of quantum walks and random walks are related through a non-trivial mapping. By employing a reliable equation of state (EOS) for pure kappa matter, we determine the mass and radius of stars containing various numbers of kappa and strange quarks. The research focuses on stars weighing up to two solar masses, with results showing that hybrid stars containing kappa and strange quarks can have greater masses than those composed solely of strange quarks. Additionally, we investigate the tidal deformability of hybrid stars and find that their properties are influenced significantly by the EOS of pure kappa matter. Furthermore, we utilize the GW170817 pulsar merger event as a reference, with our findings indicating that hybrid stars containing kappa and strange quarks are feasible. The study ultimately underscores the importance of knowing the EOS for pure kappa matter in order to make precise predictions about hybrid stars containing this phase. \\

At room temperature, the material LaAlSiO4 with a thickness of sub-nanometer exhibits a distinctive metal-to-insulator transition, making it an ideal example. This transition arises from atomic-scale disorder and results in a thickening of the electronic density due to the introduction of excess electrons. By manipulating the amount of disorder, the electrical behavior can be altered; in LaAlSiO4, this involves varying electron density while keeping the structure essentially unchanged. This unique property allows for precise control over electrical properties, aligning with the concept of prototypical characteristics. This research investigates the changes that occur at the interface of LaAlSiO4 when it's in contact with a thin layer of an identical material, altered to induce a permanent state of insolation. Utilizing advanced surface analysis tools, the study discovers that the interface exhibits a distinct electronic signature, resembling a high concentration of mobile ions. This reveals the presence of a thin layer (approximately one unit cell thick) with altered properties, caused by a permanent state of disorder. Although the insulating behavior is dominant, the interface still exhibits a mixture of insulating and metallic characteristics. This disorder causes a weakening of the interface's covalent bonds, resulting in a distortion of the electron cloud and a shift in the position of the interface's atomic structures. This permanent disorder results in a reduced electron cloud and a shift in the position of the interface's atomic structures, similar to the effects observed on LaAlSiO4 during a metal-to-insulator transition. Contrary to expectations, the interface's electronic behavior is not solely determined by the amount of disorder but rather the shape and distribution of the disorder, emphasizing the complexity of the system's electronic behavior. Additionally, the study discovers the presence of a thin layer (approximately two unit cells thick) with altered properties, affecting the interface's electronic behavior and characterized by a distinct electronic signature, resembling a reduced mobile ion concentration. This result requires further investigation to confirm the findings, highlighting the need for additional studies on the material's electronic behavior. This research reveals the intricate relationship between disorder and the material's electronic behavior, offering insights into the electronic properties of the interface and the LaAlSiO4 material. This knowledge can be utilized to explore other materials exhibiting similar characteristics, offering a comparison with the LaAlSiO4 interface and identifying areas for improvement in understanding the electronic properties of these materials. This approach allows the model to simultaneously minimize prediction errors and constraints on its capacity. We support our proposal with theoretical arguments and empirical evidence from experiments on image classification tasks. Our results indicate that the novel training method outperforms traditional techniques, particularly on datasets with limited data availability. We investigate the potential mechanisms underlying this improvement and explore the avenues for further research. Additionally, we develop a straightforward yet effective way to enhance the performance of existing models, such as the convolutional neural network (CNN) and the transformer. This method involves applying regularized training to the entire model architecture in a end-to-end manner. We conduct experiments on multiple datasets and find that the augmented training method enhances model performance, particularly when combined with the widely-used stochastic gradient variance reduction (SGDR) heuristic. Our research also examines the regularized training of models with convolutional and graph-structured data. We find that the regularized training can improve the performance of models working with image and graph-based data. We further investigate the effect of the regularized training on the convolutional neural networks by adapting it to the models with 2D and 3D data. Our analysis reveals that the regularized training can enhance the performance of the convolutional models predicting continuous outcomes. Our results indicate that the regularized training improves the performance of the convolutional models. Moreover, we analyze the effect of the regularized training on the convolutional models identifying the key features that drive their performance improvement. Our study demonstrates the broader applicability of the proposed training method across the deep learning models. The distribution of opportunities within a society often impacts individuals' future socioeconomic circumstances, affecting one generation's socioeconomic status and potentially influencing that of future generations. Due to the challenges and expenses associated with gathering data on intergenerational mobility, maintained opportunities, and their effects, existing research has largely relied on synthetic data and simulations. In contrast, this paper utilizes a unique natural experiment, taking advantage of Nigeria's post-civil war one-child-per-parent policy, to analyze opportunities and their long-term socioeconomic consequences in that country. Our findings indicate that parents living in areas affected by the war at a specific time had a disadvantage in providing opportunities for their children, a disadvantage that still exists today, even many years later. In addition, these opportunities exert significant influence on the socioeconomic status of subsequent generations. Our research also shows that the long-term effects of the war on opportunities are primarily driven by the widespread destruction of physical infrastructure it caused, as well as the resulting shift in the geographic distribution of able-bodied men. In contrast, the legacy of the conflict in terms of human life loss had no significant impact on the distribution of opportunities. In terms of economic productivity, we found that the destruction caused by the war reduced the country's long-term potential GDP by 30 to 40 percent, with these losses being predominantly concentrated in the north. Our study demonstrates the utility of natural experiments in providing precise quantitative estimates of the distribution of opportunities within a society as well as their long-term socioeconomic consequences, even in settings where data is not readily available. In addition, this research highlights the significance of identifying and controlling for confounding factors that may affect opportunities and their estimation. In natural experiments where the intervention factor has multiple observational states, utilizing instrumental variables techniques can help provide more accurate estimates of the distribution of opportunities by paring observations from similar environments and eliminating any remaining confounding factors that may remain. In natural experiments where the intervention factor has multiple observational states and utilizes observational data that may exhibit endogenous spatial patterns such as Nigeria presented in this study, in addition to leveraging the benefits of the "similar environments" paradigm offered by instrumental variables, further accuracy can be achieved by applying the "matching" technique to eliminate any remaining confounding factors that may remain. In natural experiments where the intervention factor has multiple observational states and utilizes observational data that may exhibit endogenous temporal patterns, in addition to leveraging the benefits of the "similar environments" paradigm offered by instrumental variables, further accuracy can be achieved by applying the "unit root tests combined with Difference-in-Differences time series analysis" to eliminate any remaining confounding

In solid mechanics research, a model's historical dependency is crucial for accurately predicting long-term behavior, like strain memory in plasticity. However, this history dependency is often difficult for the model to learn from past experiences, a challenge common in continual learning. Traditionally, recalibration or reinitialization techniques are used, but they either learn from related tasks by forgetting previous ones (recalibration) or start anew with forgotten knowledge (reinitialization). Neither approach utilizes past experiences effectively. 

In response, we've developed a novel continual learning method for simulating history-dependent material behavior in solid mechanics. Our method, called ECHO, emerges from findings in the neuropsychology domain. It's based on the hypothesis that the brain creates new connections between existing neurons in the hippocampus to store experiences, which are then forwarded to other brain regions. We've translated this process into a three-phase procedure: 

1. Experience extraction: Our model stores the key features of the past simulation in a specialized database, marking the initial'sensing' phase. 

2. Mapping to existing knowledge: It compares these extracted features with past simulations to select the most similar ones in the database. 

3. Updates based on past experiences: It adjusts the model accordingly by applying the lessons learned from these similar experiences, which have been accumulated in the past. 

We've tested ECHO on a representative example from the solid mechanics research community and found that it outperforms state-of-the-art techniques significantly. Our research has the potential to revolutionize the modeling of long-term behavior in solid mechanics research, a significant advancement in the field. Our code is available online for other researchers to use. 

In the near future, we plan to apply ECHO to various examples of history-dependent material behavior, such as shape memory alloys, crystalline solids, and materials with memory that behaves like a computer's memory. Our ultimate goal is for ECHO to become the new standard in the modeling of such materials. Our research will ultimately contribute to creating more accurate simulations of these materials, which in turn will speed up the development of new technologies, such as lighter airplanes and cars, and innovative sporting equipment. Optimizing motion planning for multi-limbed robots can be computationally challenging. We address this issue by introducing an efficient framework that works in tandem with a unified limbed system to fulfill task requirements in a specific environment. Our approach is composed of a multi-stage optimization protocol which synchronizes the movement of multiple limbs working in unison. This framework generates a set of joint trajectories that meet specific criteria including completion within a predetermined time and adherence to desired time-spaces. Furthermore, we reformulate the time-spaces as functions to enable the calculation of optimal joint angles for each associated time. This reformation enables us to utilize the cspace of joint angles as the primary variable in our optimization process. Our method is capable of producing realistic and collision-free joint trajectories for a multi-limbed robot under various constraints. We validate the effectiveness of this framework through successful deployments on a Panda Panda robot with results that include the sequential manipulation of multiple objects, the growth of a flower in a vase, and the playing of a simple musical tune on a xylophone using eight automated motion trials. Our approach demonstrates considerable reductions in execution time in comparison to other relevant protocols. For example, optimizing a single joint using a direct method took approximately 0.35 seconds, while our optimized multi-limbed motion planning framework took around 0.13 seconds to produce eight correlated joint angles. We develop a framework to compare the effectiveness of different quantum processes in enhancing the value of a particular quantum property within a quantum circuit. This analysis employs the concept of relative quantum entanglement to measure the gain of a quantum resource within a quantum channel. By employing this approach, we identify trade-offs between the probabilities of achieving maximally resourceful states and the associated errors. Our findings demonstrate that the trade-offs can be expressed through measures derived from the quantum resource theory, such as min-entropy, and that these trade-offs are maintained even when the quantum processes are noisy. Our study also reveals conditions under which the trade-offs are preserved in the presence of incompatibility and non-trivial quantum correlations. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of our framework in the contexts of quantum information transmission and distillation. Additionally, we examine the distillation of quantum states under concurrent and sequential transformations, and show that the trade-offs can yield valuable insights into the optimal resource preservation capabilities of these transformations. Our work contributes to the broader field of quantum resource theory, and offers a useful tool for comparing the performance of different quantum processes in enhancing the value of a particular quantum property. Investigating the dynamics of a cup of coffee during car rides has inspired various studies in the field of applied physics. In this study, we explored the dependence of this phenomenon on the cup's orientation by simulating its movement. Our results reveal that the primary factors influencing the cup's behavior are the angle of the pivot and the distance from the pivot point from the cup's center. Additionally, we identified a unique frequency specific to the cup itself. However, this frequency is modulated by the pivot angle when considering the system as a whole. We also developed an analytical model capable of providing accurate predictions about the cup's behavior under different orientations using only two key parameters, thereby confirming our simulation findings. Importantly, our study demonstrates that the cup's instability is largely determined by the angle of the pivot, rather than the cup's design. As such, drivers can prevent spilling their coffee by keeping the cup held close to the pivot point, or by placing it near the center. Crucially, for cups with a center pivot, the cup's geometry no longer affects its behavior; it only matters when the pivot point is off-center. In the extreme case where the pivot is near one of the cup's edges, the cup's design takes on less importance, and the primary factor influencing spilling is the cup's asymmetry. In this scenario, the frequency specific to the cup itself disappears, and the system exhibits only one dominant frequency. As such, the challenge of preventing spilling is largely decoupled from the cup's design and instead depends on the driver's actions. Ultimately, our study highlights the value of combining theoretical and analytical models to address practical problems in the field of applied physics. The knowledge gained in this research may one day inspire the development of effective coffee spill prevention systems. In conclusion, our study contributes to the ongoing dialogue in this field while introducing novel analytical models. The techniques employed in this research can be applied across multiple domains, and our findings may be of interest to manufacturers designing coffee cups, researchers in the field of applied physics, and drivers seeking to safeguard their morning coffee. This research focuses on identifying and analyzing various resonances triggered by Solar Radiation Pressure (SRP) for objects in a specific astronomical context. We thoroughly examined the phenomena surrounding these SRP resonances, modeling their impact on key orbital elements such as eccentricity, inclination, and longitude of the ascending node. The study found that SRP-induced resonances result in significant variations among objects with similar semi-major axes, primarily due to changes in their orientation with respect to the Sun and the ecliptic plane. Additionally, we developed closed-form approximations for key SRP-driven orbital changes, including variations in eccentricity, inclination, and the ascending node, which will be crucial in understanding the SRP-driven evolution of various celestial systems over extended time periods. By incorporating the masses of the four giant planets, our findings also accounted for the effects of gravitational perturbations from these planets, maintaining analytical expressions for their influence on SRP resonances up to an accuracy of 5%. The analysis covered a range of celestial objects, including asteroids, trans-Neptunian objects, and other various objects. It is essential to consider SRP-induced orbital changes that can lead to objects shifting out of specific astronomical categories, such as the Hildas and the Scattered Disk, which have crucial implications for our understanding of the evolution of our Solar System. Furthermore, the research highlighted the need for correct identification and analysis of objects within these resonance phenomena to gain insights into the SRP-driven orbital changes in these objects. The study also points out the limitations of using simplified models, such as Alpha, in accurately determining the orbital changes for objects farther than approximately 55 AU from the Sun. The SRP-induced orbital changes observed in the study have extended implications for various resonances triggered by the SRP, which vary vastly in their impact on the orbital elements of the objects. This study explores the benefits and limitations of utilising prior information about a treatment's efficacy from related subgroups within a clinical trial. By incorporating a shared effect for multiple subgroups, the sample size can be significantly reduced. However, borrowing information between these groups may introduce bias if their definitions aren't solely based on objective factors. To address this issue, we propose a systematic approach to defining subgroups that minimises potential bias and allows optimal statistical analysis. Our method involves a unique subgroup identification process that relies on a multivariate partitioning method, ensuring the subgroups are defined solely by the trial data to avoid external influences. After determining the optimal subgroups, we employ a meta-analytic partial pooling technique to estimate the effects of the treatments. Our approach maintains the assumptions of having a shared treatment effect while allowing the variability between the subgroups to be estimated from their specific trial data. By doing so, we can accurately assess the treatment differences while accounting for potential biases. Our method is thoroughly validated through comprehensive simulations and applied to real-world data analysis in the healthcare industry. One such application involves analyzing the treatment outcomes for patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) across various demographic subgroups, using data from the SELENA-Da study. Our approach successfully identified optimal subgroups, provided reliable estimates of the treatment effect, and confirmed the presence of notable baseline covariate effects on the outcomes. Our analysis reveals a notable bias in the treatment effect when using the partial pooling method compared to classical frequency approach. Furthermore, we investigate the treatment effect modifications due to relevant covariates using a generalised partial pooling framework, which reveals interesting insights.
