The study focuses on the design of an adaptive motion control system to implement a string-based nonlinear invariance approach in a first-order arterial road model. By incorporating a variable scalar signal, known as a "string", along the road, the system aims to overcome obstacles posed by dynamic position-dependent systems that hinder accurate tracking performance. By utilizing two adaptive algorithms based on the internal model principle, the study successfully establishes a string-based nonlinear invariance approach that ensures asymptotic tracking of the scalar signal and string variable for any finite road length, as well as string-based invariance for any road condition. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed strategy in achieving robust string invariance and precise road length tracking. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of road length variations on tracking performance. The results show that a more accurate road length estimate leads to improved tracking performance, and a optimal gain setting can be achieved through accurate length estimation. The study also assesses the performance of the proposed strategy in tracking a constant road profile. The results show that the string profile remains constant with reduced variance, and the error in length estimation remains constant with reduced variance. The study observes that maintaining a constant road profile does not impact the tracking performance of the system. The study's adaptation algorithms are tested and verified through their stability and performance in tracking the road profile. The study's results show that the string-based nonlinear invariance approach provides a robust and effective strategy for implementing adaptive motion control in a first-order arterial road model with variable length. The study's findings indicate that the internal model principle can be used to develop tracking and inversion algorithms for complex dynamic systems with position-dependent dynamics. The study's results demonstrate the effectiveness of the string-based nonlinear invariance approach in tracking and inverting a first-order arterial road model with variable length. The study's research can be applied to develop intelligent transportation systems for effectively managing and adapting to road conditions. The study's results can also impact the development of adaptive motion control systems for road-following vehicles. The study's contributions primarily impact the fields of control theory and intelligent transportation systems. The study's outcomes benefit these fields by providing a practical solution to a complex control problem. The state of the art in control theory involves one-dimensional differential equations that govern the dynamics of a process or system. A significant challenge in control theory lies in adapting algorithms developed for position-dependent dynamics to be applicable to dynamics that vary with position. The study's research addresses this challenge by developing a strategy for adaptive motion control in a first-order arterial road model with variable length.

Action anticipation in videos has numerous real-world applications, such as helping robots navigate physical obstacles. Current methods focus solely on visual data from a video's current frame to anticipate the next frame. They do not utilize the video's sequential nature or the relationship between different frames. Our research introduces an action anticipation model that incorporates elements from the video, including the spatial relationships between objects, the temporal sequence, and the object movements. Lastly, we outline the feasibility of constructing $G_2$ instantons of higher multiplicity. Our analysis provides a detailed explanation of the $G_2$ instanton space through both local and global examinations. These studies offer a valuable comparison with the properties and behavior of $SU(3)$ instantons. The JUNO experiment is an underground neutrino-oscillation project that utilizes large liquid-scintillator detectors with time-of-flight capabilities. 

Its current design consists of 20 kt of highly pure active scintillator within which 20,000 photons per cm^2 can be detected, along with 1,744 photomultiplier tubes and 20 ton water-based R7081 quenching agent. 

By harnessing 2.5 ten to the power of 35 photons per cm^2 and an 40 ns time resolution, the experiment is capable of tracking neutrinos at an energy resolution of approximately 0.03 percent for 100 MeV reactions. 

In addition, a 7 dt QFAD design helps reduce intrinsic light within the scintillator and an 300 ton instrumented control mass allows for anti-neutrino detection in an six year duration. 

Its current construction has progressed to completion with electrical and mechanical installation, electrical and mechanical testing in progress, and related functional tests set to begin in Q4 2023, followed by initial data analysis in Q2 2024. 

In scientific research, the JUNO experiment primarily focuses on measuring $\theta_{23}$, measuring the mass splitting between two neutrino states and detecting solar $\nu_{e}$ appearance within 6 years, solar $\bar{\nu}_{e}$ appearance within 10 years, and astrophysical neutrinos within 20 years, as well as numerous additional sub-projects within its research scope.

The Informer model has recently demonstrated remarkable performance in large-scale multidimensional time series prediction tasks. However, its original ensemble strategy, although boosting results, fails to exploit the complex interdependencies between different dimensions effectively. In this research, we introduce an enhanced Informer model ensemble, featuring a new ensemble model called ME-Enformer, to tackle this issue. By incorporating an inter-dimensional transformer into the original ensemble framework, ME-Enformer increases the ensemble depth and broadens the dimension-wise correlation capture, leading to improved prediction accuracy across multiple dimensions. Experimental results showcase ME-Enformer's superiority over the state-of-the-art methods on real-world multidimensional time series prediction datasets. Moreover, the associated code and data can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/J-He/ME-Enformer. In addition, ME-Enformer has been implemented in the PyTorch framework and the related benchmark benchmark1 has been introduced. Both the benchmark and benchmark code are publicly available. In terms of performance, ME-Enformer consistently outperforms the benchmarked approaches, as shown in the benchmark results. Specifically, the comparison with benchmarked approaches yields relative improvements of 14%, 16%, and 21% in metric RMSE on datasets AirQuality, M4, and M4Small, respectively. Finally, the detailed analysis of the ensemble components and the parameter sensitivity of ME-Enformer have been provided. Specifically, the sensitivity evaluation with hyperparameters indicates an optimal learning rate of 0.01 and the number of ensemble components of 5 for the M4 dataset. Moreover, the ensemble component selection and corresponding correlation analysis show the potential for further research to optimize the ensemble strategies. The theoretical validity of enhancing the depth of the ensemble model has also been verified through the inter-dimensional correlation capture analysis. As a result, the proposed ME-Enformer model boasts enhanced capabilities in this domain. We introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), an ensemble-based model that iteratively refines its predictions by analyzing the output logits. By comparing and combining predicted logits from multiple classifiers, PILE generates updated logit inputs for an ensemble re-training process. This refinement method is applied to both training and evaluation data. The PILE framework is versatile and can be applied to various data sets, with our analysis focusing on its benefits on pairwise label data. Specifically, PILE shows improvement on triplet label data when used on the results derived from pairwise labels. PILE's code and data can be accessed through the GitHub repository: https://github.com/qmroll/PILE. Our experiments comprise three data sets - the Amazon dataset, a social network dataset, and a benchmark dataset from Wikipedia - to demonstrate the effectiveness of PILE in improving ensemble models. Our results indicate that PILE enhances both ensemble accuracy and its underlying model's ranking capability. With a focus on model scalability, PILE's scalability evaluation involves scaling up PILE's training data from 10% to 100% of the complete dataset, with our findings showing that PILE's relative improvement grows in line with the size of the dataset. Furthermore, the effects of varying the number of iterators and iterators intervals on PILE's performance were examined, with our analysis indicating that PILE achieves optimal improvement when using between 1 to 8 iterators. Specifically, using every 10th percentage of the data results in the most consistent enhancements. PILE's potential applications extend beyond predictive modeling, with its utility in data augmentation and active learning techniques also being explored. With ALE being a key area of interest, the analysis of PILE's label influence becomes particularly pertinent. When assessing PILE's label influence at various stages of its ensemble, our results indicate that PILE's predictive accuracy is often consistent across different stages. Consequently, the application of PILE to pairwise labels must be accompanied by an evaluation of its efficacy on triplet labels. These fluctuations could be perceived as variations in background light and are potentially measurable through sensing technologies. We are exploring the possibility of employing an array of quantum sensors to detect these fluctuations. By utilizing the principles of quantum estimation and considering the network's geographical distribution, we examine how network topology affects the recovery of the fluctuations' power spectrum. Our results demonstrate that cooperation among the sensors improves estimation, with the level of improvement relying on the sensors' positioning and their connections within the network. We have defined a set of parameters that determine the level of improvement and have established a relationship between these parameters and the benefits gained from quantum sensing. We have also established a fundamental limit for recovering the fluctuations' power spectrum and have determined the potential for achieving an order-of-magnitude improvement with networked sensors. These findings provide a framework for the evaluation of quantum-enabled telescopes that aim to detect dark matter through intensity fluctuations in the night sky. Under the condition that the matrix alpha's spectrum lies within the exclusive half-plane of a normal lozenicspace, we establish that the basis pursuit problem yields a solution that can be expressed as a rational function of b(b). The range of its denominators is determined by a constant, dependent on the problem's parameters, and the numerator's denominator either equals one or lies within the matrix's spectrum. This result is known in the case of basis pursuit with an invertible matrix, with the present study generalizing the outcome to basis pursuit with a matrix whose spectrum lies outside a closed half-plane. Furthermore, the study shows that the basis pursuit problem may yield solutions expressed as functions of b(b) only when the matrix alpha's spectrum includes a closed half-plane. The growing field of programmable switch research is reminiscent of the era when network engineers and researchers were able to freely develop and distribute custom router software. Unfortunately, current developments in programmable switches are hindered by a lack of accessible compiler backends, which is the primary obstacle preventing researchers from contributing to and building upon existing work. To address this limitation, this paper introduces PyBCP, a novel, open-source compiler backend for various switch platforms that is built on top of BCP, a renowned technology in programmable switches. By providing a comprehensive toolchain, PyBCP empowers researchers to create custom switch firmware, thereby fostering innovation through code sharing and collaborative testing. As evidence of its utility, this study showcases a successful implementation of PyBCP, which enabled the development of a switch firmware capable of 4BIT watermarking, a feature previously only available on traditional CPU-based platforms. PyBCP is now freely available online at https://github.com/PrincetonNLP/PyBCP.

This research explores a class of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods that exhibit explicit and concise formulations, even for multi-dimensional systems. These methods naturally extend traditional Runge-Kutta techniques and can be conceptualized as exact methods for Hamiltonian problems. A key innovation here involves adapting existing techniques for analyzing continuous-stage methods to evaluate their numerical stability in complex systems, specifically those with hidden oscillations. By applying these analyses, it can be determined that certain continuous-stage methods are capable of preserving the exact solution in certain contexts, such as when dealing with damped Hamiltonian problems. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that some continuous-stage methods are equivalent to combinations of traditional Runge-Kutta stages, enabling the derivation of concise order conditions that facilitate a more efficient approach to establishing stability in complex systems, even those with multiple hidden oscillations. Two specific continuous-stage methods are identified and their explicit formulations are proposed, including one method that is a continuous analogue of the DK4 method and another that is a continuous representation of the method suggested by Cohen and Hairer. The research also examines the numerical performance of these continuous-stage methods in solving a range of exact and imperfect problems. By comparing their performance to traditional Runge-Kutta methods, it is observed that they are capable of accurately solving problems in certain contexts, with the DK4 method, in particular, exhibiting excellent results in both precise and approximate applications. Furthermore, it is noted that some continuous-stage methods may not be efficient in solving problems that are not Hamiltonian but are formulated as such, potentially introducing artificial stiffness, and that their direct interpretation may not be possible in certain contexts with multiple hidden oscillations. As such, it is suggested that these continuous-stage methods be viewed as explicit, concise, and efficient solvers for Hamiltonian problems, with potential applications in a range of precise and approximate mathematical modeling contexts. By adopting a continuous-stage approach, it is argued that traditional Runge-Kutta methods can be enhanced, expanded, and sometimes re-interpreted in new and valuable ways. With the ability to directly analyze and interpret them as exact or efficient methods for solving complex mathematical problems, new and useful variants of these methods can be developed. In conclusion, the goal of this research is to promote the adoption of continuous-stage methods as efficient and precise solvers for a range of complex mathematical problems, and to utilize them as efficient methods for solving problems in various fields that involve Hamiltonian or nearly Hamiltonian structures, in order to promote their use in solving such problems. Modern convolutional and recurrent neural networks often benefit from being treated as infinitely wide networks.  While this property leads to favorable characteristics in terms of optimization and data representation, it presents a significant challenge for efficient training in resource-constrained settings.  To overcome this limitation, we develop a novel end-to-end training method that distributes parameter training locally to individual nodes in the network.  By doing so, each node adapts its connection weights independently, effectively creating a decentralized, distributed learning system.  We derive conditions under which decentralized learning converges to a global, optimal solution, thereby leading to improved classification performance in our tested applications.  Notably, the proposed approach exhibits increased efficiency and scalability compared to traditional, wide neural network training methods.  To demonstrate its practical value, we successfully applied decentralized learning to the development of efficient models for computing hand pose from image data and for classification tasks in the CIFAR-10 dataset.  Specifically, the resulting model required significantly fewer computational resources while achieving comparable classification accuracy to state-of-the-art models.  Moreover, the developed methodology is highly versatile and can be adapted to a range of neural network architectures and data sources.  We anticipate that decentralized learning will contribute to the development of efficient, widespread, and user-friendly AI technologies.  The associated code can be found at https://github.com/Princeton-VILAB/Decentralized-Neural-Networks. To differentiate the natural movement of biological entities from the movement of non-living objects, we propose a novel approach. This approach involves treating the data as a flow, calculating the Laplacian of the flow, and assessing the inverse of the Laplacian. The results of this method can effectively distinguish the natural movement of biological entities from the movement of non-living objects. In multimodal optimization, the objective function yields multiple optimal solutions, unlike multi-objective optimization, which has solutions with varying optimal outcomes. This research investigates how an ensemble of image processing techniques applied to a binary genetic algorithm affects the distribution of solutions in the fitness landscape in a complex dataset, specifically the Kusuzan dataset. The techniques include pixel intensity transformation and a correlation-based filter, which enhance the algorithm's fitness, discovering that applying these techniques either (1) shift the distribution towards better solutions without altering their diversity, (2) diversify solutions without improving their fitness, or (3) have no impact on either diversity or fitness. This exploration lays the groundwork for developing an optimized solution pipeline. Additionally, the study examines the effectiveness of our multi-objective approach in discovering robust solutions to a feature selection problem using the Ion Channel dataset, aiming to discover solution sets with diverse properties and levels of classification performance. The results show that our approach outperforms or matches the performance of SFS and NS on the Kusuzan dataset, while the NS and SBIO baselines on the Ion Channel dataset were superior to our method in some cases. Ultimately, the study suggests that multimodal optimization has the potential to improve solution diversity but may not necessarily enhance their fitness. Nonetheless, it's worth exploring this approach as an alternative to multi-objective optimization to discover robust solution sets with varied properties. The outcome of this research also lays the groundwork for our future work in developing an optimized solution pipeline through image processing techniques applied to genetic algorithms. To tackle the excessive computational complexity of global decoding for quantum error correction, we propose dividing the decoding process into multiple parts. By applying reinforcement learning to one of these parts, we aimed to enhance the overall efficiency. Specifically, we focused on decoding the surface code with bit-flip corruption only and restricted the code size to 7x7. We developed an environment where a neural network, trained using a policy gradient method, makes decisions about which clausal constraints to activate based on the readout metrics. This approach allows us to solve a complex problem in real-time. We also achieved a significant improvement in throughput when compared to a fully global decoding method. We anticipate this accelerated switching mechanism to be valuable for rapid and adaptable surface code protocols. 

After that, we expanded our method to include phase-flip corruption. We developed a way to represent the error circulant matrix as a set of commuting Pauli strings. This approach enables us to represent constraint activation decisions in terms of the strngs' overlaps with the error matrix. We trained a neural network to make these decisions using a quantum approximate metric embedding and achieved superior performance compared to a global decoding algorithm. We also discovered that the trained neural network's corrections to the error matrix were highly accurate. This led us to apply the neural network to scenarios with multiple types of corruption. The neural network successfully handled the switch from one type of corruption to another and performed well even when the types of corruption were very different. We also observed the improvements in decoding efficiency when the network was applied to larger code sizes. 

Finally, we explored the concept of local decisions and their products on the code boundaries. We analyzed their symmetry properties and represented them as a set of dominant descriptors. We applied this approach to 5x5 surface codes and observed the reduction in complexity. This facilitated the global decoding of 7x7 surface codes for the first time. We also applied this method to larger code sizes and achieved significant improvements in throughput. This could be very useful for rapid and adaptable surface code protocols in the medium noise regime. 

In conclusion, we successfully applied reinforcement learning to quantum error correction by accelerating the switching mechanism between decoding strategies. This succeeded in boosting efficiency. Furthermore, we discovered novel tools such as the quantum approximate metric embedding and the dominant descriptors that can be utilized in the medium noise regime. These resources are now available for public use.

The process of detecting exoplanets in ground-based telescopes is a complex task due to anisoplanaticity and system nonlinearities that make data analysis extremely challenging. Current advanced wavefront sensing methods employing high-order algorithms are limited to detecting small-scale aberrations and are ineffective against larger problems. Additionally, when applied to exoplanet detection, these methods fail to consider the absorption and scattering effects that occur in the atmosphere. Our research introduces a new approach, consisting of a hybrid detector system utilizing a genetic algorithm to eliminate atmospheric distortions and improve the detection of exoplanets and mock planets in a real-world scenario. Our results demonstrate that this method enhances the signal-to-noise ratio and mean squared error when compared to existing wavefront sensing techniques, even under adverse optical conditions. It is capable of identifying morphological features of larger-scale aberrations and removing noise, allowing for a clearer image of exoplanets and mock planets. Our study marks the first step in integrating a global optimization algorithm with a hybrid detector for this application, holding promise for future improvements in exoplanet detection and image restoration. Our code is available upon request. \\

We introduce a new stochastic local-stochastic-time (SLST) model for option pricing, combining GARCH-like stochastic vector spaces in space and time, and the M\'{e}le\'{e}d-Zambrano (MZ) model. This combination addresses the challenge of negative interest rates seen in the European Overnight Comprehensive Total Return Swap market. The combination is analyzed through the two-state SLST-MZ model, which incorporates correlated stochastic vector spaces. This approach yields a highly non-trivial partial differential equation (PDE) that's challenging to solve analytically. To overcome this, we adopt the state-space approach and utilize the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the SLST-MZ system to derive both an approximate PDE solution and a closed-form European option formula. This is achieved with minimal computational effort, making it efficient for real-time option pricing. Our method's accuracy is validated through put premiums calculated using the SLST-MZ model, compared to both the Black-Scholes model and the MZ model. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability of the SLST-MZ model to price options in both positive and negative interest rate environments. Finally, we highlight the benefits of the SLST-MZ model in terms of its applicability to various option pricing tasks. This includes calculating option prices for both call and put options, as well as pricing options based on both European and American exercising strategies. Due to its versatility, the SLST-MZ model has the potential to be applied in both equity and fixed-income markets. Specifically, its capabilities extend to pricing options in markets influenced by stocks, bonds, commodity prices, currency exchange rates, and even volatility itself. In effect, the SLST-MZ model offers a powerful tool for option pricing that addresses various market complexities and paradoxes, such as negative interest rates and the associated high volatility seen in markets influenced by volatility itself. In other words, the SLST-MZ model provides a valuable option pricing framework for markets in which volatility plays a key role. This is particularly true for markets involving options on derivatives (known as options on options), as well as markets affected by cross-currency effects and the early exercise of options. In fact, the SLST-MZ model offers a highly effective option pricing system that addresses the most challenging market conditions, including negative interest rates and the associated high volatility seen in markets such as the one for European Overnight Comprehensive Total Return Swaps. The DUNE Near Detector, situated within the FASER$\nu$ tunnel, would leverage its existing detector systems to capture neutrinos. However, its design as a WCMT-based detector may not be ideal for the ultimate goal of detecting light sterile neutrinos, given its substantial background of neutral currents. By reevaluating the detector's design, specifically through the addition of a high-frequency readout of the WCMT signals, we aim to enhance its capability to differentiate between neutrino modes and improve the detection of light sterile neutrinos. Moreover, combining this upgraded detector with the optimized design of the FASER$\nu$ target, characterized by a reduced width of 10 cm, we aim to minimize losses and maximize the overall detector performance. Consequently, this upgraded, optimized detector configuration is anticipated to yield significant reductions in the $L^2/E$ uncertainty and improvements in the $Q^2$ acceptance, ultimately facilitating the detection of light sterile neutrinos with higher statistical significance. Specifically, this upgraded, optimized detector configuration is anticipated to yield a $3\sigma$ statistical evidence in approximately one and one-half to two times the duration of the initial $10^{-3}~\mathrm{eV}^2$ sensitivity for a 1300 km long neutrino path length. Furthermore, this upgraded, optimized detector configuration is anticipated to offer a 2 to 4-fold increase in the $10^{-3}~\mathrm{eV}^2$ sensitivity compared to the present DUNE Near Detector design. Conversely, for the LHC Run 4, this upgraded, optimized detector configuration may not be sufficient to yield a $3\sigma$ statistical evidence for a $3\times 10^{-3}~\mathrm{eV}^2$ sensitivity level, but may still provide a useful prototype for the DUNE Near Detector and a valuable contribution to particle physics, specifically in the form of refined detector technology suitable for future use. By contrast, for the LHC Run 5 and beyond with a longer neutrino path length of 1300 cm, this upgraded, optimized detector configuration may offer a $3\sigma$ statistical evidence for a $3\times 10^{-4}~\mathrm{eV}^2$ sensitivity level. Furthermore, this upgraded, optimized detector configuration is anticipated to yield a $3\sigma$ statistical evidence for a $3\times 10^{-5}~\mathrm{eV}^2$ sensitivity level in cases of longer neutrino path lengths

We address the issue of cluster-robust quadratic least squares estimation in the context of linear regression with clustered data, particularly when sample sizes are small. A novel estimator has been developed and is shown to be more efficient than the standard cluster-robust estimator, especially in small sample scenarios. The proposed estimator also provides better confidence intervals and test statistics, which are more accurate in small sample contexts. The findings are supported by both theoretical and empirical analysis. The method has been implemented in an R package, rcqlr, which is available on CRAN. The package includes a range of functionalities, including point estimation, variance-covariance estimation, inference, and residual analysis. The rcqlr package is compatible with the lmerTest package and provides a cluster-level version of the lmer() function from the lme4 package. The package also offers a generalization of the LM_test() function from lmerTest for model diagnostics. The package can be utilized for both continuous and binary dependent variables. The package provides support for various types of clustering (e.g. block, time, space) and includes a utility function to visually inspect residual plots for assessment of model assumptions and the effectiveness of the estimator. The package is accessible through the following CRAN URL: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rcqlr/index.html. We developed the multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) to accelerate flow simulations around complex objects by utilizing particle interactions to update fluid velocities. This approach leverages the particle's influence over a extended period, reducing the number of updates required in the fluid simulation. We optimized MTSA using various particle placement methods and evaluated its performance across a range of flow scenarios. Compared to conventional methods, MTSA yielded a speedup of up to three times, striking a balance between simulation accuracy and computational expense. Furthermore, MTSA's output matched that of precise simulations with exceptional agreement, demonstrating the technique's potential to expand the scope of computationally demanding particle-laden flow simulations. This technology now enables the exploration of complex, multi-body dynamics in relevant applications such as fluid-structure interaction and locomotion analysis. We anticipate MTSA to be a valuable tool for the simulation-based design of biological and mechanical systems. We examine the dynamics of microscopically defined particle number and its connection to macroscopically defined number in the context of black holes. Our investigation centers on the process of Hawking evaporation, and we suggest that the method used to define the number involves a complex out-of-equilibrium process involving the creation and annihilation of quanta. We explore this idea through the application of thermal field theories and the calculation of particle number both before and after the process. The results reveal that the number calculated using microscopic and macroscopic definitions differs and involves the emission of particles, a finding that supports the theory of information loss in black holes. Additionally, we adjust the emission process to make it in accordance with unitarity, an approach known as 'information preservation'. We demonstrate that, even with this adjustment, the particle number calculated using the two definitions remains disparate. Nonetheless, we discover that the difference in particle number is vastly dominant compared to the total number emitted during the evaporation process, a finding that raises hopes for the recovery of information to be achieved through further emissions. Moreover, we show that the method used to define the number involves a delay of orders of magnitude. Lastly, we examine dual definitions of number in the context of stringy fuzzballs and observe that, for certain states, the calculated particle number matches the expected values. Nevertheless, the method used to calculate the number proves to be ineffectual for determining the entropy of the dual black holes. Conversely, the alternative approach yields the correct entropy but fails to determine the number. These findings suggest that the dual definition of number remains an unresolved issue. We intend to explore this problem in depth in the future. We also propose an innovative procedure that enables one to determine the density matrix by using the microscopic definition of number and applying it to the output states. We demonstrate the outcomes of utilizing this method in the context of holographic theories, an approach that may serve as an adaptable tool for various theoretical models. Lastly, we quickly examine two conventional techniques for defining the number and determine that they are ineffective in resolving the theoretical issues at hand. Conversely, the method suggested here proves to be more versatile and effective in yielding meaningful outcomes. Moreover, the method is found to be consistent with the theory of information preservation in all the scenarios examined. Conversely, the alternative approaches fail to achieve this consistency. We thus suggest utilizing the suggested method in future research in quantum field theory. Additionally, the method proves to be an innovative way of constructing thermodynamic phase diagrams, an advantage that will be utilized in the future theoretical models

The impact of the nuclear broadening on the $W$ boson transverse momentum distribution was investigated using theoretical models of the dipole-scalar interaction. These models include the QCD-inspired Humpoid and H1 models as well as a model derived from the D0 parametrization. The analysis involved measuring the influence of nuclear broadening on the $W$ boson $p_T$ distribution and predicting its effect on the normalized $W$ boson $p_T$ spectrum at the LHC using the respective models. The outcomes of the nuclear broadening models varied significantly: while the H1 model yielded an enhancement of about 20% for the $W$ boson $p_T$ distribution, the D0 model predicted an inhibition of roughly 15% and the Humpoid model exhibited the least nuclear impact, predicting a decrease of about 30% with the inclusion of nuclear effects. When compared with the standard perturbative QCD predictions without nuclear effects, the H1 model showed agreement with LHC data up to $p_T$ values of approximately 50 GeV, whereas the D0 model deviated from measurements for $p_T$ values exceeding 20 GeV. Despite nuclear phase space restrictions, the Humpoid model failed to effectively describe experimental findings, leading to the conclusion that the H1 model provided the most suitable representation of $W$ boson $p_T$ data influenced by nuclear broadening. Additionally, the H1 model was found to predict $W$ and $Z$ boson $p_T$ distributions that align with LHC measurements, whereas the D0 model predicted an opposing trend. We examine the dynamics of a liquid jet flowing through a channel filled with a less dense fluid than itself, which flows due to gravity. This study investigates how the presence of air incorporated within the fluids influences the process. Contrary to expectations, the presence of this incorporated air significantly alters the pulse period and amplitude in systems where air is present, revealing more intricate behavior. The air-filled state assumes a distinctive state we label as "rippled" that differs from the air-free case. The incorporated air reduces the minimum cross-sectional area within the channel and often transforms into discrete air pockets. In certain situations, the pulse frequency matches the hydrostatic velocity, leading to a coexistence of two distinct flow patterns: pulses and sinusoidal fluctuations. The air-filled states show increased instability compared to the air-free scenario, particularly at lower heights. We observe the emergence of sinusoidal fluctuations in both air-filled and air-free scenarios, which show similar characteristics despite differing pulse frequencies. As the system evolves, these fluctuations develop into unstable toroidal structures. The study highlights the significant impact of incorporated air on fluid dynamics and suggests that air incorporation should be considered in the design and operation of liquid flow management systems. This requirement is further exacerbated by the need for high availability and fault-tolerance in modern applications. We illustrate the efficacy of our approach by implementing a set of sequential and parallel benchmarks that demonstrate exceptional error-resistance and high performance, exceeding traditional locking methods while providing the added benefit of static analysis verifiability. This innovation enables the detection of faulty code at compile-time rather than run-time, thereby significantly reducing the impact of errors. Notably, our benchmark suite outperforms existing memory safety checks, offering a more efficient and error-tolerant alternative. This research lays the groundwork for a new class of algorithmic services aimed at protecting data integrity, paving the way for greater reliability in software architecture. We expect this research to open doors for further investigations into the algorithmic protection of persistent data, fostering innovations in data storage and management. We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a novel approach for inferring latent topics and information sources in complex networks. By analyzing a system's temporal dynamics from multiple angles, HDTM uncovers underlying themes and the relative importance of associated factors. This model possesses the capacity to identify hierarchical structures, allowing it to distinguish between multiple levels of abstraction within an information network. We apply HDTM to analysis of both terrorist organization publications and Twitter posts, comparing its output to that of alternative methods. Our findings indicate that HDTM provides a clear picture of the network's organizational and topical structure, offering a more detailed understanding than other approaches. Additionally, HDTM's ability to analyze systems at multiple scales enables the detection of latent patterns and sources. We demonstrate this capability by analyzing Twitter data, separated into different time intervals and characterized by distinct features. Our analysis reveals the underlying thought processes and information dissemination patterns among various entities within these networks. These entities range from individual users to larger groups such as news agencies and advocacy groups. The model is made available online at https://github.com/indigojelly/HDTM. A detailed tutorial can be found at https://hdtm-tutorial.readthedocs.io. HDTM is implemented in Python, with all code and supporting documents accessible at the above-mentioned locations. By analyzing a system's temporal dynamics from multiple angles, HDTM offers a more comprehensive understanding than alternative approaches. The model's output is particularly useful in information-intensive domains such as counter-terrorism analysis and social media research, where it provides a more detailed and layered understanding of complex systems. This understanding enables domain experts to make more informed decisions regarding topic identification, information source attribution, and related domain-specific applications. Model validation is carried out through a comparison of its output to that of competing models, in this case Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Hierarchical LDA (HDP). This work examines how three-body systems behave when subjected to overbound conditions, analyzing both their numerical simulation results and theoretical predictions. To initiate the three-body escape process, we randomly altered the potential in systems drawn from the thermodynamic ensemble. By comparing these findings with theoretical estimates based on the overbound distribution, our analysis focuses on escaping probabilities, distribution shapes, and other statistical properties. Interestingly, our numerical results closely match the theoretical predictions for all considered aspects, with the exception of a minor discrepancy in the distribution's tail. Our investigation explores the application of three-body systems as proxies for understanding the overbound universe, providing insights into the broader, more complex cosmological scenarios. Additionally, our analysis sheds light on the statistical nature of these systems, yielding valuable information for the wider scientific community. Furthermore, our work paves the way for a potential extension of this methodology to four- and five-body systems, aiming to gain deeper insights into more intricate astronomical phenomena. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute towards developing general-relativistic techniques for modeling gravitational systems, especially those observed in the universe's early stages. In continuous logic, a framework for studying general metric spaces through logic,  we demonstrate that equivalence relations within this context naturally correspond to closed subsets of the space of all possible equivalence relations, equipped with a continuous metric. Furthermore, we show that these equivalence relations form complete metric spaces in their own right.  We then establish that any complete metric space can be represented as a category of structures based on continuous metric space principles.  We conclude by illustrating that complete metric spaces according to the Scott topology are a specific instance of these equivalence relations.  We finally examine the relationship between continuous and first-order logic within this context.  Specifically, we show that any continuous formula is equivalent to a first-order equivalent, and that valid statements in continuous logic correspond to their first-order equivalents.  As an added consequence, we prove that any theory in continuous logic that is initially defined through continuous metric space principles is equivalent to its first-order counterpart.  Consequently, we conclude that compactness theorems established for first-order logic extend seamlessly to continuous and metric-geometric frameworks.  We further demonstrate that any consistent complete metric space in continuous logic corresponds to a model within its associated first-order counterpart.  These findings collectively yield Tarski-Grothendieck, Lowenheim-Skolem, and fundamental categoricity theorems.  Moreover, we show that continuous logic's notion of elementary equivalence generalizes that of first-order logic, thereby yielding additional foundational categoricity theorems.  Finally, we establish that any continuous formula or statement is equivalent to its first-order counterpart relative to any given model or metric space.  Consequently, our results in continuous logic are inherently pure and first-order.  In essence, we have achieved an extension of first-order logic to general metric spaces, achieving purity and first-order-ness through the adoption of continuous metrics. This research focuses on leveraging the capabilities of singular value decomposition to track modifications within software variations. It builds upon previous work from the RSV1 paper, improving the noise resilience and computational efficiency. Key advancements include the application of the DyCST algorithm, limited SVD components, and the utilization of the k-nearest neighbor approach for neighbor selection. Moreover, we introduce a novel metric to assess model clarity based on the ratio of retained and total singular values. Our findings are validated through an experiment using 797 distinct Java projects from the PyGFZ dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Specifically, the DyCST-GFZ method exhibits exceptional robustness against noise, comparable to state-of-the-art techniques, while also demonstrating improved computational speed up to three times. Furthermore, we identify models with high clarity rates when the top singular values dominate the others, indicating a smaller number of underlying features. Ultimately, this work suggests merging the RSV1 and GFZ approaches as a viable strategy for managing software variations. Although not all features are relevant, they can be ignored, and the remaining ones provide a clear understanding of the dynamics within the system. Conversely, these techniques can be utilized for feature selection in traditional software development, helping to eliminate non-relevant features and pinpointing the ones that are vital to system performance. As a proof of concept, we utilized the DyCST-GFZ method to analyze the GFZ dataset, highlighting the role of feature extraction in both variation management and software development. Our analysis suggests that the top three features encompassed by the first three singular values predominantly affect the system's dynamics. Specifically, the first singular value is linked to feature 1, the second to feature 2, and the third to the scaling of the other features. This groundbreaking finding opens up new avenues for research, and we plan to explore these new directions in the following sections. Additionally, our approach has far-reaching implications, and we envision its utilization in educational programs centered on variation management. By providing clear insights into the underlying system and its dynamics, the DyCST-GFZ method offers a powerful tool for understanding the impact of feature extraction on system performance. Deep sequential models have significant practical value, despite often struggling with temporal data that has varying pacing and durations. To address this challenge, we develop a novel deep RNN architecture, combining spatial and temporal attention mechanisms that adaptively sample and focus on input data for each hidden state update. By utilizing an external memory matrix and selective attention sampling, our proposed model can effectively handle long sequences with numerous variables. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world data reveal our method's effectiveness in resolving the long-term issues barrier. Additionally, we assess the interplay between spatial and temporal attention mechanisms through ablation tests. In general, finding distinct subset sums within a certain range is NP-hard, even when limiting ourselves to smaller subsets no larger than a fraction of the total set size. This issue arises frequently in big data applications where sets exceed two billion elements, necessitating an alternative approach proposed in this paper. It involves distributing the elements of a set into multiple smaller groups, each producing a distinct subset sum when filled to a certain capacity. To ensure this is possible, we develop an approximation algorithm that can handle large sets, including ones exceeding one trillion elements. This solution was validated through extensive testing on various large dataset examples. Additionally, we established a theoretical limit on the quality of this solution, showing it can be no more than twice the optimal limit. Notably, this algorithm can also efficiently calculate various useful metrics, such as the minimum and maximum subset sum within a given set. One of its advantages is real-time applicability to any set, whether balanced or unbalanced. Furthermore, we found that this problem shares similarities with a campanella problem variant, though it requires a distinct subset sum for every group size from one to n, where n is the total number of elements in the set. While a solution does exist for the special case of fixed group sizes, it does not apply to our scenario, where group sizes vary and are determined dynamically. Consequently, this algorithm represents a novel approach to solving the general subset sum distinctness problem. We therefore introduce a new term to describe this challenge: the dynamically sized distinct subset sum problem. We also investigated relationships between various special cases of this problem, including ones where subsets are limited to a specific size or when the sum of their elements is known to be less than or equal to a certain value. As an added benefit, we found that our algorithm can be modified to solve two related problems, including one where we seek the smallest subset that meets a given target sum and another where we seek the largest subset that meets a given target sum. Notably, these problems were previously thought to be incoherent. We therefore provide new terms to describe these challenges: the dynamically sized minimum subset sum problem and the dynamically sized maximum subset sum problem. We established an approximation algorithm for the first of these problems, one that can be no more than twice the optimal limit, though we were unable to find one for the second problem within the same bounds. We therefore conjecture that its intractability may stem from its relationship to a special campanella problem variant, where subsets have fixed sizes and sums, and we prove this theory.

This study investigates the estimation of a scalar parameter within a generalized linear model, where the dependent variable follows a specified distribution and the independent variable follows a Poisson distribution. We consider two distinct regression settings: one with a single independent variable, and the other with multiple interconnected variables. We analyze the properties of a weighted average of estimators obtained through least squares, and demonstrate under what conditions this weighted average achieves weak convergence. We also explore the relationship between this weighted average and a maximum likelihood estimator, and derive the distributional properties of the estimators in both the single variable and multiple variable cases. Ultimately, we employ simulation to assess the performance of these estimators, including their bias, mean squared error, and ability to accurately estimate parameters under various degrees of model specification. We also introduce a novel goodness of fit test to assess the assumed distribution, and employ simulations to evaluate the test's performance across different sample sizes and error distributions. The results of these simulations indicate that the test's power increases with both sample size and deviations from the assumed distribution, and that it is most effective in scenarios where the model is poorly specified with non-Poisson error. Conversely, the test's performance is diminished in scenarios where the model is well specified with Poisson error. Consequently, the test is deemed most useful as a diagnostic tool to identify potential issues of model specification and non-Poisson error, rather than as a standalone method for assessing goodness of fit. The analysis presented in this study is original, and represents an important extension of existing work on statistical estimation and modeling. The test for goodness of fit and estimation methods proposed herein are both simulable, with code available for reproduction and future use. In the context of mean field games, the existence of an equilibrium is proven for a specific class of dynamics with constraints that adhere to standard regularity conditions. It's established that imposing more stringent regularity requirements essentially introduces obstacles, hindering the existence of an equilibrium. The crucial aspect here involves the first-order approximation of a controlled differential equation with a constrained boundary condition, drawn from a set of dynamically regular functions. This approximation drives the state and control variables towards functions that are globally smooth, leveraging the regularity of the set in question. The key to this analysis lies in the development of a new approximation technique, applicable to controlled differential equations with dynamically regular constraints. This innovative approach can also be used to derive existence proofs for equilibrium solutions in both mean field game and optimal control frameworks. Furthermore, the provided mathematical analysis is substantiated through the introduction of a specific model that illustrates the significance of regularity requirements in determining the existence of an equilibrium. The model consists of a game involving drivers with regular paths and routes that are also regularly varied, impacting traffic congestion. The equilibrium solution in this model is represented by an association of equilibrium routes and speeds, with the regularity of the speeds being a direct consequence of the requirement for regular paths. The model is then further generalized to encompass situations where the regularity of routes is replaced by variations in lane positions, demonstrated through the example of a multi-lane circular road. The analysis ultimately reveals that constant speeds are the only equilibrium in this game. The previous findings are then substantiated through the presentation of numerical simulations verifying the existence of these equilibrium solutions. The close relationship between the approximate and precise methods is confirmed numerically, showing that the difference between them diminishes as the degree of the approximating polynomials increases. The convergence observed in the numerical experiments suggests that the approximate solutions have a natural connection with monotone convergence. The derivative of the approximate solution is shown to converge uniformly to the solution of a specific cell problem, which is a constant in this example. The application of a similar approach to a two-dimensional continuous flow mean field game on a grid road also yields conclusive results. To overcome this challenge, we developed FedBuff, a novel federated learning algorithm.  FedBuff is an adaptive, online, and data-driven method that enables the server to make informed decisions at each step by effectively utilizing the received batches. Gallium nitride's (GaN) practical limitations at room temperature are attributed to its poor hole mobility.  Investigating room-temperature hole mobility in GaN by matching its lattice with two binary nitrides, ZnGeN2 and MgSiN2, we discovered that this approach significantly boosts hole mobility while keeping GaN's crystal structure intact.  Utilizing first-principles calculations within the framework of the Boltzmann transport equation, we determined that room-temperature hole mobility in GaN can be realistically increased by at least one order of magnitude through this lattice-matching technique.  The underlying reason for this improvement is the comparable sizes of GaN's lattice-matching atoms to the GaN mobility-limiting impurities in ZnGeN2 and MgSiN2, which enables minimal disruption to the GaN electronic structure.  These findings offer a new pathway to enhance GaN's room-temperature hole mobility and thus overcome its limitations.  The principles underlying this discovery can also be applied to optimizing other II-IV and III-V semiconductor materials. Over the past 15 years, research into high dimensional expanders has been actively pursued, and a significant body of work has been developed, which we are attempting to summarize and provide a comprehensive framework for understanding this work through a set of connections and analogies.
High dimensional expanders have the potential to address several key challenges in theoretical computer science; for instance, they might facilitate the construction of robust quantum-proof cryptosystems or serve as building blocks for efficient data processing and computation in high dimensional spaces.

We begin by defining key concepts related to high dimensional expanders and examine their relationships with other fundamental concepts in harmonic analysis and combinatorial geometry.
By mapping these concepts onto group-theoretic definitions, we can simplify and understand the properties and applications of high dimensional expanders.
This framework allows us to break down complex research findings into more manageable areas, such as expanding Cayley graphs within approximately transitive spaces, and exploring the characteristics of high dimensional expanders with small doubling property.

Our analysis uncovers connections between the field of combinatorics and that of quantum computing, particularly in the context of operator space theory and quantum information.
By applying a quantum probing technique, we demonstrate that certain operator space properties can be derived from classical properties of high dimensional expanders, and we show the feasibility of this approach.

We further establish links between the field of harmonic analysis and the study of group representations, and explore the implications of nearly host-dependent sum-products theorems on the eigenvalues of random graphs.

Our work culminates in a future outlook section, where we identify unresolved questions and potential areas of study, such as investigating the properties of high dimensional expanders within specific subgroups of operator spaces, and understanding their connections to quantum complexity theory. Additionally, we propose the study of a new problem which involves combining results from the host-dependent sum-products theorems and invariable sets of bounded degree, and its potential implications in the context of quantum computing. Lastly, we propose another future study which involves applying the properties of high dimensional expanders to solve a long-standing open problem in operator space theory.

the potential of models to process untrained prompts. We suggest using distribution
calculus to assess the predictive capacity of large language models. Finally, we
note that prompt encoding is a learnable factor and can be optimized to reach the
full potential of large language models.

A new level of precision measurement technology has been achieved using Rydberg atoms coupled with advanced deep learning techniques, which have traditionally been limited by extreme sensitivity to noise. Unlike conventional systems, this method can efficiently handle noise by learning around it. Our research involves a series of deep learning approaches for a Rydberg atom-based angle measurement system, which extracts information about the direction of a spin polarized atom relative to a magnetic field. These models not only increase the accuracy of the measurement but also improve its resistance to noise and deteriorating factors. A comparison of our results with the standard approach shows a significant 250-fold decrease in the level of noise that affects the measurement, indicating a substantial improvement in the signal-to-Noise ratio (SNR). Furthermore, we demonstrate that a combination of neural networks trained on simulated data and experimental measurements can achieve comparable results, thereby validating the effectiveness of our approach. This innovation presents a new direction for dealing with noise in quantum metrology using machine learning techniques. Our research has the potential to open up new avenues in this field and could soon be applied in accurate time and frequency measurements, as well as in the detection of gravitational waves. Debugging data-driven applications has become a data scientist's perennial challenge,
as issues with data can lead to incorrect model predictions and lost revenue.
Current methods involve repetitive trials and data transformations to locate
the source of errors, yet they fail to adapt to an application's specific pattern
of data evolution.
Our solution, DataScope, adapts these methods to an application's changing data
by analyzing the relationships between data attributes and generating relevant questions.
By integrating DataScope with an application's API, we collect data samples and
compute attribute statistics, then use these statistics to detect outlying data and
generate questions based on the anomalies. Evaluation with 9 real-world datasets
shows that DataScope successfully identifies the cause of data errors over other
debugging strategies. Our tool has been implemented as a Python library, available
at \url{https://github.com/PrincetonUniversity/Datascope}. Our experiments can
be replicated at \url{https://princetonuniversity.github.io/Datascope-experiments/}.

Mn$_3$Sn and variants with additional elements in the 3d and 5d series exhibit unique magnetic properties, which can be comprehended through the concept of layer polarization by spatial periodic magnetic ordering. These materials transition from ferromagnetic monolayers to antiferromagnetic trimer layers with increasing element polarization, ultimately displaying intricate entanglements in their magnetic phases. By analyzing the impact of element polarization on the crystal electric field, we establish that certain materials develop a unique trimerization effect, influencing their magnetic ground states and introducing significant magnon band gaps. The element polarization's role in determining trimerizing pressure allows us to control the transition between different trimer arrangements through external pressure. These findings significantly broaden the scope of trimerization phenomena, encompassing both magnetic and structural manifestations, offering a new perspective on this phenomenon. Moreover, we predict the presence of novel trimer arrangements and of their magnon Dirac bands within Mn$_3$VSn and Mn$_3$IrSn. These materials can serve as exceptional magnon-based topological isolants when configured in A-type antiferromagnetic arrangements. Lastly, we outline the trimerization effect's potential to create unique quantum states in elementally diverse 3d-5d superlattices and magnetically coupled trimers. These superlattices can exhibit extraordinary spin-caloric effects and enable the creation of stable magnetization polarization with electrical heat current. Similarly, they can display an anomalous Nernst effect that defies the normal inverse proportionality between the Nernst coefficient and the magnetization. These unique trimerization effects are anticipated to yield rich physical phenomena in elements and their compounds, offering new opportunities for research and development.

Hypergraphs, being more flexible graph structures, fail to be well-defined in certain contexts, primarily due to the issues of (1) ambiguity when analyzing their projections, and (2) overfitting when lacking a suitable regularization framework. Focusing on the first concern, we establish certain conditions under which projections from hypergraphs to graphs are possible and explore the challenges of reconstructing the original hypergraph from its projection. In this context, we introduce notions of 'fertility' and 'luminosity' that determine the feasibility and uniqueness of the hypergraph's projection. Our results indicate that for a given hypergraph, uniqueness is not guaranteed but feasibility is; conversely, a group of hypergraphs can have the same projection but are not equivalent. This leads to the idea of'saturation' which measures the maximum number of unique hypergraphs that can have the same projection. We provide a general formula for the saturation number under specific conditions and also consider special cases, such as hypergraphs composed of two distinct subgraphs, for which we establish a formula depending on the fertility and luminosity values. Furthermore, we introduce a new class of hypergraphs, called 'clustered' hypergraphs, for which the reconstruction from its projection is possible and guaranteed, along with certain characteristics such as a bounded ratio of vertices to edges. Our research also delves into the computational aspects, presenting algorithms to determine the clustered and fertile status of a hypergraph based on its properties, such as a given threshold for the ratio of vertices to edges, as well as finding the smallest equitable partition of a graph in time O(n^{\omega}). Our findings are further illustrated through various examples that demonstrate our theoretical contributions. In addition to these outcomes, we propose a new framework of 'fertility' and 'luminosity' for graphs based on their clustering structure, leading to new concepts and investigations. Our research provides an innovative approach to analyzing graph data, offering novel tools for understanding graph projections and clustering, which can be applied in various practical domains. Our results open the door for further exploration of the relationship between clustering structures and the characteristics of graph embeddings, thereby contributing to graph data analysis. A key factor influencing free-electron laser (FEL) output is the chirp and tapering strategies. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of different tapering methods on ultrashort pulse generation in XUV and soft X-ray FELs. We discover that a combination of partial tapering and a specific type of chirp management can significantly enhance pulse energy and improve coherence, leading to even higher gains in coherence when implemented earlier in the accelerator. Notably, this strategy also optimizes electron beam parameters, making it more feasible to implement. When in exploration mode, both agents sample a state and choose an action to maximize mutual information.
When in regularization mode, the agents sample a state but choose an action that randomizes dependence on the state.
The technique takes advantage of the contrast between exploration and regularization to efficiently estimate the mutual information.

We introduce TextWorldExpress, a significant speed enhancement for the TextWorld challenge. TextWorld is a benchmark that evaluates agents' ability to perform well in text-based game environments. The challenge, which incorporates 708 levels across eight games, has typically been solved using extensive search strategies due to the sheer size of its state space. TextWorldExpress, however, streamlines the simulation process, reducing throughput from 0.01 levels per second to 0.7 levels per second, enabling the exploration of multiple agent strategies for the first time. We utilize TextWorldExpress to analyze the effectiveness of six established strategies and identify areas for improvement in the simulation environment. The new benchmark will help advance research by allowing developers to identify the most relevant strategies for the toughest levels in the games we studied. A widely used approach in 2D and 3D object estimation involves representing objects as class-specific and category-agnostic canonical forms. Training models using this method typically relies on aligning objects to these reference forms, but the search for optimal canonical poses can be constrained by limited data availability. Past research involved searching the pose space through iteration, however this can result in sub-optimal local minima. Direct optimization methods are also impeded by the non-differentiable transformation between objects and canonical forms. Our concept of 'latent canonical pose' allows the object pose to vary across classes, and we propose a multi-stage training method to learn this pose. Our model searches the latent space stage-wise to refine the estimated canonical pose. Unlike previous research, our method does not require iteration or object alignment, and we demonstrate through experiments that it yields superior performance. We carried out a photometric observation of the Algol type star Algol~C, which is part of the triple star system Algol, during the Spring 2021 Astronomical Observation Campaign organized by the Turkish Astronomical Society and the Central Observatory. Our analysis involved analyzing the data collected from 10 hours of simultaneous time series observations taken with the 0.60-m and K0 1.2-m telescopes at the Makstad Observatory in Turkey. Our results indicate that the systems' binary star Algol~C maintains a consistent orbital period over at least the past 350 years. Additionally, the data refined the light time analysis technique's accuracy to ±0.00065 days. With our new observations, the orbital parameters of Algol~C were determined as follows: the semi-amplitude orbital period is 5.381 days, the systemic velocity is 16.29 km/s, and the velocity ratio of the stars is 0.587. Furthermore, the characteristics of the Algol~C sub-system were compared to those of similar systems. Our research also recorded significant changes in the brightness and color of the system, particularly when the longer period star was in the superior position, which indicated that the effects of Algol~C's eclipses were masked by these color and brightness fluctuations in certain observing periods and were not accounted for in previous studies. Our study further highlights the advantages of utilizing the light time analysis technique in detecting non-eclipsing binary stars with unusual orbital patterns. To facilitate future research, we have made our observational data and analysis available to the scientific community through a public repository. Additionally, our study suggests several areas for further research, including revisiting and interpreting historical records, conducting spectroscopic studies, and carrying out prolonged photometric observations. Based on our results, we recommend that the binary star Algol~C be considered for inclusion in the list of stars with unique orbital patterns maintained by the General Catalogue of Stellar Triple and Multiple Systems. Our research has also provided educational opportunities for university students and young researchers to engage in real-world astronomical research, which is discussed in the concluding section of the study. To support their research, various resources and support materials are available for download from a public repository. Our study recommends that the binary star Algol~C be considered for inclusion in future research projects that aim to study the orbital patterns of binary stars using the light time analysis technique. Our research has also gained the interest of several university students and young researchers who have benefited from the various educational resources and support

This article explores blow-up for focusing Schrödinger equations both with and without a boundary present. We demonstrate that several established methods for proving blow-up in an entirely open system cannot be applied within a bounded domain, even in cases where the solution does not remain entirely non-trivial. However, we successfully develop a new set of methods to establish blow-up in both scenarios. We also discuss how these methods can be adapted to solutions of the linear focusing Schrödinger equation in domains with various geometric shapes. Ultimately, we conclude with a exploration of the implications of our findings on the focusing Schrödinger equation within a bounded domain. Interestingly, we observe that the maximum of the solution does not necessarily reach infinity, unlike in the case of the entirely open system. We also note the existence of solutions that do not remain entirely non-trivial without experiencing blow-up. This research explores the ferroelectric field effect in ferroelectric semiconductor materials by analyzing the conduction band distortions that occur when domains switch polarities under an external electric field. Using a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental validation, our findings reveal the impact of domain switching on the conduction band profile and demonstrate the potential to leverage this behavior for the creation of ultra-fast logic circuits operating in the sub-100 ns regime. Specifically, our experiments involve examining the domain switching dynamics in BiFeO3 through the variation of the conduction band profile and effective domain size with period, and we show that these features can serve as logical inputs for building fast-response flip-flop memory cells. Our study further explores the feasibility of achieving Cascode Voltage Switching by adjusting the conduction band profile through the choice of material parameters, and lays out a path for the development of accelerated logic circuits driven by domain switching in ferroelectric field effect transistors. Ultimately, our work identifies new pathways for the enhancement of performance in integrated electronic devices.

This paper delves into resolving the issue of library congruence in the Cargo ecosystem. Cargo's dependency management system is based on libraries specified in Rust code, which poses challenges for detecting congruent library upgrades. Past research suggested several conditions for congrent upgrades of individual libraries, but it's been left whether these conditions are sufficient for solving the broader congruence problem or if additional conditions are required.  In this paper, we conduct a preliminary exploration of the congruence problem in practice, focusing on how many Cargo libraries continue to be vulnerable to known issues even after receiving updates. Our analysis reveals that roughly 30% of libraries are affected by vulnerabilities in their latest versions, and over 50% of libraries fail to address at least one existing issue, even after being upgraded to the latest version available in Cargo.  Additionally, our findings suggest that using more conservative criteria for detecting congrent library upgrades, such as considering data format changes, reveals around 20% of libraries are compatible under this standard, and using the criteria proposed by Mesnard and Moudrie, around 15% of libraries are compatible.  We also discover around 30% of libraries are compatible when the standard criteria for source code changes is applied. As for the broader congruence problem, our initial insights suggest it may be resolved using existing conditions for individual libraries, but further research is needed to confirm this, and additional criteria may be necessary. In contrast, additional criteria may be necessary for detecting congrent library upgrades based on data format or source code changes.  In terms of practical solutions, our analysis reveals library developers may be using incorrect versioning schemes that could simplify the task of detecting congruent library upgrades based on the version numbers alone for certain libraries, and using more conservative versioning schemes can prevent upgrades that conflict with contract changes. Researchers have developed various forms of Trojan attacks against neural networks, but they typically come with limitations, such as reduced effectiveness in larger networks and limited applicability to non-image data. We propose a new type of Trojan attack, which can be applied to a broader range of networks and data without compromise. The attack involves adding a minimal amount of noise to the input, which can then trigger the network to make the desired class prediction. We test the attack on multiple networks, including ResNet and Transformer models, and evaluate its effectiveness across various parameter settings. The results show that the attack can achieve success rates of up to 100% without significantly impacting the network's accuracy. Notably, the attack can be more effective in networks that have overfitting issues, such as networks trained on smaller datasets. We observe that the noise patterns resulting from the attack can provide valuable insights for data labeling and improvement. For example, the noise patterns we encountered when attacking the BIRD model included distinct patterns for distinguishing between 'bird' and 'car' images. We are introducing the ROSIE IFU, an innovative integral field unit that is set to transform the landscape of astronomical mapping. This cutting-edge instrument, featuring a vast $4.5^\circ \times 4.5^\circ$ field of view, is comprised of 16 photomultiplexer units delivering $7 \times 800$ pixels across $500$ nm to $1100$ nm, will significantly boost efficiency and spatial resolution in the mapping of nebulae, galaxies, and star clusters using the AAO:2.5m telescope at Siding Spring. Following the official launch in May 2021, we present preliminary tests that include: a) a detailed description of the instrument's calibration; b) demonstration of fine sampling through the use of a $7 \times 7$ sub-array; c) description of the multi-object capability with a pair of narrowband filters as part of a program targeting planetary nebulae; d) early science results for NGC6543 and its central star, showcasing the potential for spatially resolved spectral maps that enable time-series monitoring of the star's complex emission line spectrum. These test outcomes effectively validate the performance of the ROSIE IFU for its intended applications. Further enhancements to the instrument's software and capabilities will continue to support a diverse range of scientific objectives. Additionally, we outline the multiple avenues for future improvement, including enhanced data reduction scripts and additional scientific applications across various astronomical objects. These developments will enable the maximization of the ROSIE IFU's potential for delivering critical insights into the workings of the universe.

This framework elevates the meaning of modal operators to a high-level abstract concept, making it easier to work with. By doing so, it enables a straightforward translation into the language of functors between strict topological categories, building on similar approaches in lower-order modal logic and expanding on existing methods for adding modal features to higher-order logic. We use our framework to demonstrate that various modal inference rules, including those derived from Kripke models, can be generalized to strict topological categories, providing a valid reasoning system for the logic. We take our analysis further by exploring the following questions: How do the notions of completeness and compactness behave when defined using universal properties? Can we define model theory within the context of strict topological categories?
