The concept of strong edge-coloring in graphs was initially explored by Vizing in 1976, who proposed that every graph with a maximum degree of Δ can be assigned colors to its edges such that no two edges incident on the same vertex have the same color, with a maximum of Δ colors.  In 1990, Carloni and Mazzuoccolo conjectured that every bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 3 can be given a strong edge-coloring using an amount of colors equal to their vertex count.  After many years of research, this conjecture was finally proven by Bartusek and Zivkovic in 2021.  This paper provides an alternative proof to their work by using a different method.  Also, a related conjecture in unipancycles was proven which states that every unipancycle with a maximum degree of 3 can be given a strong edge-coloring using an amount of colors equal to their vertex count plus one.  In addition, a generalization of strong edge-coloring in graphs with a maximum degree of Δ that are composed of two partite sets was proven which states that such a graph can be given a strong edge-coloring using an amount of colors equal to their maximum degree multiplied by the number of vertices in the first partite set.  Finally, this theory was applied to solve Carloni and Mazzuoccolo's conjecture and Bartusek and Zivkovic's theorem.  All of these results were verified using a computer program with its assistance.  In addition, all verified results were incorporated into an algorithm that can provide alternative proofs to these results. Hamming graphs serve as a perfect setting to apply Szabo's support reduction technique, yielding significant improvements in certain cases. However, the enhanced results come with a cost of more complicated expressions and reduced coverages in other scenarios. This research applies a customized version of Szabo's technique to the square zeroth eigenspace of the Hamming graph H(n, q), offering advancements over previous estimates for the minimum number of influences required to support non-constant functions defined on H(n, q). Specifically, the analysis reveals that, given standard constraints on n, i, j, and q, the minimum number of influences is approximately i(j^2), with an allowable exception of O(i/j^2 + i^2/j + i^2log(i)/j) in the case of i being comparably small to j. When the values of i and j are comparable to n, an upper limit of n/(2q^(-i)) can be set for the influences, demonstrating how these findings surpass the previously established bounds. This research was inspired by the 'Influences' problem on Brainiac's Olympics, where the prize for solving it has yet to be claimed.

By formulating problem-specific constraints within a penalized objective function, neural networks can effectively tackle a wide range of inverse and ill-posed problems. However, implementing these constraints, known as problem-specific priors, remains a significant challenge due to the unique problem requirements. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach called Neural-Penalized Problem Solution (NPPS), which enables neural networks to capture problem-specific priors through penalization during forward propagation, eliminating the need for constraints. NPPS is demonstrated on recovering continuous, piecewise-linear data from noisy observations, with results comparable to established constraint-based methods. Furthermore, NPPS offers a versatile framework for addressing a broad array of inverse problems. Code is available at https://github.com/jamiewinslow/npps. NPPS has potential applications in fields such as computer tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and data denoising. For example, it could be used for recovering piecewise-constant data from noisy MRI scans or denoising piecewise-linear data. Additional details on implementing NPPS for specific problem types are presented in the supplementary materials. In future work, we aim to explore adaptations of NPPS for problem-specific priors involving smoother forms such as polynomials or Gaussian processes. We also intend to investigate connections between NPPS and Bayesian inference, as well as other deep learning approaches for inverse problems such as differentiable iridescent bas-reliefs. With its versatility and ease of implementation, NPPS offers a promising alternative to existing constraint-based methods. It provides a foundation for developing more accurate and interpretable neural networks that capture problem-specific priors in various applications. In this paper, we examine a broad range of applications where NPPS can be applied, such as recovering piecewise-linear data from noisy observations. Although the method can be easily adapted for other priors, we have chosen not to present those examples to avoid presenting multiple results. In future work, we plan to explore this possibility in more detail. For instance, we can use NPPS for recovering piecewise-constant data from noisy MRI scans or data that follows a smooth, polynomial pattern. We introduce inexact policy iteration for large Multi-dimensional reinforcement learning problems by building on the Grouped Multi-way Merge algorithm. Experimental results indicate that inexact policy iteration is 5-15 times faster than traditional policy iteration in a 10,000-state MDP, and its computation time is largely unaffected by the size of the problem when using GMM with 10-13 levels. Notably, inexact policy iteration is 2-5 times faster than approximate offline policy iteration and achieves comparable performance to deep reinforcement learning methods. Additionally, we provide a partial theoretical justification for inexact policy iteration's convergence. Based on these findings, we recommend inexact policy iteration as a computationally efficient method for large Multi-dimensional reinforcement learning problems.

The simulator is altered to reflect both the practical limitations of the system under test and the performance metrics that the tuner aims to optimize. As a result, the reinforcement learning-based tuner can focus on finding a configuration that balances speed and practicality, without being limited by unrealistic scenarios. This paper examines jets produced in collisions between protons and photons at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Our research focuses on final states containing one photon and at least one jet. To initialize these processes, we must set up the quantum boundaries involving three partons, taking into account the momentum of the incident photon. Unlike traditional jet production studies, which only involve quarks and gluons, our investigation requires incorporating the full set of parton momenta, as well as the effects of photon recoil on the parton initial conditions. To develop the parton initial conditions, we utilize the BHS and GLS factorization schemes. Our analysis shows that, in the BHS factorization, the parton initial conditions are largely independent of the photon momentum. In contrast, the GLS factorization yields parton initial conditions that vary significantly with the photon momentum and are strongly connected to it. Furthermore, our work reveals that, in both factorization schemes, the parton initial conditions exhibit distinct transverse momentum and direction dependencies, which are notably different from that of the photon and are influenced by it. Our research also shows that, in the BHS factorization, the parton initial conditions' rapidity distribution is directly linked to the rapidity distribution of the photon, whereas in the GLS factorization, the parton initial conditions' rapidity distribution can diverge from the photon's at high rapidity. Our findings strongly suggest that the parton initial conditions' unique transverse momentum and directional dependencies, which differ from those of the photon, are responsible for the observed cold nuclear matter effects on photon-jet production observed at the LHC. Our work paves the way for a fresh understanding of jet production in proton-photon collisions and encourages the use of factorization and parton initial conditions to study the subject further. Our research also extends the applicability of factorization and partons to a previously unexplored realm of processes. Moreover, our analysis suggests the presence of an interference term in photon-jet production that could be detectable through differential measurements and may be an important aspect of the process. Finally, our work opens up the possibility of using photon-jet production as a probe to investigate and discover new, exotic states that may not interact via strong forces. This study evaluates alternating versions of Apéry-type series and reveals they exceed even the highest level of colored multiple zeta values (colMZVs). We confirm this by demonstrating they surpass even the colMZVs found in the expanded form of (x_1+x_2)^n. Additionally, dense sets of colMZVs related to these series are identified, particularly for the type involving square roots. To fully comprehend these results, even for finite values of n, a suitable representation of colMZVs is needed. This paper introduces an innovative method of colMZV expansion using a novel notion of 'alternating with respect to a color' (AWRC) series. A practical approach to calculating double parton distribution functions (DPDs) within the framework of a given parton model is to represent DPDs in terms of products of single parton distribution functions (PDFs). However, such an approximation may not be suitable at small $x$ and is likely to fail when DPDs exhibit rapid $k_T$-dependence. 

In the literature, DPDs have been redefined in terms of impact factors that describe the transition from a hard process to a soft region, and it is proposed that DPDs can be determined through a comparison of two-loop cross sections for double-parton scattering processes at NLO. 

Our work suggests that, in the context of a given parton model, DPDs can be calculated at the next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) in the approximation where the transverse momenta of partons are small relative to the scale $\sqrt{Q^2}$, and these calculations can be done through an actual computation or by using an approximation in terms of products of PDFs. 

Furthermore, it is found that when the approximation holds, the NNLO DPDs will agree with the next-to-next-to-logical approximation in the rapidity region where the approximation holds in the differential cross section for double-parton scattering processes at $x \sim 10^{-2}$ and $k_T \lesssim 2$ GeV. 

In the case where DPDs are defined through a comparison of two-loop cross sections for double-parton scattering processes, the NNLO DPDs will also agree with the next-to-next-to-logical approximation in the $k_T$ dependence up to $k_T \lesssim 2$ GeV. 

In the application involving the Basso-Keating-Stewart DPD framework, the $k_T$ dependence of DPDs is found to be outside of the region where the approximation holds, and as such, the NNLO DPDs will not agree with the next-to-next-to-logical approximation in the $k_T$ dependence.

This study explores the process of drop formation that occurs when a liquid film surrounding a fibre undergoes cooling, causing the liquid to solidify and shrink. As the liquid solidifies, it slips off the fibre due to their differing phases, creating a gap that grows and eventually forms droplets. Unlike other methods of drop formation that rely on external factors such as pressure or surface tension, this process arises solely from the slipping motion of the liquid against the solid surface, making it unique and fascinating. Using advanced imaging techniques and analytical tools, we observe and study the drop formation process in detail, and develop a theoretical framework to model and understand the underlying dynamics. Our findings reveal that the drop formation method and size depend crucially on the relative phases and slip conditions of the liquid and solid surfaces. Traditional methods of modeling duration often rely on the assumption of a fixed at-risk population, analyzing how covariates affect the likelihood of events occurring within a certain time frame. This assumption is not always feasible, particularly in scenarios involving non-proportional hazards and dynamic at-risk populations. To address these challenges, a new model has been proposed that uses the cumulative distribution function to model duration and separates the effects of covariates and time. This approach involves modeling the expected duration for sub-populations of interest, based on relevant characteristics, by integrating the hazard function and an unspecified density function. To implement this model effectively, specifications for both the hazard function and density function must be established. Notably, the proposed duration modeling technique differs from conventional methods in its ability to handle sub-populations with non-proportionate hazards and dynamic at-risk statuses. To evaluate the proposed model's assumptions and performance, numerical analyses and a real-world data set have been employed. Ultimately, this technique can be applied to assess the effects of covariates on event occurrence rates among at-risk populations under dynamic circumstances. To illustrate the model's utility, a real-world example has been provided, demonstrating its utility in investigating non-proportionate hazards in sub-populations and dynamic at-risk situations. Additionally, simulations have been conducted to evaluate the proposed model's numerical performance. Selected findings from these simulations are presented below. Further details regarding the simulations, along with their results, can be found in the report by Li et al. (2023). To facilitate parameter estimation for the proposed duration model, an established method has been adapted, along with two alternative methods identified for this purpose. To begin with, the adapted M-estimator method has been explored. To seek alternative solutions, both the weighted M-estimator method and the log-spline based AIC selector method have been examined. Notably, the log-spline based AIC selector method exhibits promising results, particularly in its ability to determine the optimal number of knots required for effective model estimation. To evaluate the proposed estimator methods, a series of Monte Carlo simulations have been conducted. To seek feedback from the statistical community, a preliminary paper on this topic has been shared, with feedback received from several experts. To seek additional input, a survey has been created to gather feedback from the statistical community. Occupancy modeling plays a significant role in ecological research and is often used to analyze species presence/absence data. By integrating historical occurrence data and current detection data, researchers can make more accurate inferences. Current frequentist methods analyze the two data sources separately and then combine the results. However, this approach may not always yield the most reliable inferences, especially when data are imperfect. We present a new Bayesian framework that enables a single analysis of historical and current data and also allows the estimation of variability in occurrence data. This framework is similar to standard detection modeling but with several key enhancements. We demonstrate the benefits of this new framework through simulations and real-world applications, and show that it yields more efficient results and more accurate estimates of variability in occurrence data. Additionally, this framework can be used to estimate the variability in presence/absence data without the need for replicates, making it a useful tool for researchers working with real-world data sets. We provide a publicly available R program that implements the new framework. To model the intrinsic variation seen in type Ia supernovae, we developed a Bayesian framework using Gaussian process regression. By incorporating a correlation penalty into the model, we can enforce smooth relationships between SN properties and improve the modeling of their collective variability. Applying this approach to a combined dataset of 54 and 101 supernovae, we found that the correlation penalty helps to reveal relationships within the data that weren't apparent before and boosts the signal-to-noise of the overall variability signal. The analysis also confirmed that a scale model consisting of early photometry and velocity components is necessary to fully capture the variability. Introducing a correlation penalty improves the modeling, increasing the likelihood that the variability signal isn't simply random noise. Furthermore, we demonstrated that marginalizing over model parameters doesn't significantly diminish the variability signal, and that a correlation penalty enhances the modeling of the collective variability in SN Ia. The analysis primarily focused on signal extraction rather than noise characterisation, and we didn't attempt to fit SN Ia spectra in this study. The dynamics of particle transport within a channel with a swirling flow have been investigated both experimentally and numerically. In the experimental component, the interaction between a plume and a vortex in a channel with a square cross-section was studied under conditions where the plume exhibited either higher or lower density compared to the surrounding fluid. Our findings were then compared to numerical simulations using a two-dimensional model that accounted for the effects of turbulence on fluid flow and particle transport. In cases where the plume had a higher density than the surrounding fluid, our observations showed that particles tended to move downwards due to a form of 'counter-density' entrainment, resulting in a maximum percentage of particles being transported downwards of approximately 300%. Existing model checkers for multi-threaded programs, like McMini and its predecessors, have shown promise but have been limited by their speed, which has been dictated by the memory available on a 32-bit machine. This constraint has prevented them from fully verifying multi-threaded operations. In response, the McMini team has revised the model checker to utilize more than the minimum amount of memory that the Java Virtual Machine allows for. Specifically, they developed an iterative deepening model checker that segment the single thread of execution in a multi-threaded program along temporal axes, elevating McMini's scalability to match the memory capabilities of a 64-bit machine. As a result, the revised model checker has outperformed its predecessors by factor of 3 on smaller multi-threaded programs and by factor of 200 on a benchmark of single thread that converts infix to postfix notation. Furthermore, the revised model checker has successfully verified the multi-threaded operations of a Java implementation of a lockless queue that had eluded earlier model checkers. In addition to these advances, the McMini team has revised the model checker to utilize multiple processor cores when available, effectively boosting performance by factor of 2 on a multi-threaded server program and factor of 4 on a multi-threaded client-server program. Lastly, the McMini team has developed an initial tool to verify the multi-threaded operations of a real embedded device in real-time. Despite reaching the memory limits of the device's processor, the model checker was able to verify single thread that performed a variety of critical tasks, including managing a queue, acting as a client-server, and controlling input/output operations. In conclusion, the revised model checker has reached new heights of scalability and efficiency, exceeding the performance of its predecessors by factor of 200, verifying complex multi-threaded programs that had been out of reach. In addition to these advances, the model checker has successfully verified the multi-threaded operations of a Java-based lockless queue and achieved real-time verification on an embedded device. This method is applied to the $N=2$ superconformal field theory in three dimensions to form a supergravity framework, which is then used to create a supergravity expansion technique. This expansion technique can be employed to calculate various physical properties in supergravity systems and is shown to be consistent with the principles of quantum gravity and low-energy effective theories up to a specific order. Furthermore, the development of the supergravity framework in this paper can be generalized to other supergravity theories in four and eleven dimensions. The presented method is based on previous work by Friedan and Kent and involves connecting supergravity to the underlying quantum gravity and effective theories through a modular approach that utilizes the supergravity's anomalies and the expansion technique. This connection allows for the identification of several key physical properties and allows for the formulation of quantum gravity at a low energy level. We analyze the combined system of a magnetic film, connected to two superconducting strips, moving at a gap frequency. By integrating out the superconducting leads, we obtain a closed micro-magnetron model that generates robust non-linear magnon behavior. We demonstrate that this model exhibits consistent solutions representing magnon phase shift, persistent current, and stored energy. It is observed that this model replicates the known characteristics of magnon beam delay, trapped current, and energy storage, as well as predicting new features. Notably, we find that this model predicts a greater delay for higher-frequency magnons, and its non-linearity can change direction based on the magnon's frequency. The findings indicated that local news volumes declined significantly due to the pandemic, with content shifting towards pandemic-related topics, often reflected negatively. The research also revealed regional differences in pandemic news, with some locations receiving more coverage than others, and varying levels of positivity in editorial opinions across different areas. Overall, the study provides insights into local news responses to the pandemic, highlighting the influence of geographic location, population characteristics, and economic conditions on pandemic news. Additionally, the study addresses broader societal questions by investigating how local news reflected community concerns, fears, and perspectives during crisis situations. The ability to systematically extrapolate beyond initial training data limits is a crucial property of models, especially when dealing with limited datasets. However, in the context of Language Models, extrapolation is largely under-determined due to non-differentiable components such as pre-training, data selection, and data quality. This work proposes a novel analysis that uncovers an underpinning issue with extrapolation in Language Models: they often confuse it with data augmentation. By examining BERT and BART models, our study reveals that extrapolation is often achieved through augmentation in simplified scenarios or compromised in complex cases. Additionally, our investigation links the successful extrapolation of BART, a sequence-to-sequence model, to its ability to handle out-of-frame inputs. A new training objective, called Input augmentation with Data Mimicry (IDM), is developed to enhance BART's extrapolation capabilities. IDM encourages augmentation by cross-tuning the input and utilizing data that's similar to the initial training data. This objective improves BART's ability to handle various extrapolation challenges, such as counting, coreference, and text classification, while our study also sheds light on the inherent ambiguities of extrapolation and augmentation, highlighting the difficulties in achieving reliable and natural behavior beyond initial training data limits. Overall, our investigation demonstrates that extrapolation is an intricate property that's challenging to achieve reliably without addressing issues of data quality, data augmentation, and data representation. Based on these conclusions, we suggest future research should concentrate on developing novel methodologies that automatically transform inputs to achieve successful extrapolation. This research has significant implications for the broader NLP community as it seeks to achieve reliable and natural behavior of Language Models beyond initial training data limits. With the growing importance of Explainable AI, our study also explores the potential of identifying augmentation inputs for BART through attention analysis, feature importance, and perturbation-based methods, concluding that the current attention-based interpretation is insufficient to drive data augmentation. Nonetheless, our investigation indicates that attention-based methods can effectively identify inputs that are similar to initial training data, such as fake sentences for text classification, whereas perturbation-based methods can only partially mimic data augmentation in the presence of augmentation. This research has significant implications for the broader NLP community as it seeks to achieve reliable and natural behavior of Language Models beyond initial training data limits. the xor operation to merge and compress partial answers from counting algorithms. 
This research revamps the technique, proposing new constructions and evaluating its 
performance through experiments. The findings indicate that xor filters typically require 
less memory and run faster than conventional Bloom filters, while also yielding similar 
false positive rates. The main disadvantages of using xor filters are the increased computational 
cost of construction and deployment, as well as dependence on specific frequency counts. 
Offline construction allows for a single, lengthy Computation, after which deployment 
can occur in real-time. We suggest xor filters as a suitable choice when a moderate amount 
of memory needs to be saved and superior speed is desired, especially for applications 
where frequent offline recollections are required. The code and experiments are accessible

This research examines the time scales inherent in Intraday Market Data, both large and small. Large time scales were found in past transaction evidence and are influenced by market opening and closing periods. This discovery aligns with existing knowledge. However, the analysis uncovers a novel observation: the time span between transactions determines the magnitude of market directional force. This is in line with the principles of self-similar behavior. Conversely, smaller time scales were not clearly determined in past transaction evidence. However, simulated data with randomly varying price and volume generated on minute-by-minute basis supports the idea that there is no significant market directional force at this scale. Furthermore, an algorithm was developed to identify the most influential companies driving market direction on large time scales. It is shown that the market direction on these scales is largely dictated by the largest companies by market value. Finally, the research demonstrates that market directional force across all time scales is largely driven by price and volume fluctuations in individual stocks rather than any market-wide factors. Unlike existing theories, the findings suggest that market directional force is not an inherent characteristic of market dynamics but rather a consequence of individual company dynamics. It is also shown that market dynamics are purely random in nature, eliminating the need for any autoregressive elements. In conclusion, the research offers a new perspective on market dynamics, attributing market behavior to individual company actions rather than any market aggregate factors. LITERATURE REVIEW: The Dow-theory, developed by Charles Dow, is the longest-running market analysis approach (now in its 100th edition) and the only approach to forecast markets, providing specific buy and sell indicators. In contrast, the Bollinger on Bollinger Band approach uses moving averages and volatility measures to identify trends. Despite its effectiveness, the approach has significant draw-downs and failed to prevent significant losses. Similarly, the RSI approach uses the Relative Strength Index to identify overbought and oversold conditions in markets. However, the approach has inherent flaws, leading to false signals and market losses. In comparison, the research-based time scale-based approach has several advantages over existing market analysis methods, including superior performance, reduced risks, and accurate trend identification. VALUATION: The valuation multiple, based on earnings, price, and dividend figures, failed to accurately predict short-term market behavior. In contrast, the research approach uses individual company dynamics to identify market direction on large time scales and market dynamics at smaller scales. Using real market data, the research approached accurately identified short-term trends and outperformed existing market analysis methods, including technical indicators

Our proposal, FLVoogd, is the first federated clustering approach that balances efficiency, fairness, and reliability. This innovative system utilizes a two-phase approach with active learning to determine data inclusion for training. Firstly, it engages human reviewers to assess suspicious submissions. Untrusted submissions are labeled as'reject' and do not contribute to the model, while benign submissions are labeled as 'accept' and used for training. This ensures that only trustworthy data is utilized. Secondly, the accepted data are efficiently labeled using Bayesian learning to maximize the effect on the clustering model. Our experiments demonstrate that FLVoogd achieves high accuracy and fairness, surpassing existing solutions. Additionally, it protects personal information and prevents data exploitation by federated servers. Its adaptability and scalability also enable it to thrive in diverse, large-scale settings. Overall, FLVoogd is the first federated clustering approach that integrates human and machine intelligence to establish a culture of trust on the global internet. Deepfake media have become increasingly realistic, posing significant issues for real-world implications. As their realism improves, they are more likely to influence people's beliefs and spark real-world events. Despite the growing importance of controlling the amount of misleading information, current methods are limited in their ability to manipulate continuous video footage. Our proposed approach allows for the creation of realistic individual frames in a video, without the need for prior knowledge or the full video content. We achieve this by developing a technique to craft novel control frames that align with the underlying video. Our goal is to enable the creation of artificial videos that are both visually plausible and dynamically consistent. Upon evaluation, our method outperforms existing techniques, producing high-quality results in line with state-of-the-art generative models. Moreover, our method enables the creation of artificial videos from single images, outperforming existing approaches in both visual and video metrics. Our code and model will be made available.

Research into neural networks, particularly those inspired by the McCulloch-Pitts model, has been revived by the success of deep neural networks in various applications. Our study contributes to this resurgence by examining a supervised, gradient-based learning approach for a multilayer network built around the McCulloch-Pitts neuron. We show that even without relaxing the original neuron's discrete output constraint, it is possible to train this network and achieve accurate classification of complex patterns, such as the exclusive OR function. Our work also draws a connection between the original Hopfield network and a deeper McCulloch-Pitts network, indicating that the former can be viewed as a specific realization of the latter. Consequently, the trained McCulloch-Pitts network represents a generalization of the Hopfield network's dynamics, offering improved learning capabilities. We support our findings with numerical examples that verify the applicability of our theory. Our analysis sheds new light on the neural network literature, particularly regarding the trained network's robustness to perturbations and the existence of multiple, local optima. Our results may also influence the design of novel hardware for deep neural networks. The significant advancements in Scene Text Recognition (STR) have been hindered by the lack of inclusion of Out-Of-Vocabulary words in traditional models. To address this gap, researchers have developed a new dataset of Oxford English words with full vocabulary coverage. Our study focuses on integrating this dataset into the STR task and evaluates various modeling strategies. Additionally, we have developed new baseline models for Out-Of-Vocabulary words and assembled a comprehensive test suite from the dataset and existing benchmarks in the field. The study's findings show that models can achieve a high accuracy of 90% for less frequent words and the development of this test suite will facilitate further research into STR, particularly in less frequent situations. The proposed dataset and test suite, as well as baseline models, are now available for public use. Our work on this problem can be accessed at https://github.com/asharakeh/oxford_english_dataset. Our research on integrating the dataset into the STR task can be found at https://github.com/asharakeh/OxfordEnglishSTR. In contrast to the conventional approach of assuming that Out-Of-Vocabulary words do not exist, we have explored a more practical scenario where such words constitute 15% of the total. Our analysis of the characteristics of this subset reveals that a substantial number of these words have similar spellings and may cause confusion for the model. To address this challenge, we have developed a new strategy of using similar-looking words as pseudo-out-of-vocabulary examples during the training phase. The proposed approach has demonstrated significant improvements, with an overall accuracy of 93.65% on the Out-Of-Vocabulary subset and 96.13% on the In-Vocabulary subset. Our work also involves the development of test suites for various benchmark datasets, including ICDAR 2015, ICDAR 2019, and the newly created Oxford English dataset. Our analysis of the performance on the Out-Of-Vocabulary challenge shows that while significant progress has been made, there is still room for improvement, and the creation of this test suite will facilitate further research into this field. Our study is the first to tackle the Out-Of-Vocabulary problem in the realm of Scene Text Recognition, and our proposed approach has shown promising results, with an overall accuracy of 93.65% on the Oxford English dataset. Our work is publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/OxfordEnglishSTR. Our research on integrating the dataset into the STR task can be found at https://github.com/

Detecting abrupt shifts and individual failures within sequential data is a difficult task, especially when resources are limited. To address this challenge, we developed a new method called Isolate, a online algorithm designed for setting and detecting changes. Machine learning models depend on large datasets of labeled data; yet, the time-consuming process of annotating these data, especially for expensive tasks, limits the use of available data. A technique called selective labeling cuts costs by limiting the labeling of training data to specific, hard-to-reach cases only. This paper explores how to apply selective labeling by identifying the most challenging instances. In various experiments across multiple datasets and models, we found that relying solely on model predictions isn't enough and that we need to combine this with other factors such as data structure and utility. By taking an active learning approach and considering both utility and easy access, we were able to accurately identify the instances that require labeling in selective labeling scenarios. This method performed comparably to other methods that relied on utility or other factors in different contexts. Furthermore, we found that when we integrated selective labeling with data collection policies, we were able to limit the number of labels needed to the same extent as if we had collected labels for all data from the beginning. This method saved us the cost of annotating data selectively. Our work was performed on graph-based data but can be applied broadly to any domain where there are issues with data scarcity and limited resources for annotation. Notably, we saved computational resources by limiting the number of labels and reduced the risk of overfitting by limiting exposure to easy data. This method is resource-efficient and effective in saving costs associated with data annotation. Our code is available on GitHub for reproduction of our results. This method helps address these issues by limiting the number of labels needed while focusing on the instances that are critical to model performance. This indicates that our method is effective in identifying the instances that require labeling and can be used to limit the number of labels needed while still achieving good results. The interface between EuS and InAs has shown promising properties to manipulate spin and carry significant electronic charge. An understanding of the electronic structure at the interface is crucial but difficult to determine directly, so computational models are utilized to investigate this phenomenon. In this study, the density functional theory with the use of a patching potential and a cluster perturbation method is applied to determine the electronic structure of the EuS/InAs interface. Our results show that the dispersion at the InAs valence band maximum arises from charged states originating from the interface interaction, while the top of the EuS valence band is isolated due to a barrier created by the interface dipole. Additionally, our analysis reveals the presence of a complex energy spectrum associated with the interface, which is closely linked with the antiferromagnetic lattice distortion of the EuS layers. Our findings also demonstrate that the perturbation induced by the interface affects the InAs conduction band, leading to a band shift and increased interaction when comparing with the properties of InAs alone. A detailed examination of the interface shows that the average distance of the interface charge distribution does not solely depend on the InAs relaxation height observed in the EuS/InAs quantum wells. Instead, it is influenced by the amount of EuS monolayers and antiferromagnetic layers present. Our study provides comprehensive insights into the electronic structure of the EuS/InAs interface, which is essential in understanding the properties of the interface and its potential applications in the manipulation of spin and electronic charge. Our results can serve as a reference for the experimental investigation of the interface, and the interface properties can be modulated through the variation of the interface monolayers for new device applications. Moreover, our analysis indicates that the interface effects are not confined and could influence the properties of the InAs conduction band. Due to the presence of the interface potencial, the charged states at the interface do not follow the symmetry of the zinc-blende structure at the InAs valence band maximum. Instead, the interface charge distribution is more prominent compared to the top of the EuS valence band, which is shielded due to a dipole created at the interface and can be affected by varying the number of monolayers. We establish a enhanced version of Borel Wadge determinacy within projective determinacy, which in turn gives us an improved version of Borel Wadge determinacy. This in turn allows us to prove a more robust version of Arhangel'skii-Shapiro theorem. Furthermore, our findings imply that second-order arithmetic is equivalent to a certain system of transfinite arithmetic with quantification over Borel sets. Lastly, we demonstrate that the axioms of extensionality and choice can be fully incorporated into our framework of projective determinacy. 

In contrast to Borel Wadge determinacy, which can be proven to require large cardinal axioms when assumed to fail, our findings show that projective determinacy is sensitive to the existence of cutters for certain projective sets, with its non-implication by second-order arithmetic being equivalent to the failure of cutability for projective sets with a specific property. 

Also, the proof strategy for our result differs significantly from previous proofs of Borel Wadge determinacy, with the main difference being the integration of projective set theory into our model, which allows for a more direct demonstration of determinacy for certain classes of games compared to Borel Wadge determinacy. 

We note that while our results primarily focus on the analysis of Borel games, our findings of projective determinacy and Borel Wadge determinacy do encompass certain classes of games involving choice functions that are not necessarily Borel. Similarly, our findings of determinacy for certain classes of games involving cutters for projective sets with a specific property also encompass determinacy for certain classes of games involving cutters for Borel sets with a similar property. 

In terms of related work, our findings of projective determinacy can be seen as an enhancement of a previous result by Steel which focused on the determinacy of a certain class of games involving projective sets with a specific property, while our findings of Borel Wadge determinacy can be seen as an improvement of a previous result by Aschenbrenner which focused on the determinacy of a certain class of Borel games. Furthermore, our findings of the equivalence of second-order and transfinite arithmetic with quantification over Borel sets is an enhancement of a previous result by Cunningham which focused on the equivalence of second-order and transfinite arithmetic with quantification over a certain class of sets.

The merger of two compact stars, such as neutron stars, is a critical astrophysical event that allows us to examine diverse, complex phenomena in a single observation. Observing the gravitational wave from the merger through the lens of general relativity is complemented by the electromagnetic radiation, providing a wealth of information about the coalescing stars. Specifically, the analysis of gravitational waves offers precise measurements of the stars' spin, size, and composition, whereas electromagnetic observations reveal details of the post-merger state, such as the appearance and mass of a neutron star disc and the behavior of the shock jet. By merging these two perspectives of the merger event, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical processes involved. Consequently, the analysis of multi-messenger observations of neutron star mergers has become a vital area of study, supporting the development of advanced hydrodynamic simulations and analytical models.

Here, the author presents a comprehensive review of the significant advancements achieved in the analysis of neutron star merger simulations. The analysis is organized according to the frequency range of the gravitational wave, starting from higher frequencies in the upper section and descending to lower frequencies in the reverse. This presentation covers key aspects of the merger process, beginning with the final inches of the merger of the two neutron stars, through the collapse of the initial core, the formation of the substellar object known as an hyperon, and down to frequencies as low as $10^{-4}$ Hz. The author provides an in-depth examination of the analytical models used in each segment, accompanied by the most recent and sophisticated simulations available in the literature.

In addition, the author also delves into specific topics, such as the origin of the electromagnetic radiation produced during the merger, the structure of the shock, the formation of the hyperon, and the behavior of the system at low frequencies. The discussion on these topics is based on the latest findings and is designed to guide both novice and seasoned researchers through the subject. The author hopes that this comprehensive review will serve as a useful resource, bridging the gap between the complex theoretical models and the complex astrophysical phenomena involved, and ultimately contributing to the development of more precise tests of general relativity. Our approach to recognizing hand-drawn mathematical symbols relies on a basic k-neighbor classifier that operates within a predefined feature space defined by a HOG-SVM system. In this context, the HOG-SVM system serves as a domain expert, responsible for extracting the underlying mathematical concept from input images and encoding it into feature space. The k-neighbor classifier then utilizes the features generated by the HOG-SVM system to determine the nearest class representatives for the input image provided by the domain expert. Following the initial HOG-SVM classification, the HOG-SVM system is disabled, and the modified features are passed on to a second HOG-SVM system, known as the predictor, which performs fine-grained classification within feature space. This two-stage classifier achieves a performance boost of up to 15% compared to the existing state-of-the-art, resulting in an overall accuracy rate of 73.86% across all mathematical symbols. Additionally, the complex design of our approach may offer insights into developing advanced machine learning systems that are easier to validate and certify. Moreover, the intricate nature of our approach may contribute to the development of more sophisticated algorithmic methods that are amenable to certification and validation. For instance, the use of Taylor expansions could facilitate the assessment of uncertainties in the reliability of our classifier. Our two-stage classifier has been carefully tailored to operate within feature space, and its design may be extended to other domains to create advanced machine learning systems capable of producing certified outcomes. We found that more connected networks tend to allow epidemics to spread widely and precisely, while less connected networks limit their spread. Additionally, our analysis revealed that higher network integrality can either accelerate or slow down an epidemic, depending on the specific conditions. Notably, we discovered that more fragile networks are susceptible to rapid and widespread epidemics, while less fragile networks are able to resist the spread of the disease. Our findings provide valuable insights into the spread of epidemics in networks and can inform public health policies. Moreover, we make adjustments to the existing bounds for estimating the twin prime count, a problem first addressed by Brun, and leverage this revised estimate to compute the twin prime count for specific cases, namely $(x, x+2)$, where $x$ ranges from $10^4$ to $10^5$. Additionally, we extend this generalized Sieve to other prime pairs $(p, p+4)$ and establish a new representation for $p+4$ as a product of two codes, one related to $p$ and the other to its quadratic Gauss reduction, both of which are based on L-functions. This generalization allows us to explore the precision in approximating $p+4$ through its factorization into these codes and assess how close we can get to an optimal estimate. Finally, we outline potential future applications of this generalized Sieve, such as impacting polynomial modular reduction, and examine the possibility of extending this Sieve to other types of prime pairs $(p, p+6)$. Nevertheless, such an extension appears to be significantly more challenging than $(p, p+4)$. Lastly, we briefly explore connections between the generalized Sieve and other mathematical concepts, including the L-functions, modular forms, and toric codes, all of which share intriguing connections with prime numbers and their relationships. By leveraging these connections, we can gain valuable insights into the primes themselves. Due to the complexity and intricacy of these prime-related concepts, we have chosen to introduce them in a logical and easy-to-follow sequence, thus allowing less experienced mathematicians to gradually build their understanding of these advanced mathematical ideas. In conclusion, this generalized Sieve offers a versatile tool for exploring prime pairs at the cross-section of number theory, algebraic geometry, and information theory, and has the potential to contribute meaningfully to the field of number theory. We present a modular control system consisting of multiple levels of decision-making. Our system is specifically designed for mobile robots equipped with a sonar sensor array to improve navigation in dense environments. This innovative sensing technology provides detailed information about the robot's surroundings at close range but is limited in its long-range capabilities. We address this challenge by developing a hierarchical control structure that separates higher-level decisions from sensing details at lower levels. This breakdown allows us to focus on optimizing navigation through a localized area while considering the robot's position and orientation as its primary factors. Our layered control system is composed of three interconnected levels: the first handles low-level details such as sensor data interpretation and movement control, the second manages mid-range tasks including rotation, and the third makes long-range decisions such as when to rotate in response to the robot encountering obstacles. We utilized an asynchronous message-passing system to connect these levels, enabling them to operate independently, even in real-time. Our approach proves to be both efficient and adaptable, with navigation capabilities consisting of approximately 80 lines of code, including comments and space. Experimental results confirm that our method is both effective and lightweight, making it suitable for navigation in dense environments. This paper integrates the pessimism principle into a modified Thompson sampling, enabling efficient learning of an optimal dynamic treatment policy with minimal sample efficiency in the context of multi-armed bandits with hidden and unobserved patient characteristics. The model assumes patient characteristics evolve over time in response to historical treatments and observations. The proposed algorithm uses a compact latent variable representation to approximate the patient population's distribution, learned through online sampling and a variational objective that balances exploratory and predictive goals. The algorithm then uses the sampled characteristics to make informed treatment decisions, enhancing both pure and regret-optimal dynamic treatment policies. The method's asymptotic optimality is verified through theoretical analysis, and its practical efficacy is demonstrated in simulation-based experiments. Finally, the algorithm's effectiveness is validated in two real-world scenarios involving COVID-19 treatment protocols. The code for the algorithm can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/alexstrammer/PATNT. We establish a formal equivalence between nonlocality, contextuality, and relevance, four concepts of quantum embeddedness that have been considered distinct. Our analysis reveals that different scenarios are connected through correlations stemming from shared quantum states, enabling a reduction to a single framework. Furthermore, we introduce a set of necessary and sufficient conditions, encompassing all four properties, that a single quantum state must satisfy. These conditions are based on specific transformations of the quantum state and are related to each other via relationships stemming from compositions and contexts. Our work provides a unified method for extending the study of these properties from individual experiments to any experiment and for generalizing them from specific outcomes to any outcome. Additionally, we demonstrate that nonlocality and contextuality can be quantified by measuring constraints on the quantum state, thereby allowing a comparison of the properties in different scenarios. Our findings are validated through a comprehensive analysis of the Bell, Mermin, and Conrad nonlocality inequalities, as well as the contextuality inequality proposed by Howard et al., using various resources, including higher-dimensional systems. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the nature of quantum mechanics and its implications for the boundaries of classical reasoning. Our methods are accessible and can be appreciated through a more intuitive approach, as well as through a more formal approach. Our software implementation allows for the computation of the properties, the inequalities, and the quantum states that satisfy them, as well as the determination of the closest classical states, making it an invaluable resource for researchers and students. Our work is documented in a research paper and is based on our previous article, our presentation, our interview, and our chapter. Our implementation is designed to be modular and can be applied to any problem in the field of quantum embeddedness, as well as to any problem in the field of relevance theory, as evidenced by our application to latent variables, our application to quantum estimation, and our application to conflict resolution. Our work is also general enough to be applied to any problem in the field of measurement uncertainty analysis. Our study is the first to examine the complete set of conditions for a single quantum state in the context of nonlocality, contextuality, and relevance, as well as the first to demonstrate the equivalence between nonlocality, contextuality, and relevance that arises from shared quantum states. Our work is original, as evidenced by our references, and contributes to the advancement of the field of quantum embeddedness, as well as to any problem in the field of algebra, as evidenced by our abstract, our presentation, and our code. We analyze the analog of the generalized Polya theorem in the context of p-adic solenoids. To accomplish this, we first establish a functional equation, and then solve it using D. Bertrand's functions with a restricted value range. Next, we demonstrate that these solutions form a subgroup of the solenoid's automorphism group. Additionally, we address the raised questions concerning the existence of solutions with a period and the case of adic solenoids in relation to the standard real case. 

In the case of a finite adic system, we successfully find solutions with a period. On the other hand, for an infinite adic system, we prove the non-existence of such solutions in the form of a periodic function. Finally, we explore the transition to the real case, highlighting the differences between function-valued solutions and those interpreted as collections of real numbers. 

This research also leads us to define and study a new topological group, which we denote as $\Delta_G(\Bbbp^1)$, consisting of function values defined on a set of p-adic intervals and taking values in $ \Bbbp^1$. Similar efforts have been applied to investigate other analogs of the generalized Polya theorem in the context of locally compact abelian groups. 

Also worth noting is that this article draws heavily from the excellent textbook by M. Hazewinkel, N. Zierman's Ph.D. dissertation, and D. Bertrand's influential papers. 

In the context of p-adic solenoids, we have chosen to focus on systems with a finite number of transitions. This allowed us to obtain a comprehensive understanding, but raised questions about systems with an infinite number of transitions, which we have partially addressed. In particular, it is uncertain whether solutions with a period exist in such systems, which we conjecture to be the case. In contrast, solutions with a period do exist in the form of a periodic function, but this requires collection of real number-valued solutions. To evaluate the effectiveness of multiple clustering approaches on species occurrence data, we conducted an experiment using 30 datasets from the Occurrence dataset from iNaturalist. We compared the results of four clustering methods: k-means, PCoA with Bray-Curtis distance, PCoA with Jaccard distance, and hierarchical clustering with Ward linkage, measured by the Calinski-Harabasz index and Silhouette score. Our findings show that the performance of each method varies across different datasets, and none of the indices consistently identify true clusters. However, hierarchical clustering is perceived as easier to use and more flexible than the others. Ultimately, the choice of clustering method and assessment metrics should be based on the specific research question and objectives. All data and code used in this study are openly available on the GitHub platform at the specified URLs. Additionally, a package named clustertest is being developed for reproducibility and future testing of clustering methods. Currently, it is accessible through the development version at https://github.com/jgabry/clustertest.

A low-dose image reconstruction model aims to mitigate noise in Computed Tomography (CT) imaging.  Existing low-dose techniques are primarily based on 3D iterative reconstruction methods taking non-local information and prior information into consideration, but they often require significant computational resources and may not fully utilize prior information due to assumed noise statistics.  Other deep learning-based approaches focus solely on using residual connections or separate noising modules, failing to account for non-stationary noise and non-uniform illumination in practical CT scanning operations.  In contrast, this research introduces a new deep learning-based model that incorporates prior information and considers non-stationary noise and non-uniform illumination, enhancing image texture and clarity while reducing noise.  The model's effectiveness has been validated through numerical and visual analyses, demonstrating improved image quality and robustness against varying noise rates.  Furthermore, it has been successfully applied to 320-slice scanners to produce high-quality, low-dose images.  In particular, it significantly enhances noise resistance and image quality at ultra-low doses equivalent to 0.15 mGy.  Compared to other state-of-the-art methods, it produces superior image quality with increased iteration stability. Previous research into Bayesian Program Learning revealed that the framework could generate realistic handwriting samples with just a few training examples. Yet, the generated handwriting often contained structural errors, such as incorrect stroke sequences and orientations. To address these issues, a new model called Grammatic Program Learning (GPL) has been developed. GPL introduces a novel explanation for BPL that uses context-free grammars to define the sequence and connection patterns of drawing actions. Contextual factors in the environment, such as the location of previous strokes, now determine which production rules in the grammar should be used. Through the application of Monte Carlo Bayesian inference, the model learns the most suitable production rules from a given dataset. Our tests using the UNIPEN dataset confirm that the new model significantly outperforms BPL in producing realistic and structurally correct drawings. Moreover, the generated samples exhibited a high level of similarity to samples from the same class. Our findings demonstrate that GPL presents a viable solution for applying BPL in a more practical manner. We suggest a storage system to expedite the computation of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements. It comprises a hierarchical database that groups potential matrix elements by characteristics derived from the momentum space geometry. Such characteristics include the three-body Jacobi momenta, intrinsic orbits, and the direction of the relative momentum between the non-active nucleon. This scheme reduces memory needs by a factor of 10 and 100 for all-to-all and local interaction schemes, respectively, and makes it feasible to store the magnitudes of these interactions directly within computational codes. We evaluate the effectiveness of this storage system in generating non-vanishing three-nucleon interactions, and examine its implications on the phase shift distribution and the breakdown of the 'chain of bundling' approximation in the non-relativistic nuclear force environment. Moreover, we outline pathways for applying this storage system to extended models that incorporate isospin and momentum space deformations. Finally, we consider its applicability to extensions involving relativistic and mean-field theories. We visualize a potential future adaptation of this storage system for beyond mean-field models, and outline its potential for a common utilization across various nuclear force realizations. Additionally, the source code for the storage system and related utilities is made accessible through the open-source GitHub repository 'nmst-utils'. In this paper, the authors present a novel memory allocation framework, DynaSOAr, designed to address the shortcomings of traditional allocators. By combining static and dynamic allocation methods, adapting to application memory patterns, and optimizing so-called "best-effort" memory requests, DynaSOAr significantly outperforms state-of-the-art allocators, offering two to 14 times faster memory allocation, 35% to 80% reduced overhead, and 100% reliability. The authors' experimental results show that DynaSOAr's static allocation phase can automatically determine the required memory block count for most applications in a few milliseconds. This study tackles two challenges. Firstly, we develop a metric to measure the robustness of decision functions in scenarios with uncertain environmental parameters. This metric guides the choice of decision functions that can withstand parameter fluctuation by minimizing potential losses. Next, we apply the developed framework to the problem of predicting stock prices, which involves uncertain parameters. We use the daily price movements of Apple, Amazon, and Google from 2015 to 2019 as our case study. By leveraging the robust optimization framework, we identify the most resilient models for forecasting price movements and compare their performance with a benchmark model that assumes perfect knowledge of parameter values. The results indicate that more robust models can achieve better average returns on investment compared to the benchmark model. Specifically, models chosen using a robustness measure that protects against up to 30% of possible parameter values yield a 10% to 15% higher return on investment than models chosen using the maximum expected return criterion that assumes perfect knowledge of parameter values. Moreover, these robust models often provide more accurate forecasts than models chosen using the maximum expected return criterion, especially in scenarios that are 30% or more different from the assumed parameter values, where their forecasts are on average 12% to 18% more accurate than those of models chosen using the maximum expected return criterion. In particular, our robust models exhibit an average return on investment that is 16% to 20% higher than models chosen solely to maximize expected return. The study's findings demonstrate the value of using the proposed robustness metric in guiding the selection of decision functions, which can result in better performance even in scenarios that are not as uncertain as those initially considered. By adjusting the threshold for robustness, decision-makers can balance the level of uncertainty protection against the potential performance sacrifice and choose an appropriate model. Ultimately, the proposed framework provides an actionable method for managing uncertainty in decision functions that can be applied broadly across various domains. Furthermore, we examine the influence of different communication strategies, asynchronous updating methods, and buffer sizes on the convergence rate, and investigate the benefits of using an asynchronous gradient method in parallel environments. We conclude that the asynchronous algorithm can achieve a comparable level of convergence to its synchronous counterpart, and can even outperform it in certain situations. Additionally, the study highlights that the choice of asynchronous updating method and buffer size has a substantial impact on the convergence rate, and points to the 'double buffer' strategy as a promising option for achieving optimal results. Employing an ensemble of size k involves running k separate forward passes in the network, yet there's a possibility that multiple models being evaluated could share some computed features, making the process less efficient. To optimize the ensemble process and minimize redundant computations, we propose a novel method, Feature-Elimination Vote (FEV), which reduces the efficiency gap by identifying and eliminating unnecessary features from being computed across models. By leveraging the characteristics of FEV, we also introduce two enhanced ensemble strategies, FEV with Model Pruning (FME) and FEV with Model Selection (FSE), to achieve the same goal. By comparing these methods with Weighted Vote and Error, our experiments demonstrate that FEV, FME, and FSE consistently outperform them in both runtime and accuracy. Moreover, our analysis reveals that FEV and its variants are particularly beneficial when dealing with larger-scale image classification tasks. To facilitate the use of these methods, we have also introduced an open-source tool called EvalEnsemble, which enables the evaluation and comparison of ensemble classifiers. Quantifying the uncertainty of predictions is a pressing issue in deep learning, as current techniques lack formal justification and rely on inaccurate statistical assumptions. We address this challenge by developing a novel approach that uses the variational inference framework to represent the uncertainty of predictions as the posterior distribution of the model given the observed data. Notably, this method can be generalized and applied to complex models that are difficult to theoretically analyze. We justify our approach through the lens of Bayesian statistics and establish a variational Bayes representation of the uncertainty, which is then approximated using the Stochastic Gradient Episodic Memory (SGEM) algorithm. We evaluate the proposed method on a range of benchmark datasets and compare its performance to established metrics, such as the Expected Calibration Error, Predictive Variance, and Relaxed F-score, as well as a new metric we developed, the Intervaled F-score. The results show that our method outperforms the traditional Monte Carlo dropout approach and yields more accurate calibrations and predictive measures when combined with the Intervaled F-score. Furthermore, the proposed method provides insights into the posterior uncertainty of model parameters and can inform hyperparameter tuning. The code for the proposed method is freely available on GitHub at the specified link. Additionally, the predicted uncertainties for the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets can be accessed through the deepblue repository. Feedback and suggestions from the deep learning community are welcome and encouraged. Further research applications of the proposed method are presented in the accompanying document. Based on these findings, we conclude that the proposed method is a viable solution for quantifying the uncertainty of predictions in deep learning. The technical details of the proposed method are presented in the stocasticity section of the document. The proposed method can be applied to various machine learning algorithms by substituting the computational graph of the model and the observed data into the variational inference framework. The variational Bayes representation of the uncertainty is represented by the following mathematical expression: $\mathcal{P}(\theta|\mathcal{D}) \proportional to \mathcal{L}(\theta) \mathcal{P}(\theta)$, where $\theta$ represents the model parameters, $\mathcal{D}$ represents the observed data, and $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ represents the likelihood function. However, the phenomenon of PPT squares - states expressing positivity through classical data - appears to disappear in infinite dimensions. Notably, research has identified a distinct category of operators associated with PPT squares in tensor product systems, which share certain operational characteristics. The key contribution of this paper lies in establishing a one-to-one correspondence between positive operator-valued measures (POVMs) and PPT squares in tensor product systems, thereby expanding the understanding of PPT squares in such systems. The study further explores their application to consistency assessment of quantum channels in the context of PPT-preserving transformations. It is observed that while local PPT squares enable consistent one-qubit measurements, this is generally precluded for PPT squares of broader scope, with the notable exception of special cases. The investigation also examines the properties of entanglement-assisted protocols for PPT squares and local PPT squares, drawing connections with optimal transport and related problems. The study concludes with an analysis of PPT squares arising from Seidler's example in the context of simplex-embeddings. The research offers a series of open questions and outlooks for future investigations. The companion material includes additional mathematical contributions. Within the cell body, materials are transported through the process of receptor-mediated endocytosis and, subsequently, dissolved or consolidated into transport vesicles that travel along microtubules, eventually undergoing exocytosis at distal locations. A key aspect of this process involves the energy generated by ATP hydrolysis facilitated by motor proteins in the microtubules' dynamic structures. Banks incur significant losses due to fraud, which can be attributed to unauthorized transactions on customer accounts. To prevent this, banks need to monitor account transactions in real-time and block invalid transactions. The validation process involves verifying the transactions against the banks' rules and regulations to ensure compliance. Currently, this process relies on predefined rules based on experts' experience, but this approach has its limitations as the rules do not cover unknown future threats. Furthermore, manually expanding the rules to account for new accounts is impractical as it requires constant updating. To alleviate these issues, a novel machine learning technique called Generative Validation Graphs (GVG) is introduced. GVG utilizes a generative model to create valid transaction patterns, which are then used to classify suspicious transactions as invalid. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, with an accuracy rate of 92% for unseen data, along with accurate prediction and detection rates. Additionally, the integration of GVG into a banking system enables real-time invalid transaction classification, enabling the automatic refinement of rules as the model is updated. The technique also facilitates the creation of realistic invalid transactions for testing and training, utilizing the estimated posterior distribution as a reference. Furthermore, the methodology includes an invalid transaction generation method called Discriminative Invalid Graph Generation (DIGG), which enables the construction of valid graphs for comparison purposes. By analyzing the conditional probability of a category given the observed data under this model, a Bregman divergence metric can be derived. By examining the metric's properties, we find that its extreme points correspond to categories capable of providing unique categorization. We also show that metrics derived from this model are essentially non-confusable. We have implemented a method in R that enables the computation of Tversky distances for any multinomial data. This algorithm allows the optimization of Tversky t-treewidth metrics using an efficient graph-theoretic approach. We have applied the metric in two contexts: assessing the uniqueness of category labels, and identifying non-confusable categories for data such as human responses and automated output data. For example, when analyzing responses from the Lexical Subtype Identification system, we successfully identified distinctive labels and the minimal set of labels for each type with high confidence. Similarly, when examining human judgments, we successfully identified distinctive labels and the minimal set of labels for each type with high confidence. A widely recognized issue in vision research, image deblurring is crucial for mitigating the effects of blurred images. Recent advancements have focused on incorporating attention mechanisms to improve deblurring performance, yet most studies overlook the connection between deblurring and image segmentation, although they share attention-based characteristics. This study proposes an innovative deblurring framework that incorporates a reblurring module to enhance the attention mechanism's guidance for more effective image restoration. Furthermore, we develop a new UNET-like architecture with attentional features within the encoder and a reblurring module within the decoder to facilitate seamless end-to-end training. Experimental results confirm that our proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of visual evaluation and objective metrics. Additionally, we provide ablation studies and comparative analyses to validate the reblurring module's contribution to the overall deblurring effectiveness. Recent research has demonstrated the capacity of chemical reaction networks to represent complex, evolving systems, influencing discussions on autonomic learning and intelligence in biology. Inspired by these discoveries, a new field of study, known as biochemical cognition, is emerging, which seeks to investigate how CRNs can be used to model cognitive processes, similar to those found in neurons. To facilitate this line of research, a computer program, called BioCHIMIC, has been created, which enables researchers to simulate CRNs with complex dynamics, assisting in evaluating hypotheses and identifying patterns, such as oscillations and incremental changes, associated with cognitive processes. By utilizing BioCHIMIC, researchers can explore the properties of these networks and observe meaningful behaviors, which can inform their design, shedding light on the underlying biological mechanisms, which can be applied to advancements in artificial neural networks. For example, a study using BioCHIMIC simulated a network capable of learning binary numbers through an incremental learning process, which showed promising results, demonstrating the potential of this tool in exploring the intersection of biology and artificial intelligence. By combining theoretical and practical approaches, this program caters to researchers from various fields, such as systems biology, computer science, and electronics, enabling them to explore the practical applications of biochemical cognition, where the boundaries between biology and artificial intelligence become blurred. We investigate how these graphs can be fully destroyed by removing t-copies and derive specific code rate results under various minor destruction scenarios, even considering the worst-case analysis. To support our findings, we offer several best-known examples of minimal linear codes with specific parameters. Furthermore, in the graph context, we establish conditions and relationships, particularly examining how t-copies affect the existence of complete graph minors $K_t$ and rooted branch sets in a given graph, which is of particular interest in the graph coloring problem. These findings contribute valuable insights to both coding theory and graph theory. We present an intuitive destruction method grounded in graph coloring, which yields an almost immediate correlation between the applied code linear error correction capacity and the graph's coloring number. We also explore multiple destruction methods based on graph invariants such as treewidth, fractional isomorphism, and the Szemer\'edi--Koml\'os theorem, providing novel applications and tight bounds in both coding and graph contexts. These new destruction methods grounded in treewidth and the Szemer\'edi--Koml\'os theorem yield particularly significant results, especially for t-copies where t is not too large. Notably, in the non-critical t-circuit scenario, we discovered that destroying t-circuits using t-copies may not be feasible, which prompts the exploration of associated graph invariants, including the branch number and the minimal linear doubly cyclic matrix over a Galois field. This research focuses on an adaptive algorithm employed in online linear optimization tasks.  Key insights into its behavior can be obtained by examining the cost function's properties.  If the cost function is convex, the algorithm achieves near-optimal results.  In contrast, if the cost function is concave, the algorithm attains a performance rate of $O(\sqrt{Mt})$, where $M$ and $t$ represent bounds on the duality gap and time, respectively.  A pivotal question remains whether any adaptive algorithm can guarantee a better or similar performance rate than $O(\sqrt{Mt}/\Delta)$ for general online linear optimization tasks, where $\Delta$ represents a bound on suboptimality.  Our findings refute the conjecture that $\Omega(\sqrt{Mt}/\Delta)$ is an inherent lower bound for any adaptive algorithm.  We prove that by applying a non-decreasing adaptation strategy, the algorithm can guarantee a performance rate of $O(\sqrt{Mt}/\Delta^2)$.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that this new guarantee can be improved under specific cost function properties to achieve a performance rate of $O(M\log t/\Delta^2)$ when the cost function is quasi-convex and $O(M\sqrt{t}/\Delta^2)$ when the cost function is concave.  We stress that our findings provide performance guarantees that are independent of the unknown model parameters, a key advantage over traditional convex optimization techniques.  Finally, we perform experimental evaluations to verify our theoretical findings and showcase the algorithm's robustness against adversarial perturbations.  Our code is available at https://github.com/ashishgupta93/adaptive-algorithms.  Our approach is novel and can be generalized to various adaptive algorithms, broadening its applicability and efficacy.  Our analysis is rigorous and the algorithms are computationally lightweight, a key consideration for numerous real-world applications.  Our analysis is the first to address adversarial perturbations in online linear optimization tasks.  Our findings are the first to establish the algorithmic performance guarantees of adaptive algorithms.  Our experimental evaluations are the first to demonstrate the efficacy of adaptive algorithms in multi-round online linear optimization tasks.  Our study is the first to generalize the quasi-convex cost function property to multi-round online optimization tasks.  Our study is the first to establish the algorithmic performance guarantees of adaptive algorithms in multi-round online optimization tasks.
