Deep Learning, specifically particular network architectures, can be reinterpreted in a new context through the application of message passing on graph structures. This is achieved by analyzing existing CNNs and fully connected neural networks in the framework of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). A general framework is introduced that allows any neural network to be reinterpreted on graph structures. This framework demonstrates that interpreting neural networks on graphs provides valuable insights into how information is passed between nodes. By applying this framework, GCN mechanisms can be identified within CNNs, illustrating the similarity to localized convolutions in the graph domain. Conversely, fully connected networks correspond to fully connected graph structures. Furthermore, by analyzing neural networks within the graph domain, it becomes evident that neural networks utilize message passing to extract meaningful features from the input data. This understanding enables the design of neural networks tailored to the graph representation of the data, resulting in improved representation of the data for further processing. This is demonstrated through the application to chemical compound recognition. Additionally, any neural network can be expressed as a GCN on a specific graph structure, providing insight into its functionality. This is exemplified using the ResNet architecture. Lastly, GCNs can be expressed as neural networks on specific graph structures, illustrating the duality and equivalence of the two. This is demonstrated using the Bipolar Bipolar Graph, resulting from the application of the framework to a fully connected network. To alleviate the limitations of self-training in enhancing parsing performance, we have developed a novel approach called Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST). This method tackles the issues of weak labels and data contamination by incorporating context-aware neighbor aggregation in sentence classification. DCST also takes a hierarchical approach, contextually aggregating tokens within sentences. Through iterations of self-training, DCST refines its models, ultimately leading to superior results. Our research specifically using DCST on the North American Treebank demonstrates its effectiveness, achieving an 8.1% improvement in parsing accuracy using just 50% of the original dataset with enhanced supervision. Furthermore, DCST outperforms other techniques in unsupervised and semi-supervised parsing tasks. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenChaoForum/DCST. DCST has been added to the CoNLL shared task website https://conll-st.org/. Additionally, our baseline models' hyperparameters and results can be found on the CoNLL website at https://conll-st.org/2021/task4/index.html.

We establish that linear systems of equations over a finite field are constructively representable in the context of PVP, and this representation is even CPT-definable when considering systems of equations where the coefficients are distinctly valued. In contrast, we find that this representation is not complete for the PVP class when the coefficients can be equally valued. Building on this finding, we prove that the existence of solutions for systems of equations is CPT-definable under specific conditions but not generally so when the coefficients can be equally valued. In a separate set of results, we show that the problem of determining whether a system of equations has solutions over every possible finite field is CPT-definable. Additionally, we find that this problem is not CPT-definable when considering all possible fields, but it becomes so when the coefficients are distinctly valued. In the process of achieving these findings, we establish an alternative formulation for CPT-definability using a specific type of elementary formula and prove that the isomorphism problem for algebraic closures of finite fields under distinct coefficient values is CPT-definable. An n-tuple is considered nontransitive if, in a matrix where the main diagonal consists of n distinct numbers, the relative differences between adjacent elements lead to inconsistent order comparisons. The largest possible value in these differences is denoted as d(n). If d(n) exists and is finite, the question arises as to whether d(n) can be expressed through the sum of an integer k and a positive rational number r. This problem has been resolved for the case of n = 6, revealing that d(6) can be represented in the form of k + r, where k equals 4 and r equals 1/42. To address this issue for general n values, a theoretical framework is introduced and utilized to determine d(n) for n = 7, 8, 9, 10. Additionally, it is demonstrated that for large n values, which exceed 449, d(n) is greater than or equal to the value of (n-2)/2. Furthermore, it is shown that if d(n) matches the lower bound of (n-2)/2, then n must adhere to a specific pattern, consisting of 2 at the end, followed by an alternating sequence of 3s and 4s, starting from the beginning. Next, in the context of infinite sequences of numbers, conditions are established under which two consecutive terms of the sequence can be regarded as interchangeable, leading to the concept of _twin transitivity_. It is revealed that not all nontransitive tuples have twin transitive counterparts, and under what conditions they would have such a twin. Finally, in an unrelated area of study, the concept of'smooth' and'sharp' transitions is introduced to analyze the behavior of the n-tuple's difference distribution as n gradually increases. Additionally, it is shown that for large n values, which exceed 449, the'sharp' transition occurs at n = 6, and then the difference distribution continuously evolves from n = 5 to n = 6. The proliferation of software systems worldwide has led to a major issue: many of them are burdened by the overhead of executing unnecessary features. This excess can result in prolonged startup times, increased memory usage, and a higher risk of security breaches. This research investigates a novel approach centered around the concept of "compactness," aiming to reduce the attack surface and improve the system's efficiency by stripping away nonessential capabilities. A cutting-edge technique is developed to accurately identify and eliminate the options that are never enabled or used throughout the system's lifecycle. Our study employs a cutting-edge metric to gauge the compactness of systems, utilizing this metric to gauge the compactness of 302 applications across seven open-source repositories. The findings reveal that the average factor of reduction for (1) startup time, (2) memory usage, (3) lines of code, and (4) dependencies is 1.45, indicating a substantial compactness advantage. Additionally, removing nonessential capabilities appears to have a positive effect on the system's startup time, memory usage, and complexity in many instances. However, this comes with a risk of introducing instability in some cases. Based on the compactness levels, the research distinguishes between three distinct categories of software: extremely compact (top 10%), somewhat compact (middle 40%), and compact-malicious (lower 50%). Interestingly, every single extremely compact system utilizes the Java programming language and all belong to the Apache software family. Conversely, the lower compact-malicious group comprises software from various programming languages, primarily consisting of systems that score somewhat compact in the compactness metric. The research uncovers that the compact-malicious group notably stands out in terms of the following: (1) higher likelihood of security breaches (10%), (2) increased memory consumption (1.23 GB), (3) larger codebase (3.2 million LOCC), (4) greater number of features (143), (5) higher lines of code per developer, and (6) longer compilation times. The analysis indicates that compactness has an inverse relationship with the system's size, complexity, and memory consumption. Importantly, removing nonessential capabilities does not always ensure improved performance, especially when stability is compromised. The findings suggest that compactness offers valuable insights into system efficiency but should be coupled with stability metrics for a more comprehensive understanding. In light of the presented results, the concept of compactness emerges as a useful metric to gauge system efficiency, detect vulnerabilities, and guide development decisions. ECG signal analysis carries significant importance in medical diagnostics for heart condition monitoring and prediction. In this research, a denoising approach for improving deep learning-based ECG signal analysis in deep bed noise is proposed. The approach utilizes a patch-based method to compare ECG time series with a denoised version, aiming to identify and analyze periodic patterns. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through comparative studies on a well-known public dataset, involving a comparison with established state-of-the-art techniques. The results show that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art performance in deep bed noise conditions, with a significant improvement of 15.6% and 12.5% respectively, over the current best techniques for signal classification and inter-beat interval estimation. The application of active force systems in various experiments has been widely embraced, and it is often characterized by oscillations resembling those of simple harmonic motion. However, fundamental questions remain about whether active force systems inherently exhibit harmonic behavior or if more complex anharmonic forces can produce similar results. In our study, we investigate fluctuations in both harmonic and anharmonic force systems and find a distinct variation in their behavior. Specifically, we identify a divergent fluctuation trend in anharmonic systems, producing irreversible work and distinct oscillation characteristics. These findings suggest that anharmonic forces play a crucial role in active force experiments and may offer novel opportunities for optimizing swarm behavior. Moreover, our research lays the groundwork for developing more efficient and dynamic optimization methods in swarm robotics. This occurs because the fluid dynamics of the falling snowflakes are influenced by their mass, whereas in general, lighter objects in fluid dynamics are affected by gravity and drag. When considering the mass of the snowflakes, their settling velocity increases linearly, exceeding expectations based on drag alone. As a result, there is a critical mass above which larger and lighter snowflakes are unable to take advantage of this effect, enabling a range of snowflake sizes to settle at a speed close to the terminal velocity. Deep learning techniques have enabled the creation of detailed, realistic datasets and data mixes using probabilistic generative models. However, these models fall short in addressing the underlying structure of a dataset, particularly one composed of diverse, real-world domains with varying resolution levels. To address this limitation, we introduce the Conceptual Generative Disentangled Synthesizer (CGS), a new deep generative model capable of producing high-resolution syntheses in multiple domains while identifying underlying conceptual factors. By disentangling both domain and category-specific factors from the input data, our model is able to produce sharp, realistic samples in each domain, and, upon manipulation of these factors, our model can efficiently generate novel, unseen data mixes and domain-specific samples. Moreover, we show that our model is effective in learning category-specific factors from domain-invariant data, and, upon removal of domain-specific factors, our model is able to transfer learning to a target domain with minimal data. Our model is evaluated on the challenging task of generating face images in the wild. Our research introduces the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), an innovative approach for data compression and restoration. By maintaining the integrity of input data through dual encoding and decoding processes, BCAE enables the detection of manipulations via internal consistency analysis. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of BCAE in identifying artificial manipulations within images and videos, surpassing the performance of conventional data compression methods. Additionally, BCAE facilitates the extraction of reliable features for various machine learning applications. Furthermore, the BCAE's unique design facilitates the creation of synthetic data for training models, a valuable resource in machine learning. In particular, we utilize BCAE to develop a novel method for generating synthetic images using the FID metric as the optimization target. This generated data is found to be effective in model training, as evidenced by our experiments. The proposed BCAE, associated code, and supporting materials are available at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/BCAE. In terms of efficacy, the BCAE's embedded data compression capability compares favorably to state-of-the-art methods, including the Joint Image Compression autoencoder (JICE), and Mechem's compressed expanded JICE (MEJICE). More specifically, the BCAE outperforms JICE and MEJICE by 9% and 11%, respectively, in terms of accuracy in manipulating synthetic data. In terms of compression ratio, the BCAE surpasses MEJICE by 14%, while matching the performance of JICE. The 2DFID benchmark has been established to evaluate the effectiveness of data compression methods in detecting artificial manipulations. In accordance with this benchmark, the BCAE outperforms established methods like Proton, Proton+ (proton+), and the EfficientNet-based proton+ by 26%, 16%, and 14%, respectively. Moreover, the BCAE exceeds the efficacy of Proton and proton+ by 16% and 6%, respectively, in terms of compression ratio. In addition, the BCAE outperforms other data compression methods, such as the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and the Hybrid Image and Text AutoEncoder (HITEA), and the EfficientNet-based proton+ by 44%, 10%, and 14%, respectively, in terms of compression accuracy. In terms of compression ratio, the BCAE surpasses proton+ and EfficientNet by 16% and 14%, respectively, while matching the performance of CNN and exceeding HITEA

Immunotherapies for colon cancer have shown promising results when treated
with checkpoint inhibitors, but response rates are typically low and lasting
remissions are rare. To enhance anti-tumor effects, a combination of Doxorubicin
and IL-2 has been used, primarily to stimulate an immune response. However, the
tumors' ability to stop this response and establish resistance is a significant obstacle.

To overcome this limitation, investigating the specific mechanisms colon cancer
uses to thwart immunotherapies is essential. By targeting these mechanisms, we can
develop novel strategies to overcome treatment resistance. To identify key targets,
we analyzed the gene expression profiles of colon cancer cells treated with Dox,
IL-2, and Dox+IL-2, as well as their transcription factor profiles.

Our results show that Dox+IL-2 treatment significantly alters gene expression
and triggers a dramatic change in the cell's chromatin landscape. Notably, the
combination induces wide-spread removal of nucleosomes across the genome.
Although Dox+IL-2 treatment leads to increased expression of immune-related
genes, the combination's effects on the broader transcriptome are dominated by
temporary and directed changes in gene expression related to cell cycle and
apoptosis.

Unexpectedly, the analysis reveals that Dox+IL-2 treatment promotes enrichment
of nucleosomes in gene bodies and broad-scale elimination of nucleosomes in
intergenic regions, accompanied by increased H3K4me1 enrichment and bivalent
domain formation. Our findings indicate that Dox+IL-2 treatment induces a
distinctive nucleosome reorganization, promoting linear chromatin and altering
long-range chromatin interactions.

To investigate the effect of Dox+IL-2 treatment on nucleosome reorganization at
the single-cell level, we developed a multi-color imaging approach that
revels the reorganization's significant variability across cells. Our results show
that Dox+IL-2 induced nucleosome reorganization is characterized by extensive
interactions between distinct chromatin regions, promoting a more open and
dynamic chromatin state.

Our study provides the first evidence of the reorganization of nucleosomes in
colon cancer cells treated with Dox+IL-2, shedding light on the complex
interactions between chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Moreover, the analysis at
the single-cell level uncovers the reorganization's variability, paving the way
for the development of novel strategies to target colon cancer's ability to resist

In this research, we focus on the end-to-end communication network consisting of a single transmitting device and multiple receiving devices. We aim to determine the optimal transmission strategy across all devices to maintain the lowest possible age of information (AoI). Unlike traditional network simplicity assumptions, here we consider individual AoI and enable device grouping. We are interested in finding the optimal transmission schedule for a discrete, asynchronous, time-varying network. To resolve this problem, we developed an algorithm that identifies the optimal transmission strategy for any given network configuration. We also demonstrated that allowing device grouping enhances AoI performance compared to grouping all devices together. In addition, allowing individual device scheduling yields superior performance but comes at the cost of increased computational complexity. We used our algorithm to evaluate the optimal transmission strategy in two network configurations: a random geometric network and a square layout with uniform node distribution. For the latter, we proved the problem's hardness as an NP-hard instance and proposed a sub-optimal heuristic algorithm. Through our analysis, we identified key parameters that significantly affect the optimal AoI performance in both network configurations. We also showed that the average AoI performance can be achieved with a subset of the network configurations. Our comparison between the random geometric and uniform square layouts revealed the inferior AoI performance in the former and the superior AoI performance in the latter. Furthermore, we observed the existence of a trade-off between throughput maximization and AoI minimization. To facilitate practical algorithm application, we also analyzed the optimal transmission strategy for specific network configurations with limited device numbers. Our results indicate the ease of computing optimal strategies in two extreme scenarios: all devices either have infinite or zero transmission rates. Additionally, for a random geometric network with a large number of devices, we identified a suitable approximation algorithm that yields a sub-optimal throughput with an achieved age of information. Our comprehensive study sheds light on the complexity of end-to-end network optimization for age of information and throughputs. It also highlights the benefits and drawbacks of individual scheduling, group averaging, and grouping strategies. To the best of our knowledge, this research is the first to address throughputs in tandem with age of information in wireless networks. Our findings in this area can inspire future investigations. Our algorithmic findings can be applied in numerous practical scenarios, and our theoretical analysis can influence the design of real-world wireless networks. Our results can guide the development of practical transmission strategies that minimize age of information while maximizing throughputs in wireless networks with complex topologies. This research focuses on demonstrating helicity conservation for weak solutions in specific function spaces and obtaining an $L^2 \to L^{\infty}$-estimated annealed approximation of the Euler equations, analogous to the approach taken by Cote, Masmoudi, and Roudnev in their work on the Navier-Stokes equations. We also explore a new approximation method for the Euler equations, which yields a solution with significant regularity. This solution can be extended in time and is stable with respect to perturbations. Notably, this approach diverges from other known methods, such as those discussed in Chorin's article on the initial boundary value problem of the Euler equations. Furthermore, this new method can be adapted to obtain conservation of helicity in specific function spaces and to establish $L^2 \to L^{\infty}$-estimated weak solutions of the Euler equations. Additionally, we use a approach similar to that of Brezis and Van Neumann to establish the existence of a weak solution of the exterior problem of the Euler equations. Finally, this new method can also be adapted to establish the existence of a weak solution of the exterior problem of the Euler equations with non-zero rotation. Identifying changes or events in evolving networks, or dynamic graphs, is crucial in many areas but remains challenging due to the non-fixity of network nodes. To address this issue, we introduce a new method called DyGED, a BERT-based approach that models complex network changes and event correlations. By effectively leveraging the BERT architecture to capture the dynamics of network changes and incorporating a Bilinear Attention Layer to capture event relations, DyGED achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple test datasets. Moreover, our approach is suitable for real-world applications as it can handle large-scale networks, providing a scalable solution. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ju-stu/DyGED. Experimental results demonstrate that DyGED outperforms existing methods, including GED and DeepGED, as well as BERT-based approaches without attention mechanisms. Notably, DyGED excels at event prediction, improving upon GED and DeepGED by 4.25% and 3.13%, respectively. Furthermore, its event-relation modeling enhances the accuracy of event classification, surpassing GED and DeepGED by 4.17% and 3.04%, respectively. Our analysis suggests that DyGED's success stems from its capacity to long-range attention and its ability to capture the semantics of network changes, including event-induced structure changes. Consequently, DyGED offers a more robust and effective approach to understanding complex network changes and event correlations. To facilitate research, we make our test datasets available online at https://github.com/ju-stu/DyGED. In terms of scalability, DyGED requires relatively minimal computational resources, with its ability to handle large-scale networks, including networks with 2000 nodes and 5000 edges (similar to Twitter), and networks with 5000 nodes and 20000 edges (similar to StackOverflow). Therefore, DyGED presents a highly practical solution for real-world applications. The first project examined how the initial conditions of a point source in an infinite incompressible fluid affect the resulting shock wave patterns. The second project involved analyzing how these initial conditions influence shock wave convergence in a more complex geometry. The third project focused on using numerical simulations to generate maps of fluid flow parameters in a collapsing void in a long, thin cylinder. This project introduces MrSARP: a hierarchical deep-generative model with multiple levels of detail, used for synthesizing image details at different resolutions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MrSARP by generating synthetic images from the Street View house numbers dataset, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, MrSARP enables the generation of new views for existing images, allowing for exploration of the model's latent space and discovering novel street scene configurations. We provide supporting code and model weights on our website at: https://jerrynovack.github.io/MrSARP. MrSARP is built using TensorFlow and JAX, with a detailed explanation available in this GitHub repository: https://github.com/JerryNovack/MrSARP. We envision MrSARP as a platform for collaborative research, promoting the exploration of hierarchical deep-generative models through user-contributed new views, latent space explorations, and model re-definitions. We invite researchers and practitioners to join us in shaping the future direction of this project, as outlined in our proposed research agenda, also available on our website. Ultimately, our goal is to make MrSARP a beneficial resource for the synthetic view generation community.

This study investigates a population-level interpretation of actor-critic algorithms, specifically examining rewards-discounted expectations in the context of variational free energy. We demonstrate that these algorithms formulate a variational free energy minimization problem, establishing a connection to the Gibbs measure generated from the q-function. The study analyzes multiple algorithms - EM, persistent EM, and its population-level interpretation known as the natural policy gradient (NPG), as well as its biased variant (BTPO). While EM requires the efficient computation of the Gibbs measure's density function, real-world applications often employ Monte Carlo estimations due to the high computational expense. In an attempt to mitigate this, NPG and BTPO leverage multiple trajectory iterations to estimate the Gibbs measure's density function. However, the latter uses temperature exploration, a BTPO-specific modification, to stabilize its sampling method. The study reveals that BTPO can be viewed as a variant of persistent EM with temperature exploration, both at the individual and population-level interpretations. Furthermore, the theoretical framework developed in this study allows for analyzing the NPG and BTPO algorithms with on-policy trajectory sampling. In addition, the results show that BTPO is a consistent estimator of the Gibbs measure's density function, while NPG and BTPO are shown to be consistent estimators of the optimal policy when applied to MC settings with stationary distributions. This research focuses on the transmission resonance that occurs when piezoelectric materials are placed in close proximity to each other, specifically at normal incidence. By applying the Abromovich and Breitzer condition to non-uniformly thick surfaces, we demonstrate that complete transmission is possible in these materials, provided they meet a specific surface requirement. Our analysis shows that this requirement is fulfilled by materials with symmetric piezoelectric properties, regardless of their thickness. We further develop an analytical model to determine the resonant frequency of the transmitted wave, which is found to be equivalent to a quasi-Rayleigh surface wave propagating at the material interface. These findings are verified through numerical simulations. Additionally, we investigate the one-dimensional scattering configuration and reveal that the scattering response is unaffected by the scattering angle when the frequency matches the complete transmission frequency. Consequently, this "flat" point in the dispersion relationship can be exploited to image materials with low acoustic impedance using piezoelectric transducers, as confirmed by numerical estimations. Finally, we apply this principle to realize acoustic imaging of metal surfaces, which is otherwise challenging due to its high acoustic impedance. By adjusting the frequency to the complete transmission value, we can effectively "match" the impedance at the metal-air interface, enabling clear imaging of metal surfaces using a piezoelectric transducer. These findings have promising implications for acoustic non-destructive evaluation and metal surface analysis. Additionally, this concept may be extended to achieve "at-normal" total reflection with acoustic metamaterials, by designing a single-layer meta-structure with an equivalent acoustic characteristic impedance equal to that of water. This can be achieved through numerical optimization of the meta-structure's parameters, by applying the complete transmission condition as the objective function. Consequently, this concept can be applied to develop acoustic wedges with meta-structures for improved acoustic coupling and reflection control. These findings are verified numerically for a specific wedged metal sample. Furthermore, the complete transmission condition can be utilized to design acoustic meta-structures that facilitate total reflection at normal incidence, by optimizing the layer parameters to meet the complete transmission requirement as indicated by Abromovich and Breitzer. This total reflection can be utilized to create ultra-low Q-factor acoustic resonators with high energy loss, by surrounding a very thin acoustic meta-structure with water. We investigate a system of interacting polariton condensates, presented by two coupled microdisk cavities, separated by a thin gain layer and embedded in an electromagnetic field. The spatial modulation of the excitation beams' focus can control the inter-cavity coupling and establish non-equilibrium steady states. Utilizing numerical simulations based on the Master-Equation approach, we demonstrate the emergence of memory effects in the system's output spectra and introduce a model to characterize temporal conjugacy. Additionally, we identify conditions allowing the establishment of temporal conjugacy in systems with uneven beam convergence and discuss its application in setting up memory traps and revealing the system's past influences on its current behavior. Moreover, we establish a relationship between temporal conjugacy and the phenomenon of phase diffusion in the system. Lastly, we examine the consequences of modulating the beam convergence, leading to the creation of polariton systems capable of self-bioming and exhibiting distinct phase diffusion properties in both the system's past and present. The study paves the way for experimental investigations of these phenomena in micro-cavity-based polariton condensate systems. The presented concept of spatial modulation of the beam convergence may find additional applications in the management and manipulation of polariton condensates using complex optical schemes. For example, it could enable the creation of polariton lattices with adjustable connections between distant sites, or the construction of polariton circuits with adjustable gates and non-equilibrium memory. Furthermore, it could also be applied in the development of new techniques for analyzing polariton systems with unique properties and for investigating non-equilibrium phenomena in quantum systems.
